An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time of $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This estimation was achieved by studying $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decays in association with a prompt $J/\psi$ particle decay into $K^+K^-$, which was detected using the LHCb detector. By utilizing likelihood ratio tests, decay time distributions of signal and background samples were determined, and an estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ branching ratio was calculated as $(3.6\pm0.5\pm0.3)\times10^{-6}$. Additionally, an upper limit of $4.9\times10^{-6}$ was set for the $B^0_s\rightarrow \phi\phi$ branching ratio at 95% confidence level, and lower limits of 0.88ps and 0.87ps were established for the $B^0_s$ meson lifetimes in different decay modes.

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a distributed control problem for a stochastic evolution equation. To achieve this, we applied the finite element method to achieve a non-ambiguous solution, utilizing a gradient-based algorithm to solve the control problem, and we established the existence and uniqueness of the solution at each discretization step. When using a specific algorithm, we proved the existence of the solution at each iteration of the algorithm, and we established the convergence rate of 1/4 for the algorithm. To apply these results to a particular stochastic evolution equation, we showed that the solution exists and is unique for a given control problem, and we established the decay rates of the terms in the equation, which are necessary for the convergence rate analysis. To study the convergence rate of the algorithm, we analyzed a particular example where we showed that the solution of the control problem belongs to a given class, which is necessary for the convergence rate analysis, and we found the convergence rate of the algorithm to be one-third.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory allows for a precise assessment of their large-scale anisotropical patterns. Re-analyzing extensive groups of cosmic rays with energies exceeding 4 EeV, specifically those with zenith angles between 60 to 80 degrees and distances from the Galactic Center of up to 60 degrees, we have identified areas of significant and minimal cosmic-ray concentrations in the sky. Our study reveals that the most densely populated areas are concentrated in the Galactic Center direction and surrounding regions, whereas the least densely populated areas are located in the direction of the Large Magellanic Cloud and nearby regions. We also observed that the most sparsely populated areas are situated in the vicinity of the Sculptor Galaxy Group. Our findings are consistent with theoretical predictions suggesting that extremely energetic cosmic rays may originate from galaxies with black holes that reside at the center of galaxy clusters. We have estimated the height above which cosmic-ray densities are unaffected by the presence of the Galaxy, placing it between 3.2 to 4.0 kiloparsecs in distance from the Earth. Our analysis of energy spectra for the most and least densely populated areas revealed that their patterns are comparable, with energies in the range of 0.57 to 0.67 EeV. This paper proves that every graded quotient of a Zinbiel algebra has a solvable derivation hierarchy. Additionally, it demonstrates that a Lie algebra must be of characteristic 2 in order to have derivations that act trivially on all elementary symmetric polynomials. This implies that a Zinbiel algebra's annealing hierarchy is unaffected by its Lie algebra structure. Moreover, it can be shown that a Zinbiel algebra's annealing hierarchy is equivalent to its pre-Lie hierarchy, and this equivalence holds without the condition of being of characteristic 2.

Using ALICE, the acceptance of the V0 multiplicity and photon-triggered neutral pion pairs in the forward acceptance of the ALICE CPV0 detectors was measured in Pb-Pb collisions at an energy of 5.02 TeV. These measurements were carried out over a transverse momentum range of 0.6 to 4.0 GeV with assistance from the TPC and HMF detectors to ensure accuracy. The results were then compared to similar measurements in In-In collisions at an energy of 5.44 TeV. The findings were also used to determine the fluctuations in flow angle and magnitude in Pb-Pb collisions. The results showed that the ratio of flow fluctuations to initial conditions was relatively constant across a wide range of transverse momentum. Additionally, the results were compared to theoretical predictions based on the ALICE-L3 transport model and the iEBE-VISHNU v1 transport model, and were found to be in general agreement.

Maintaining accurate data is crucial for any information system, and having a method to handle inconsistencies is vital. Although the theory of a specific type of inconsistency, known as paradox, has been extensively explored, it's relatively rare in actual data sets. On the other hand, another common inconsistency, caused by missing values, can be quite pervasive. In this paper, we'll be examining the relationship between these two kinds of inconsistencies and will provide a three-step procedure to handle one type of paradox when there are data sets that contain both missing values and relationships between data columns. This process includes identifying the type of paradox, determining the appropriate course of action, and calculating the resulting data set. We'll also be testing and comparing our approach with existing methods using a variety of data sets.

This study introduces a novel stochastic process, the Poisson Autoregressive process of order p with time-varying parameters, designated as PADP. This model, which expands upon the fixed-parameter PAD (Poisson Autoregressive of order p with distributed shocks) model, allows for changes in parameter dynamics over time. We establish a rigorous mathematical framework for PAD by verifying the existence of moments of sufficient order and establishing that the tail distribution of the process remains alpha-stable, thus ensuring the existence and uniqueness of a stationary distribution. We also prove the convergence of a discrete-time PAD to a continuous-time PAD. To estimate the parameters of the PAD model, we utilize quasi-maximum likelihood estimation, which is based on a third-order weak consistency result for the ordinary generalized method of moments estimator.

Elevated object recognition in cluttered and partially occluded environments poses a significant challenge. To break free from this constraint, object recognition is often performed in controlled environments where objects are fully presented. However, in many real-world scenarios, objects are frequently seen in cluttered and partially occluded states, as observed in various applications such as robotics, self-driving technology, and medical imaging. In these settings, object recognition can be simplified by representing objects as partial point clouds, which can be efficiently processed using neural networks. Although significant progress has been made in the field, there's still a notable gap in overcoming the challenges posed by the limited amount of training data and the lack of robust object representations. In response to these difficulties, we introduce Neural Descriptor Fields, a cutting-edge object representation method that combines the strengths of grid networks and permutation-equivalent networks to accurately classify objects across various poses and orientations. In comparative trials conducted on four datasets, Neural Descriptor Fields consistently outperformed current state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating its superiority in object recognition tasks. In addition to its enhanced performance, Neural Descriptor Fields also offers a compact object representation that significantly reduces the training data required, a crucial advancement in the field.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, it has been confirmed that the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity fulfills the exact O(N) scaling behavior, thus demonstrating its universal characteristic for all O(N) universality classes that contain non-trivial critical behavior. It has also been determined that the exponent that governs the position of the singularity in the specific heat depth variable is exactly 1, thereby not exhibiting any dependence on the critical exponent $\Delta$ that defines the non-trivial critical behavior. The analysis of the symmetrizable O(2) model, which exhibits a first-order phase transition, was performed as a specific example, along with the prediction of the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity approaching zero as a boundary value as the system behaves non-trivially at its critical point.

In statistics and physics, when working with random energy landscapes and interacting spins, a key challenge is navigating non-convex energy surfaces. This package of results provides a framework for exploring these surfaces, specifically the application of the Sudakov-Fernique convex distance theorem to the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model, which was previously inaccessible due to the presence of a non-convex energy landscape. This achievement is made possible by a recent advancement in statistical physics, known as the post-AMP method, which enables the efficient computation of spin correlations near the free energy's minimizers in a wide range of models, including those with interacting spins. This post-AMP technique, originally developed by M. J. A. Husek, has been adapted for use in this context. As a direct consequence of these developments, it has been proven that the free energy of the SK model exhibits local curvature, a result that can be viewed as a variation of the original argument presented by T. M. Rudd and M. J. A. Husek. As an expansion of the earlier analysis in (Rudd and Husek, arXiv:2005.11313), the current study includes an enhanced estimation of the free energy's second-order derivatives, which have been found to be proportional to the square of the order parameter for temperatures below the critical point. As a result, this research has created a new foundation for predicting the behavior of the order parameter in the power-law regime characterizing

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving reliable and precise measurements of aerosols requires addressing several complexities. Primary challenges arise when converting counts of photons into units of optical depth and identifying suitable calibration factors. Another significant challenge is removing variability in source flux, which can take on different patterns and magnitudes, further complicating the process. Additionally, the method we're using to analyze the data, namely slope-inverse, has its own limitations and assumptions that need to be met in order to yield accurate and consistent results. Not to mention that the presence of scattering particles affects the phase curve in a non-linear manner, which can be remedied by employing a more complex model, but this introduces another calibration factor that requires precise determination. Furthermore, the influence of aerosol particles can be observed in both the phase curve and the spectral energy distribution of the star, which can be distinguished and removed through proper data analysis, but this too introduces another source of uncertainty, which can be quantified but needs to be taken into consideration. By addressing and overcoming these challenges and complexities, it's possible to extract valuable information from the data, which can be used to calculate the optical depth of the atmosphere with a high degree of precision, as demonstrated by our results using data from the Filter-Photometry from the STEREO mission, which yielded an average optical depth of 0.38, with a standard deviation of 0.01, over the course of a

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using only an RGB-D image has gained significant interest, with numerous approaches employing projection clustering and correspondence learning, and others using neural networks with vast training datasets, respectively. To circumvent the requirements for extensive training data and precise initial object descriptions, our method, DeepHMap++, leverages both strategies by combining projection clustering and correspondence learning. In the proposed pipeline, DoF pose estimates are generated from clustered features through correspondence learning, and a neural network refines these estimates using the input RGB-D image. The network is designed to process objects with complex geometries and variable resolutions, and is trained for a limited set of objects with only a single RGB-D image per training sample. Our system, DeepHMap++, demonstrates superior performance on the COX dataset, outperforming the current state-of-the-art by a significant margin, and is also applicable to estimating the pose of specific objects within a scene.

We present GGLasso, a Python library for solving a broad category of graphical models, specifically Ising models, which are defined by their energy function and evolved through time-based Markov process. This package offers a range of methods for estimating model parameters and selecting regularization strengths in both sparse and non-sparse contexts. The package's capabilities can be applied to various graphical models, including directed, undirected, semi-conditional, and time-varying graphs. We introduce the neighborhood change distribution (NCD) as a novel approach for modeling and estimating the dynamics of graphical models. The package is designed to work seamlessly with two popular machine learning platforms, scikit-learn and TensorFlow. GGLasso is an open-source Python package available for public use on GitHub.

Using Langevin dynamics, our proposed method quickly and efficiently explores a molecule's configurational space by applying a gentle random kick at each time step, making it ideal for large biomolecules with complex interactions. By analyzing a wide range of proteins with different sizes, we demonstrate that our approach achieves optimal results when a brief period of fast simulation is followed by a longer period of more precise configuration validation, outperforming existing methods by up to tenfold in terms of computational efficiency without compromising accuracy, according to metrics such as root mean square deviation and configurational entropy.

Our new method calculates a comprehensive eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks by simultaneously considering the degree of node importance in one specific layer. We used the Bradley-Munkres algorithm to match nodes across different layers and employed a new variable to represent a node's importance in one specific layer. We then calculated the centrality of a node in the combined network by solving a new system of equations. For two-layer networks, we established a relationship between our approach and existing methods, showing that our results align with previous findings. We validated our new framework and discovered that it can distinguish between two types of node connections: those that contribute to the overall centrality and those that influence the centrality within a specific layer but not the overall centrality. We also introduced an iterative algorithm to calculate the centrality of a large network and observed that our results conform to established principles, such as the distribution of random networks and the effects of adding new nodes to an existing network.

Recently, we generated a set of second-order differential equations, which include both the Einstein and Einstein-Dirac equations, using the variational approach in $R$-Minkowski spacetime. Here, we apply a change of variable to transform these equations into their differential form, obtaining the fundamental quantum mechanics equations including the Schr\"{o}dinger equation, Klein-Gordon equation, and Dirac equation.

When spheres enter water surface, they encounter significant resistance, creating areas of sealed water in the process, known as craters.  The speed at which this crater forms significant impact on the safety of various objects, including ships, vehicles, and aerial devices.  To better understand this phenomenon, researchers studied high-speed water entry of spheres, revealing that at extremely low speeds, a pocket of air remains trapped beneath the surface, while at very high speeds, this air is forced out of existence.  In the present study, researchers focused on an unexplored speed range, capturing the process in slow motion to analyze the behavior of air and water under these conditions.  Using these images, researchers developed a statistical model to calculate the height of the air pocket, or "crater height," based on the speed at which the sphere enters the water.  The results of this study can be applied to the design of ships, vehicles, and aerial devices to ensure their safety in the event of water landing.

In this study, we examine the impact of M-theory's higher-dimensional extended objects on the symmetry of a Minkowski 4-dimensional spacetime within the framework of effective field theories based on Type IIB superstring theory. We concentrate on the interplay between the Chern--Dermendyev S-duality in E8(8) gauge symmetry and the effects of the D3-brane and the Kalb--Ramperton field, and we show that while the D3-brane preserves the E8(8) symmetry, the Calabi-Yau's Kahler form breaks the S-duality symmetry. We also demonstrate that the generated four-dimensional effective actions exhibit both the instanton and monopole terms, and the effects of the Calabi-Yau's Kahler form can be represented by a generalized $\theta$-term, which is invariant under the combined transformation of the Kalb--Ramperton field and the axion field. We further analyze the impact of this operator on the Calabi-Yau's topology and identify it as the source of the non-perturbative symmetry-breaking that leads to the generation of the neutrino mass and matter arisal in four-dimensional spacetime.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits highly complex electronic interactions, with strong competition between them leading to distinct outcomes: in one scenario, tightly bonded electrons form strong bonds with minimal energy difference, while in another, they exhibit minimal interaction with each other, with a notable energy gap. These results explain the observed band structure, orbital weights, and energy gaps in this material, with implications for its magnetic properties and behavior under external electric fields.

Researchers studying quantum physics have long been interested in the behavior of small systems at equilibrium, especially when they're subject to various external influences, notably in semi-light and cold-atom research. The lack of substantial coupling between these systems and their surroundings allows for minimal interaction with their environment, resulting in minimal Bosonization effects. In contrast, excitons in solid-state systems exhibit significant interaction with their environment, leading to pronounced Bosonization effects and intricate many-body dynamics. A recent study on exciton systems, facilitated by advanced computational methods and accounting for both local and non-local interactions with the environment, reveals massive Rabi spreading and the presence of giant fluctuations when the number of excitons is substantial, even in the deep linear regime typically found in other systems with much weaker coupling. These findings are made possible by the unique properties of excitons, which can exhibit both dark and bright states, and could be experimentally verified through the study of fluctuation dynamics or various many-body phenomena exhibited in semiconductor microcavities.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D non-symmorphic wallpaper network lattice made up of carbon atoms, specifically a novel 2D nanocarbon structure, and we demonstrate the possibility of positioning a significant band gap's edge, including the desired Dirac point, within a tunable range between approximately 0.8 eV and 2.8 eV through chemical modification, utilizing an ab initio approach. We have identified two distinct variants of this lattice: one with a hexagonal symmetry that includes a Dirac Fermion pocket at the K-point, and another with an orthogonal arrangement that features a quadratic saddle point and a van Hove singularity, both of which can be isolated from other band edges or connected to other band edges at the gamma-point, with associated electronic and optical properties. We have further explored the potential for functionalizing this nanocarbon structure by chemically substituting some carbon atoms with heteroatoms, which allows us to control the band structure through adjustment of the on-site energy, and as such, this structure offers significant promise for applications in nanoelectronics, photonics, and chemistry.

In the context of quantum states and operations, coherence plays a crucial role in maintaining and manipulating quantum information. Quantum states of single photons serve as a vital component in generating coherent phases through the process of quantum-optical catalysis, facilitated by a beam splitter and a parameterizable unitary operation, U. Here, we investigate the possibility of the U operation being realized using a Mach-Zehnder interferometer. By examining various configurations of the interferometer, we can determine the conditions under which U leads to the formation of coherent phases in the form of single-photon catalyzed states, specifically cat, Trine, and Pentine states. Moreover, we investigate the effect of imperfections in the device, such as partial transmission and phase error, on the generation of these states. Additionally, we propose a method for generating the Trine and Pentine states, beginning with a coherent state and employing a sequence of beam splitters and the process of quantum-optical catalysis.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in analyzing complex geometries. This paper serves as an introduction for researchers outside the field to understand the formalism and its benefits, as well as a literature review for established experts in the field. It begins by explaining the Newman-Penrose formalism and its benefits, then reviews the application of the formalism to solve Einstein's field equations in complex geometries, specifically in the context of the G'0 G00 Weyl tensor decoupling problem. It also discusses the Weyl curvature conjecture and its relationship to bivector analysis, and concludes by examining the Weyl curvature index in bivector analysis, including its mathematical representation and a discussion on its implications for the Weyl conjecture.

To create a model that can predict polymer structures based on NMR spectra, we've developed a statistical approach using linear regression and integer programming. First, we use linear regression to estimate peak intensities from a initial guess of the polymer's carbon skeleton, and then use integer programming to refine the prediction by re-arranging the carbon atoms based on peak intensities, chemical shifts, and connectivity constraints derived from the NMR spectra. By iteratively applying linear regression and integer programming, we can recover the polymer's structure and chemical reactions used in its synthesis. We tested this method on actual NMR data and compared it to other existing techniques, demonstrating its superiority in recovering polymer structures and reaction information.

Recently, medical image analysis has relied heavily on advanced models with vast amounts of data, often with limited consideration for dense sampling restrictions and computational costs in clinical settings. This study postulates that, with suitable data preparation, dense sampling can be efficiently achieved for clinical use. A novel neural network architecture called the Dilated Dense Focus Unet (DDAUnet) was designed to validate this hypothesis, featuring unique dense transverse and longitudinal connections that enhance sampling efficiency without compromising performance. DDAUnet was applied to esophageal tumor segmentation from CT images, with preprocessing techniques developed to accelerate training and inference. The results showed that, with adequate data preparation, DDAUnet achieved comparable performance to rival models with increased sampling costs. Furthermore, using a subset of the training data as pseudocoloring significantly enhanced the performance of DDAUnet, with notable improvements in Dice scores and Inference Time. The findings of this study are relevant to various medical image analysis tasks and provide a framework for developing clinically suitable models at reduced data sampling costs.

Multilingual individuals use language mix to effectively convey information, incorporating rules and characteristics from multiple languages in a single text document. This code-mixed language presents a significant challenge for traditional NLP models and requires a more nuanced understanding that considers the intricate relationships between mixed languages. In a bid to promote innovative research and address real-world problems, the Code-Mixed NLP track at AFNLP 2021 features four cutting-edge tasks, including a code-switching generation challenge, a named entity recognition task for three language combinations, a part-of-speech tagging challenge for two language pairs, and a sentiment analysis task for five code-mixed languages. In this paper, we discuss the prevailing theories and empirical evidence related to code-mixed languages, analyze the tasks and datasets in the NLP challenges faced by multilingual communities, and discuss the implications for code-mixed NLP research.

The perception of neural network-generated image descriptions can be challenging to assess, even for human subjects. This paper investigates the process of gathering and analyzing ratings from humans who evaluated the image descriptions produced by a neural network. It also explores the connection between these ratings and the accuracy of the associated object classifications. Further research is conducted to compare the ratings and classification probabilities and is completed in the context of a specific benchmark for image description evaluation. It is hoped that the methods presented in this paper can serve as a starting point for developing and evaluating the neural network in question.

Tantalum oxide Ta$_2$O$_5$ is a significant material in both theoretical and applied contexts, with a versatile energy band structure and potential uses in electronics, optics, and catalysis. However, the lack of a well-defined lattice structure at room temperature makes it challenging to study and apply this material. To better comprehend the Ta$_2$O$_5$ lattice structure and energy band structure, we utilized the generalized gradient approximation in DFT to consider three possible structure configurations: monoclinic, orthorhombic, and rutile. By examining the total energy of these configurations, we found that the energy difference between the monoclinic and orthorhombic structures is less than 10 meV per formula unit, indicating that these structures are nearly degenerate. To resolve this degeneracy, we applied Monte Carlo simulations with random displacement of atoms in the monoclinic structure, which led to a transition to the orthorhombic structure at about 500 K. To facilitate experimental identification, we calculated the phonon dispersion curves for both the monoclinic and orthorhombic structures and suggested possible experimental pathways to determine the lattice structure based on Raman and infrared spectroscopy. To investigate the energy band structure and chemical reactivity of Ta$_2$O$_5$, we performed the GW method and calculated the binding energies of molecules adsorbed on the surface, which showed that the energy band structure and chemical reactivity are insensitive to the

The Big Shift in US geography during the COVID-19 pandemic, characterized by increased mobility within urban areas and decreased interaction between them, had a significant impact on the spread of misinformation among Reddit users. Our analysis of voting history and post contents on Reddit sites, specifically r/vaccines and r/Coronavirus, revealed that the rate of misinformation being voted highest among the top 10 posts also increased during this period. Notably, the rate of this type of activity was higher in urban areas with greater mobility, further supporting the significance of the Big Shift in spreading false information. Our research suggests that the acceleration of urban migration during the holiday season was another crucial factor contributing to this trend. By examining the statistics of Reddit users' locations and activity, as well as Reddit's algorithm for ranking posts, our study provides a unique perspective on the dissemination of misinformation in the context of the Big Shift, with potential implications for combating the spread of false information in a rapidly evolving social media environment.

In the context of teaching robots via demonstration, understanding the acoustic elements of instructions plays a significant role in enhancing learning efficiency and accuracy. By analyzing audio signals, researchers can gain insight into a student robot's performance, learning progress, and eventual skills acquired. This study delves into the specific acoustic features of speech associated with teaching robot manipulation tasks. A comprehensive examination was conducted to identify the distinctive acoustic patterns in three key regions of a demonstration: task introduction, learning process, and final execution. Utilizing these patterns, a decision-making process was implemented to determine the most effective way to provide feedback to the robot during learning. The research demonstrated that by incorporating features from the initial and middle regions of a demonstration, a 6.01% improvement in accuracy and a 10.2% improvement in time to achieve a desired level of proficiency could be achieved. The study's findings provide a tangible foundation for the incorporation of acoustic analysis in teaching robots and offers guidance on selecting relevant features and the decision-making process in question.

A novel method has been discovered to apply Euler-Arnold equations in a way that identifies intricate characteristics of conformal field theories at their boundary. Originally developed to describe the transportation of fluids and the translation of shapes, our work demonstrates the mathematical framework's ability to explore boundary conformal field theories through the use of a specific closure operator. By analyzing the properties of this operator, we can uncover in-depth information about the boundary's behavior in the context of the Weyl anomaly, and determine if a given boundary is conformally invariant or not. Additionally, our method can be applied to the study of the ultraviolet behavior of quantum field theories, specifically those that involve the removal of singularities from the energy-momentum tensor through the implementation of certain symplectic symmetries.

Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are expected to be highly reliable and perform well for a broad user base. Despite their widespread use, many automated testing methods exist for automated testing of these systems, specifically in regards to voice interactions. This paper presents an automated testing framework specifically designed to streamline testing of conversational agents in a heads-up display car environment, with features such as voice command processing, visual display verification, and validation of conversational flows. This testing framework can be configured to mimic various testing scenarios, including both simple and complex conversations. With its ability to execute tests across different environments and report on results, this paper demonstrates the capabilities of the testing framework through an example implementation of a conversational agent for a car dashboard.

Cross-domain recommendation has been a highly sought-after area of study, as it enables the sharing of valuable information and resources among different domains with little to no direct interactions. In multi-sparse-domain settings, recommendations are made across multiple domains with limited data, posing significant challenges in modeling and representation. Existing methods typically focus on either incorporating external information or leveraging the internal structure of the data but often overlook the inherent sparsity and heterogeneity of the domains. In this work, a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Cooperative Recommendation (MSDCR) is proposed to address these challenges by utilizing a dual-path strategy to combine item interactions and attribute-based preferences. Item interactions are modeled through the use of graph neural networks to capture the global patterns, while the attribute-based preferences are represented as weighted sums of attributes that capture the local characteristics. The framework is further enhanced with a dual-learning mechanism that encourages an exchange of knowledge between domains and a sample-based epistemic loss that promotes model diversity. The evaluation of MSDCR on real-world datasets shows its superiority over existing methods with more realistic domain settings, highlighting its potential for scaling to dense cross-domain settings.

Hypatia is a generic solver framework based on Julia, designed to tackle complex mathematical problems quickly, and it features an intuitive command line interface for easy problem formulation. The core of Hypatia utilizes the generic solver interface to integrate with backends, such as Julia's built-in solvers, JuliaMath's SDPA, and MOSEK, a commercial optimization solver, to rapidly solve a variety of problems, including nonlinear equations, quadratic programming, semidefinite programming, and nonlinear least squares, by simply specifying problem parameters and solution targets. With its modular design, Hypatia allows users to easily exchange backends in response to changing project needs, support for both command line and Julia API interfaces, and a comprehensive documentation resource are also available. As an example application in algebraic geometry, Hypatia is used to calculate a Riemann-Roch theorem, previously proven by its creators, and it can be freely downloaded from GitHub at the address https://github.com/kr0t0s/Hypatia.jl.

The increasing reliance on artificial intelligence has led to a growing interest in generalizing learned knowledge across diverse, previously encountered environments. In the context of medical imaging, such as brain MRI, there's a significant need to generalize knowledge across varying conditions, including different scanners, protocols, and technical specifications. In a study using MRI data from 181 subjects scanned on six different machines, researchers investigated the challenge of predicting image quality and identified key factors including scanner, protocol, and noise levels. They then explored several strategies for generalizing the knowledge across various conditions and tested the effectiveness of their methods using brain segmentation on MRI scans, with the aim of determining whether image-based features could be used to predict the quality of the image and, if so, what image-based characteristics were necessary for this prediction. The study demonstrated that it's possible to predict the quality of MRI scans and identified the factors influencing this prediction, with implications for the assessment of image quality and the development of protocols for future scans.

To analyze the effects of private electric vehicles on a distribution network's stability and congestion during outages, a new methodology is presented which considers optimal charging strategies for vehicles at various distances from the substation using a multi-agent optimization framework. By taking into account the resilience indicators, congestion costs, and limited network information, a decentralized decision-making approach is implemented for private EV owners. The methodology is tested on a simulated network with private EV owners in Los Angeles, revealing that the number of private EVs within a mile from a substation can significantly impact repair priority, with approximately 300 to 400 vehicles per mile typically being most beneficial, and that private EV charging schedules are influenced by time-of-use rates, battery sizes, and charging speeds, with time-of-use rates and battery sizes particularly notable in their impact. Furthermore, designating private EVs as repair assets can reduce congestion costs by 13% to 17%, increase the number of repaired segments by 10% to 15%, and decrease repair duration by 12% to 18%, with time-of-use rates and battery sizes contributing to these outcomes.

In highly dynamic environments with numerous agents, including those that move freely and those on set paths, meeting goals can be challenging to achieve due to frequent collisions and limited visibility. A major obstacle in overcoming this challenge is the lack of a well-defined concept of motivation, which is critical in driving decision-making and path-planning strategies. This work introduces a novel approach to meeting other agents in a dynamic world by establishing a motivation framework that accounts for the relative positions of agents and using it to create a distributed decision-making process that prioritizes meaningful encounters. In testing this approach on freely moving agents, it outperforms the current state-of-the-art method in the TMAS domain and matches its performance in the SUMO domain, and in testing it on a more complex scenario involving both freely moving and guided agents, it shows a significant improvement over the current best results.

Recently, a novel tin-based half-heel structure, related to the AuCu$_3$ type, has been reported, and it exhibits intriguing physical properties, including metallic conductivity, itchy magnetism, and a distanced insulating bandgap, varying from 0.1 to 1 eV, with different electronic configurations possible. In the presented work, the XSn$_3$ (where X is Gd or Cm) and Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds were studied using the self-consistent and plane-wave method within the framework of DFT+U. The optimized crystal structure, band characteristics, and magnetic and Fermi surface properties of these compounds have been determined and analyzed in their ground state condition. The investigation reveals that GdSn$_3$ exhibits ferrimagnetic behavior, and the band structure shows a significant indirect bandgap of 0.85 eV, whereas CmSn$_3$ shows a complex magnetic arrangement, and the band structure indicates it has an indirect bandgap of 0.12 eV. The study also shows that CmSn$_3$ has a more substantial bandgap than GdSn$_3$, and the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ compounds exhibit unique physical properties that can be controlled by varying the Gd to Cm ratio.

Using a 5 GeV dataset, the D0 detector requires an inner layer vacuum pressure of 0.01 to 1 atmospheres to maintain proper function. Increasing pressure in the outer layers of the hadronic calorimeter by 1 atmosphere would allow for a 20% increase in accepted cosmic data, and would also permit the use of liquid scintillator instead of gas as a readout material in the outer layers. This could result in the prediction of additional baryon and meson masses, specifically with masses greater than 4.5 GeV for baryons and 3.8 GeV for mesons.

The fundamental theorem established by Coxter and Mathieu in 1977, which classified finite Coxeter systems with irreducible generators and a symmetric matrix, has been expanded upon in this paper. It has been shown that every Coxeter system of type B, with a symmetric matrix, can be broken down into a product of three distinct systems: two isomorphic systems of type A, and a discrete system. This decomposition was achieved through the application of a previous, more general theorem from Coxter and Jones.

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and assuming GR as the underlying theory, a team of researchers calculated the weak lensing convergence displacement distribution for a SN Ia with an average luminosity, and then fitted the convergence displacement parameter to 69 data points from the sample. They found the best-fit value to be (0.686 ± 0.016) × (σ8 Ωm0 / (0.3))2, which is in line with similar studies. Consequentially, they used this value to place constraints on the matter density and Hubble constant using the Pantheon dataset in a weak lensing limit, and found the resulting (H0 / (100 km/s1))2 and (σ8 Ωm0 / (0.3))2 combinations to be in good agreement with other methods of estimating these values, albeit with somewhat larger errors due to the influence of SN Ia absolute magnitude dispersion and the assumption of a perfect lensing map, and also investigated the impact of weak lensing on SN Ia distances by calculating the standard deviation of the mean SN Ia stretch and E1-E2 cross term, and found it to be (0.05 ± 0.01) × (σ8 Ωm0 / (0.3))2, which is in line with other methods of estimating this value, and further explored the possibility of using the Pantheon SN Ia sample to place constraints on the matter density and Hubble constant using the

The integration of T-shaped nodes into silicon-on-insulator material could significantly enhance the efficiency of optical telecommunication systems. We investigate the T-shaped node's performance, analyzing its characteristics and behavior under different incident conditions. Using the finite-difference time-domain method, we examine the T-shaped node's electric field distribution in three variants and its impact on terry surface gratings. The results show that the T-shaped nodes with a 500 nm height exhibit improved performance when integrated with a 500 nm period terrys grating, demonstrating a 2-fold increase in the averaged optical intensity compared to a 1000 nm period grating. Additionally, the T-shaped nodes' performance is influenced by their form, with a node featuring a 2 um x 2 um cross-sectional area exhibiting the highest averaged optical intensity, an average 20 times greater than a conventional node.

For our assessment of deep object detectors in context for our proposed method, we used the COCO dataset with its native context, but we've also presented guidelines for applying our assessment to other datasets. We've demonstrated that evaluating object detectors on a single image can be an acceptable substitute for evaluating them on a set of images in context, albeit with the caveat that it's essential to use a diverse and representative image dataset. We've found that evaluating object detectors on isolated images yields results that closely resemble those obtained when evaluating them on a set of images in context, as measured by both average precision and recall. We've further analyzed our findings by examining the performance of different object detectors in various task categories, discovering that the difference in performance is more pronounced for category detection than for segmentation, and that it's more significant for smaller object detectors than for larger ones. We've also explored the role of context by examining the performance of object detectors on images with large foreground objects, discovering that it's more susceptible to surrounding context than those with small foreground objects. We've further analyzed our findings by examining the performance of object detectors on images with occlusions, discovering that it's more resistant to surrounding context than those without occlusions. We've also examined the relationship between performance and semantic segmentation masks, discovering that it's more correlated with performance in context than performance in isolation. We've further analyzed our findings by examining the performance of object detectors on images with semantically similar backgrounds, discovering that it's more resistant to surrounding context

Some important conditions on the domain $\Omega$ are also established, including a key result for a system that includes the critical growth exponent for a certain class of functions belonging to the Sobolev space, and another result for the system when it excludes this exponent. The key results from this paper can be seen as advancements or alternatives to some existing multiple solution theorems in the scientific literature. The research presented here builds upon the results obtained by Li and Yang in 2019 and Adgey, Serrin, and Tang in 2019. We derive new concentration inequalities where the variance term in the parabolic regime takes a different form, specifically, for sums of Bernoulli trials whose random variables have a weakened negative correlation property, we obtain a variety of concentration inequalities with improved variance terms, including a log-Sobolev inequality with an adjusted exponent, a Gaussian bound with an adjusted exponent, and an entropy bound with an adjusted exponent, all occurring in the parabolic regime, with strengthened assumptions on the joint distribution of the Bernoulli trials. Furthermore, with independent and identically distributed Bernoulli trials, we obtain a log-Sobolev inequality with an exponent two, with a special case where the trials have a reversed Hellinger distance of two, with additional results on the Talagrand's convex distance, with strengthened results for the entropy bound with an adjusted exponent, all with varying exponents depending on the specific measure used.

A closed symplectic $6$-manifold $M$ is defined as one that meets the criteria of having a differential $2$-form without a local annihilator except at a set of points with a specific Bianchi identity hold. This guideline results in a classification of closed manifolds that are not capable of being represented as the outcome of a particular embedding process called "twofold conjugation", thus indicating that all such manifolds fall under the category of being aspherical. It is also established that there are an infinite number of distinct closed symplectic manifolds that cannot be smoothly mapped onto each other, in contrast to a previous conjecture stating there were none. Additionally, it is demonstrated that a $2$-form can always be adjusted to make a closed Riemannian $6$-manifold become a closed symplectic $6$-manifold, provided certain curvature conditions are met.

In the course of a kidney transplant, after a patient's blood type is matched with a donor's, other factors such as the compatibility of an individual's immune system, the source of the donor, and the priority of the patient's waiting list are considered to determine whether to proceed with the transplant. In many transplant programs, a score is used to evaluate these factors, and patients are ranked according to these scores. The question of whether to accept an unmatched kidney has been examined in the literature, with the aim of minimizing the time a patient spends on the waiting list, with the constraint that the score of the unmatched kidney is known. In the present study, a control theory approach is applied to determine when a patient should accept an unmatched kidney, with the aim of minimizing the time spent on the waiting list, with the score of the unmatched kidney and the score of the transplanted kidney as the controls. The study also examines the impact of delaying the decision to accept an unmatched kidney until it becomes a match, or until it reaches the bottom of the waiting list. The study shows that only patients with the highest scoring kidneys on the waiting list should accept an unmatched kidney, with the condition that the score of the unmatched kidney is greater than the score of the top kidney on the list by more than one unit.
