This paper performs a comprehensive mathematical analysis of the correlation between the meaning of words and their classification as either informal or formal within the context of the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Dictionary. The study utilizes the geometric structure of word embeddings to visualize the relationships among the dictionary's 2,110 unique words. Although prior research found a strong link between word embeddings and many linguistic characteristics, our work reveals a more complex connection at play. We show that the design of the dictionary and the distribution of word embeddings do not align perfectly, with many words classified as similar tones being designated as distinct in the dictionary. Furthermore, we found that the design of the dictionary favors certain binary classifications over more granular ones, which could be reflected in the categories used by dictionary compilers. To support our claims, we developed a novel method for conducting t-SNE with dictionary-based labels, which we applied to both the original dictionary and an expanded version containing more nuanced categories. Our findings have implications for both scholars using the dictionary and those developing word embeddings.

This article presents the SISO-OFDM and MISO-OFDM based IDEA counterparts, which include detailed channel and signal processing descriptions, gain analysis, and simulation results for SISO-OFDM and simulated and real-data for MISO-OFDM.

This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries.

In complex multiplayer games with multiple agents, identifying stable states of strategy equilibria can be crucial for achieving optimal outcomes, but often such methods fail due to equilibria multiplicity, making it essential to consider an explanation for the predicted behavior. We introduce the first general approach to learn an explainable equilibria in multi-agent games using deep neural networks, without relying on the uniqueness of an equilibria. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our model by training it on two simple multi-agent games and show that it can de facto find the unique equilibria in these cases. Furthermore, our model is applied to a more challenging game, namely a learned equilibrium in a multi-agent deep learning testbed, which involves four agents interacting through deep neural networks. We also analyze the impact of an overfitting on the model and discuss several important implementation details. We compare our model to a baseline method and discuss the results of an experiment where it is trained on a large dataset consisting of 32 agents interacting in a deep learning network.

An analysis of a stochastic epidemic model on a changing contact network is conducted, where an infected individual immediately removes the edge with another randomly selected individual upon becoming infected, and then the model is expanded to a compartmental model, known as an ordinary differential equation (ODE) model, which describes the changes in the numbers of susceptible and infected individuals over time. By applying a stability analysis in the vicinity of an endemic equilibrium, the conditions required for the epidemic to become endemic are determined as specific parameters being above a certain threshold, and it is also found that the epidemic will eventually become endemic if these conditions are met, in addition to it being observed that the time it takes to occur can be substantial, even in models where the network changes very quickly.

A comprehensive framework has been developed to address challenges in fitting PDFs to data, incorporating external information, dealing with biases, and managing systematic uncertainties. The framework, highly effective in small PDF fitting, also shows potential benefits for larger fittings, such as that for combined PDF and Higgs boson production data.

To enhance the effectiveness of experience replay in policy optimization,
variance diminution techniques can be applied to both policy values and
value functions. By taking the latter approach, we propose a novel method
to modify the replay buffer, reducing the variance of visits frequency to
the same actions. This results in the visits frequency distribution in the
buffer being more representative of the exploration behavior. We call this
method Variance Diminution based Experience Replay (VDRER). We also
theoretically and experimentally demonstrate that VDRER leads to a more
precise estimation of the policy's expectations and consequently, a more
efficient optimization process. By integrating VDRER with policy optimization
algorithms, we achieve the state-of-the-art performance on various challenging
benchmarks, including the Atari games from the Arcade Learning Environment.

In our analysis of conversational dialogue, we face numerous possible responses 
to any given history, leading us to believe that a fixed action space cannot 
aptly capture the complexity of our model. To address this challenge, we apply 
a significant amount of effort into constructing a large set of actions for 
our dialogue system, consisting of over 3000 unique actions across twenty 
domains. We achieve this by employing a combination of rule-based and neural 
approaches to define our action spaces and learned policies to determine the 
next action within each conversation. Our system, called MultiTalk, features a 
novel way to express actions and a simple yet effective reinforcement learning 
strategy to efficiently discover optimal policies. Through our experiments on a 
large-scale dataset, we demonstrate that both action spaces and learned 
policies can generalise effectively to new, previously unseen conversations. 
Furthermore, we find that incorporating a wide range of actions in our system 
can result in significant improvements in diversity without suffering a notable 
decline in coherence, and that additional techniques such as salience masks 
and concurrency can lead to notable gains in both coherence and overall score. 
MultiTalk can be found at https://github.com/nyuvg/mtalk.

We've developed a highly efficient method for conducting accurate $N$-body simulations in various cosmological contexts, with a focus on modified gravity theories. This method, which leverages an assumption of conformal coupling between dark matter and dark energy, allows for a significant reduction in the computational time needed for $N$-body simulations while maintaining the ability to differentiate between different modified gravity models and standard $\Lambda$CDM. By developing this method, we've created a data pack containing $N$-body simulations for a range of modified gravity models, which can be used in conjunction with post-processing tools for observing the cosmic large-scale structure. These tools, designed to analyze the distribution of galaxies within massive cosmic surveys, can recover the effects of modified gravity on dark matter distribution by analyzing the clustering patterns of galaxies. By recovering the power spectrum of dark matter from these analyses, we can differentiate between $\Lambda$CDM and certain modified gravity models, such as $f(R)$ and $f(G)$, with the help of a Bayesian framework. With the ability to recover the effects of modified gravity on a wide range of scales, we can also test the Poisson equation and recover the behavior of these models at the cluster and galaxy group level.

Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops the imaginary surface along a parameter $\kappa$-family of boundary curves, and we establish a correspondence between such pairings and $\kappa$-family CLE $_\kappa$ decorated with $\kappa$-family SLE $_\kappa$ paths driven by the Dyck Brownian motion. This extension generalizes the results of Miller and Sheffield from $\kappa=2$ to $\kappa \in (1,4)$ and extends the relationship between Gaussian free fields and SLE  $_\kappa$ driven by the Loewner-Waterman measure from one boundary component to $\kappa$-family CLE  $_\kappa$ driven by the Dyck Brownian motion on the curves defined by the parameter $\kappa$-family SLE  $_\kappa$.

MediaWiki's versatility goes beyond its success with Wikipedia, being an effective tool for collaborative project work, according to the insights gained from its development history and the accounts of its users in this paper. We present the results of a survey aimed at researchers and academics who utilize Wiki platforms in their projects, as well as a retrospective analysis of Wikipedia's development and usage. Both studies provide valuable insights into the features of Wiki platforms that support collaborative work and offer suggestions for their improvement. The findings from both surveys and the analysis of Wikipedia's development and usage can be applied to the development of Wiki platforms and related software.

When applying acoustic forcing to a turbulent jet flame, the flame's shape changes, 
which in turn affects the flame's response to acoustic waves, 
due to a coupling between the flame's shape and the surrounding flow. 
To study this interaction, a mathematical model was developed 
by combining two existing models: one that predicts the flow and combustion 
in a jet flame, and another that predicts the flame's response to acoustic 
waves based on temperature and chemistry properties. 
To simplify the model, several assumptions were made, 
including that the flame's shape changes slowly compared to the flow, 
and that the acoustic waves do not significantly impact the flow. 
To validate the model, measurements of a jet flame were analyzed, 
which showed that the model could accurately predict the flame's response 
to acoustic waves when the forcing is weak, 
but struggled with a flame that had a highly irregular flame shape. 
To improve the model for such flames, it was suggested to use a more complex mathematical model 
that takes into account the chemistry of the flame, 
or a model that predicts the flow and combustion in the flame based on the flame's shape. 
To apply the model to a real-world scenario, it was proposed to use a linearized model 
of a flame in a channel with a perforated wall, 
which could help reduce the cost of developing models for actual flames.

In the scenario where neutrinos interact with ultralight dark matter, the decay of ultralight dark matter caused by neutrino scattering would result in the conversion of dark matter into energy, affecting its overall density and, in turn, impacting the dynamics of the universe during its early stages of formation. This phenomenon would lead to a specific oscillation pattern in the distribution of dark matter, potentially detectable through its influence on the phase and coherence of cosmological modes. On the other hand, the interaction between neutrinos and dark matter could also modify the energy spectrum of beta decay, potentially allowing for its identification through more precise measurements of $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay half-lives, and providing a novel approach to interpreting the outcomes of Big Bang Nucleosynthesis and the resulting matter and energy composition of the universe.

Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on a specific invariance principle, this paper derives the nonlocal gravity equation, demonstrating that its form is consistent with the underlying invariance structure. We show that the (0,2) nonlocal gravity equation corresponds to the (2,0) metric tensor component of the symmetric and traceless part of the energy-momentum tensor. We also discuss the relationship between nonlocal gravity and f(R) gravity, and the stability of nonlocal gravity equation in a classical context.

Our analysis combines data from comprehensive genomic experiments and genome-wide association studies of 18 human characteristics. To pinpoint regions of the genome linked to each trait, we correlated results from genome-wide association studies with information on gene function, expression, and other factors. We also examined the proportion of the genome associated with each trait, both across the 18 characteristics and in relation to their functional categories. Our analysis revealed that traits associated with gene expression tend to affect genes directly, whereas those not associated with gene expression may influence the genome indirectly. We found that certain traits, such as blood types, are linked to a small number of genes, whereas others, such as height, are connected to a large number of genes, albeit with a minor effect on each one. We found that regions of the genome associated with each trait, on average, account for around 1% of the genome, with some traits, such as lung function, associated with a much larger area, around 10%. We also determined that certain traits, such as type 2 diabetes, are linked to specific genomic regions, whereas others, such as coronary artery disease, are linked to more widespread areas of the genome. We ended up creating a database that combines data from comprehensive genomic experiments and genome-wide association studies of 18 human characteristics for further study.

The ATLAS and CMS experiments at the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) employ a minor selection system to enhance signal-to-background ratios in searches for new physics. While traditionally sensitive to specific characteristics such as transverse momentum and multiplicity, recent studies have explored the introduction of machine learning models to optimize particle combinations known as'subets' or'minor systems' for physics analysis. Researchers have successfully implemented custom-designed subets at the CMS experiment as part of jet characterisation and quark/gluon discrimination, and have found that certain combinations related to hadron production exhibit unique dependence on proton-proton scattering angle, effectively emulating the physics environment at the Tevatron.

Observations of some variable sources in the Milky Way center using the ROSAT and Chandra telescopes have led to the identification of 21 X-ray binaries containing neutron stars that have gone through a quiescent period. If the recurrence times of these binaries are analyzed, a pattern emerges, with times falling into distinct groups - roughly one day, from 50 to 70 days, around 90 to 100 days, around 140 to 150 days, around 160 to 170 days, around 190 to 200 days, around 360 to 370 days, around 390 to 400 days, around 460 to 470 days, around 490 to 500 days, around 530 to 540 days, around 560 to 570 days, around 590 to 600 days, around 630 to 640 days, around 660 to 670 days, around 690 to 700 days, around 730 to 740 days, around 760 to 770 days, around 790 to 800 days, around 830 to 840 days, around 860 to 870 days, around 890 to 900 days, around 930 to 940 days, around 960 to 970 days, around 990 to 1000 days, with some sources having times that cannot be determined. By considering the likely viewing angle of these sources and accounting for the Earth's interference, the average recurrence times can be calculated, with values ranging

The rate of change in crystal lattice positions, described by atomic displacement fields, determines the impact of laser radiation on electrons and can either slow down or speed up relaxation times, depending on whether it's out of sync or in sync with the natural oscillations of electrons, respectively. The influence of laser radiation on electrons and the resulting effects on their behavior can be examined by calculating the impact of laser radiation on the positions of atoms in a crystal lattice and then using this information to determine the effects of the resulting interactions on various phenomena. The calculations of this impact were initially limited to static atomic displacement fields, but it now becomes possible to examine the effects of laser radiation on the behavior of electrons in solid materials, taking into consideration the dynamic movement of the atomic lattice. It has been discovered that the frequency of atomic displacement fields can either match or differ from the energy differences between atomic levels, and that the direction of these fields can be either aligned with or pointed away from the momentum of electrons. It has been found that the interactions between the movement of the atomic lattice and the movement of electrons are influenced by the mass of the electrons, the energy they possess and the direction of these movements, and that these interactions can either speed up or slow down the relaxation times of electrons, and even cause them to move in the opposite direction, and that the movement of the atomic lattice can also affect the behavior of the spin of the electrons, and that these interactions vary across different materials and cannot be ignored when examining the effects of

When constructing natural language processing systems for generating natural language, designers typically select a single variety of language, often based on written inputs, to create both the input prompts and the output responses. In the context of natural language processing tasks like machine translation and text summarization, researchers typically train two separate models, each optimized for a different variety of language. In contrast, a newly proposed universal generative dialogue framework, NUDGL, processes multiple varieties of language by training a single model to engage in conversation with itself. This model takes two forms of input: an initial statement and a response format in which the output should be presented. Utilizing Natural Language Inference as a guiding framework, the model generates output in a variety that aligns with the predicted characteristics of the input statement. According to our experiments, by training this simple system, we can achieve significant improvements in tasks like machine translation, text summarization, and text generation, particularly when there is a significant discrepancy between the input statements and the desired output format. We also explored applying NUDGL to natural language tasks by simply redefining the input statement and response format, and discovered that it can be used to create diverse natural language dialects, including those with a more formal tone, different sentence structures, and various styles of writing, all without the need for large amounts of training data. When used in this manner, NUDGL can be seen as a type of text style transfer, and our results suggest that it is possible to train models

The occurrence of flares and rotationally induced pulsations on low-mass stars could be influenced by their rotational velocity, due to their oblateness. Despite this factor's importance, it remains unknown for the majority of low-mass stars. This study numerically simulates rotating stars with masses similar to those of red dwarfs, specifically subdwarfs and subgiants below 0.45 solar masses, using a range of metallicities. The simulations, which take into account the conservation of angular momentum and mass redistribution through gravitational settling and thermal mixing, result in accurate reconstructions of various low-mass stars' rotation velocities. Our research also identifies the limits up to which these sub-stellar objects can rotate before they split into multiple fragments or experience severe oscillations, and our calculations are suitable for applying this knowledge to a range of low-mass stars, including subgiants, subdwarfs, and red giants under the influence of rotation.

The technique of amplitude analysis in hadron collisions requires an understanding of factors affecting the accuracy of results, including the impact of experimental conditions, statistical data, and kinetic energy. A well-defined framework is proposed to assess the reliability of individual measurements and overall analyses, with the potential to identify areas for improvement in experiments, such as increasing the size of available data samples. This approach can be applied during data collection to inform decisions about the quality of amplitudes to measure and the precision of analyses, and can be useful for both established experiments and potential upgrades.

A new model has been proposed to explain the progression of external shock Grand Energy Release events. The suggested model accounts for the interplay between two phases of the shock: a phase where the shock encounters a high density of electrons and a phase where it encounters a lower density. This model also takes into consideration the effects of a variable density of electrons, which were assumed to be constant in previous models. The result is a natural explanation for the observed curvature in the spectra of relativistic jets. A new set of equations has been derived to describe the dynamics of the model, which includes a variable density of electrons and provides a general expression for gamma as a function of time. The result has been tested against existing data from Gamma Ray Burst observations and shows that it is consistent with the data, using the same parameters that were previously used to describe the same events. The model has been applied to three different types of observations: observations of the peak frequency of spectra, observations of the temperature of spectra, and observations of the luminosity of jets. The result has been that the model is able to accurately describe the dynamics of all stages of the shock, from the early stages to the late stages, with a high degree of precision. The result has been quantified by calculating the precision of the model as follows: the model has been found to calculate the peak frequency of spectra with a precision of 0.05, the temperature of spectra with a precision of 0.05, and the luminosity of jets with

Bipartite graphs represent a fundamental concept where two distinct groups of vertices are connected by edges between them, without any connections within each individual group. This type of graph has numerous practical applications (in statistics, genetics, and electrical engineering) and is also closely related to various important theories (such as matrix permanents and ranks, and the stability of linear systems). The current study focuses on an optimization problem where the objective is to minimize the number of connections between two groups of vertices by removing edges, under the constraint that a specific property (namely, having access to a particular subdeterminant) is maintained. A key contribution of this research is the development of an exact algorithm that solves this problem in time that is exponentially bounded by the number of edges, making it the first such algorithm for this class of problems.

Recently, researchers have successfully implemented bipedal locomotion in various settings, though it hasn't been easy. For a long time, scientists and engineers have been fascinated by the efficiency and balance-achieving capabilities of humans walking. To enhance stability and prevent falls during locomotion, an investigation into thruster-assisted bipedal motion is presented in this study. To achieve this, a simplified model was used to analyze the effects of direction and force produced by thrusters on a bipedal robot. To validate the model, simulations were conducted in Saplab, and in this study, an experiment was set up in a small pool to replicate the thruster-assisted bipedal locomotion scenario. To facilitate this, a bipedal robot and a control system were developed and tested on land before being taken to the pool for further testing. The results from pool tests showed that thrusters can improve the stability of a bipedal robot during locomotion, but they cannot be used to provide additional propulsion when the robot is already moving. To achieve this, further research is required. To achieve robust and efficient bipedal locomotion on land, a separate investigation is recommended.

We define a particular type of valued domain, which we call a T-domain, whose associated map from maximal ideals to the set of valuations can be extended to a map from all ideals to the set of valuations. We then establish that every T-domain is essentially the same as a domain whose associated divisorial ideal class group is finitely generated, providing a new frame of reference for this well-studied ideal class group.

In order to reduce energy consumption and heat generation, a method has been proposed to efficiently set CPU frequency levels by creating a hierarchical framework consisting of multiple layers of frequency scaling. Based on empirical observations and workload characteristics, an algorithm has been developed to determine optimal frequency levels across three distinct layers, taking into account data processing patterns, memory access behaviors, and other workload traits. A proposed design has been explored, which has been shown to be feasible in modern CPU architectures, and has been validated through simulations using real workloads from various applications. The results demonstrate that, without any performance degradation, CPU frequency can be set as low as 200MHz, leading to significant reductions in energy consumption and heat generation.

In the field of robot grasping and manipulation, a crucial step in problem-solving involves disentangling the configuration of grasped objects. A key factor in achieving this is the understanding of how links are connected, either classically or welded. For classical links, a rotation or translation in one object affects the same type of movement in the connected object, whereas in welded links, a change in one object results in the same type of movement in the connected object, but in the opposite direction. We have developed a method for determining the type of connection between objects and have applied it to a problem where the disentangling of grasped objects is necessary. The developed algorithm was initially created for classical links by Girard and Burdick, but we have refined it to handle both classical and welded links. The new algorithm was tested on a set of examples, including a problem with a complex setup of both classical and welded links.

We have demonstrated that an invariant from the Vassiliev bi-space, accurate to order three, may be represented as the coefficient in a particular iterated integral, namely the Fox-Hatcher loop calculation applied to a specific polynomial equation, involving the Alexander-Conner polynomial and its derivatives. Notably, this representation sets a precedent for a broader principle: any 1-cocycle in the Vassiliev bi-algebra generated by the Kauffman polynomial can be expressed as the coefficient in an iterated integral of the type of the Fox-Hatcher loop calculation, related to a polynomial equation with coefficients from the torus invariant.

In a collaborative setting, multiple agents, each tasked with a different project, can enhance their individual progress by working together and sharing resources. We have investigated a model where agents with varying objectives can choose to work together and achieve a common goal, and have derived the optimal cooperative policies that maximize overall progress. We have also established a framework for implementing an efficient decentralized strategy, achieved through a key distribution of values associated with each project, and have shown that this approach leads to a distributed policy that approximates the optimal cooperative outcome with a known level of accuracy. We have further explored a more complex scenario where agents can switch between multiple projects, and have a range of results related to project synchronization. We have also provided a comprehensive study on the performance of our proposed algorithm through simulations.

In Federated Learning, trained models are generated through collaborative efforts between remote devices and a central server, without the need to exchange sensitive information, thus preserving user privacy. Despite this benefit, research has shown that a malicious participant can successfully compromise privacy by simply adding a small amount of manipulated data to the learning process, a technique known as privacy assaults. In this study, we focus on private assaults in vertically Federated Learning, a variant of FL where organizations with access to different types of data collaborate to train a model. We examine several strategies for a malicious participant to breach privacy by manipulating data in the client or server, and demonstrate the effectiveness of these techniques, along with potential deterrents that can help prevent such privacy assaults from occurring in the first place. Our research in this area can be applied to VCFL and other versions of FL.

Kernel methods in machine learning are highly effective, yet the computational expense of matrix operations and training times associated with standard kernel functions hinder their practical applications. To overcome these limitations, Random Fourier Features were proposed by Smola, Coelho, and Le, in 2007, providing an alternative method to calculate kernel functions using random transformations, thus reducing the computational burden. In this research, we build upon their work by creating a data-dependent kernel feature transformation, which results in our method outperforming RFF in many instances, without the limitations of requiring a predetermined bandwidth. Our approach is particularly effective when applied to support vector machines, and our experimental findings, using datasets from the UCI repository and a kernelized k-means clustering algorithm on synthetic data, demonstrate significant improvements over the original RFF and standard kernel functions in both training times and classification accuracy.

In our study, we establish the fundamental theorem that any permutation group acting on a set with the structure of a Cartesian product can be effectively characterized as the result of a specific action of combined discrete groups on a corresponding product. This distinct classification allows us to identify the individual component groups that make up the original permutation group and determine its corresponding defining equations. Our research provides an original solution to a problem posed by Cameron, which involves determining the composite groups that form the basis of a given permutation group acting on a set with the structure of a Cartesian product.

We investigate conformally flat hypersurfaces of S(n+1) with non-negative sectional curvatures, defining a function F related to the n-th root of the Riemannian volume form, proportional to (R_\infty - (n-1)(n+2)r^{-2})^2, where R_\infty denotes the asymptotic curvature at infinity and r is the distance function to the conformal compact hypersurface. We show that any compact hypersurface without boundary or with boundary that is mean convex or satisfying a certain pinching condition, with respect to a specific Mobius inversion, with non-negative sectional curvatures and with asymptotic curvature at infinity satisfying a given inequality, contains a neighborhood where F is defined and non-negative, with the exception of a finite number of points.

In a time-switching wireless power and information transfer (WSNIT) system, one frequency band is used for data transmission and another for energy harvesting, with separate resources allocated for each service. We investigate a scenario where multiple users, each with distinct requirements for data rates and energy capacities, coexist in a wireless network. Our goal is to optimize the allocation of time, power for transmission, and power for energy harvesting for each user, as well as the frequency band for each user, in order to meet their respective needs while minimizing overall power expenditure. By developing mathematical models and utilizing numerical data, we examine various factors influencing optimal results, including the number of users, available frequency bands, time frames for data transmission and energy harvesting, data rates, energy capacities, and the level of power expenditure.

Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for analyzing the impact of malicious attacks and natural disasters in various contexts, including computer networks, urban planning, and biology. Researchers often use percolation theory to study the effects of node removal on networks, especially in vulnerable areas such as forests, power grids, and the human immune system. A key aspect of percolation theory is the analysis of the component size distribution in random cluster configurations, especially in quadratic networks, scale-free networks, and tree-like networks. A recent study examined the distribution of avalanche sizes in a Cayley tree network using percolation theory and Monte Carlo methods, providing insights into the effects of model parameters on the distribution of avalanche sizes and offering a framework for comparing the vulnerability of different network types based on the distribution of avalanche sizes.

The sensitivity of advanced gravitational wave detectors is limited by the noise caused by the debris ringing of massive mirrors. To overcome this limitation, a novel dark port technique called the sloshing-Sagnac interferometer has been proposed, where the mirrors are actuated to counteract the signal noise. However, the effectiveness of this method depends on the precise alignment of the recycling mirror and mirrors, which can be challenging to maintain in reality. In this research, the requirements for the shape and position of the recycling mirror in a advanced gravitational wave detector, specifically the GEO-HF setup, were investigated. It was found that the optimal design of the recycling mirror could be very different from its current form. A suggestion is made to use a cylindrical shape with a length to diameter ratio of around one, which could minimize the curvature of the light path and make it easier to maintain the alignment. This research also explored the application of the sloshing-Sagnac technique to other advanced gravitational wave detectors, including a proposed detector with a laser interferometer configuration, where the end mirror of an optical cavity is used as the test mass. This design could eliminate the need for actuating mirrors and reduce the noise caused by the laser, allowing it to be below the shot noise limit.

Recent advancements in MIMO technology have been successful with the XL-MIMO random access protocol due to its ability to provide high data rates and low energy consumption. A key assumption in existing research, which enables efficient cross-layer design, is the non-intersecting visibility region of bases. However, the existing literature lacks mathematical proof for this essential feature. In the existing research on scheduling and transmission protocols, the visibility region of bases is often considered as non-overlapping, with the exception of the proof provided in this work, which shows that visibility region overlap can occur under certain conditions. Furthermore, we investigate the impact of overlapping visibility regions on packet collision probabilities and provide theorems on the relationship between the angle domain packet allocation and the visibility region matrix. These theorems can be used to develop new algorithms for the optimal packing of bases in XL-MIMO systems.

Recent high-resolution observations in the millimeter to near-infrared range have revealed that young stars' surrounding disks exhibit patterns of sinuous curves or forked shapes. Researchers proposed that vertical shear instability in disks could explain the formation of these curves, and it was shown that this instability could lead to the creation of bridges, arcs, and shells within the disks. In the second part of this study, we used numerical data from simulations of unstable disks to estimate the dimensions and orientations of these curves, assuming that the features are caused by the movement of dust particles. This analysis was achieved by recreating the conditions of the shearing disks and calculating the paths of dust particles under the influence of the perturbations caused by VSI. This process allowed us to determine the observable characteristics of the curves, taking into consideration the effects of the inclination of the disks and the direction of their rotation. We also simulated the observations of these curves on the disks using the radiative transfer code MCFOST, which revealed that the peaks of the curves would shine brightly in the continuum at mid-infrared to near-infrared wavelengths, and that the curves would appear more pronounced when the disks are viewed at a shallow angle. We further analyzed the predictions of the models by comparing the predicted dimensions of the curves with the actual sizes observed in the disks, which revealed that the predicted sizes were generally larger than the actual observed sizes, although this discrepancy could be explained by the effects of the beam filling factor, which would result in the observed

Researchers analyzed recent measurements of neutron skin thickness in lead using an electro-magnetic process, as well as predictions from various models, including the "Big Apple" parameterization of the symmetry energy's density dependence. Although the spread of calculated skin thicknesses narrowed with the inclusion of astrophysical constraints, it still showed significant variation. This persistence of variation raises questions about the accuracy of the density-dependent parameterization and highlights the significance of further experimental and theoretical efforts to refine the understanding of the symmetry energy.

We investigate the accuracy of Molmer-Sorensen gates in quantum systems that incorporate multiple motional modes within an optical trap. By conducting simulations, we identified preferred trap configurations that minimize the effects of frequency drift and mode crosstalk, leading to the implementation of highly precise Molmer-Sorensen gates. For example, in an arrangement featuring three motional modes, a gate accuracy of 99.97% can be achieved, even when subject to a 10 Hz frequency drift. We also explored the effects of varying trap configurations, as well as the impact of mode crosstalk, and our results show that balanced trap configurations consistently yield the most reliable outcomes. Furthermore, we found that frequency-stable gates can be achieved using a simpler balanced configuration, achieving a gate accuracy of 99.95% with a 1 Hz frequency drift. We believe that by employing balanced trap configurations, it is possible to build quantum systems capable of executing Molmer-Sorensen gates with a high degree of precision, even in noisy environments.

Recently discovered layered crystals, such as Anderson-Taichi phase Pd(Se$_{1-x}$Te$_x$)$_{23}$ and Pd(Te$_{1-x}$Se$_x$)$_{23}$, exhibit unique properties that are characterized by coexistence of Te and Se atoms within the same lattice unit cell, allowing for the adjustment of band structure and electronic interactions through chemical doping. In this work, synthetic Pd(Te$_{0.5}$)$_{23}$ is theoretically investigated as a model for strongly correlated metals with Dirac electrons. Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that this material exhibits significant electronic interactions and exhibits linear energy dispersion near key points in the Brillouin zone, along with significant orbital and spin polarization of electrons. The results of our calculations are further analyzed using a combination of theoretical methods to understand and predict the material's properties and behavior under different conditions. Notably, we find that this material exhibits ferromagnetic behavior at the atomic level, but exhibits complex interactions that may lead to various outcomes, including the stabilization of unusual charge density waves or the generation of a spin-orbit coupled Fermi surface. By controlling the arrangement of Te and Se atoms, this material may serve as an ideal model for the study of interacting Dirac electrons in a three-dimensional space and can be used to create a solid-state platform for the study of interacting relativistic electrons.

Researchers explored the constraints that can be placed on a specific parameter in the Standard Model, related to the interaction between a particular neutrino and a heavy neutral lepton, which could influence the behavior of neutrinos at the TeV scale. They examined the sensitivity of two experiments to this parameter: the NA62 at CERN, which can detect the absence of a specific neutrino interaction, and a future SHiP experiment that can place more stringent limits. By analyzing decay patterns of which particles can be produced from certain mesons, they determined the expected rates of decays of two types: one where a neutral lepton is created and another where it is not, and calculated the NA62 sensitivity to this parameter based on its accumulated data set. In the process, they identified the limiting factors in their calculation, primarily related to detector acceptance and efficiency, and also explored the NA62 potential in detecting two types of decays: $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$ and $K^+ \to \gamma e^+ N$. Depending on the neutral lepton mass, they found the NA62 sensitivity to this particular neutrino interaction to be more restrictive than other constraints, and in some cases, even more limiting than the SHiP constraints, with a figure of merit indicating the NA62 can place limits on this interaction at a level of $10^{-16}$ when the neutral lepton is lighter than 100 MeV.

Neural language models have significantly outperformed $N$-gram models in many tasks, yet our experimentation reveals that $n$-gram models can excel when used as a component in a neural setup, specifically in a task we call "neural text creation." In this process, a decoder generates text based on a combination of a latent code and the input, with the goal of creating coherent and diverse sequences of text, with an emphasis on novelty. We discovered that when we train the encoder to produce codes that, when combined with an $n$-gram language model, accurately replicate the original text, the generated text exhibits significant improvement, with a notable increase in novelty, according to our metrics. Notably, this approach allows for the creation of novel texts that are tailored to a given context, with applications in fields such as storytelling and recommendation systems. With an emphasis on simplicity, our method is effective when used with an $n$-gram model trained on an extensive corpus, with an analysis of the interplay between the parameters of this model.

Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios with limited and occluded data remains a significant challenge. Since training and deploying monocular 3D face reconstruction models heavily rely on data with similar viewing angles, they tend to struggle with significant angle changes, especially 90-degree rotations. To address this issue, researchers have explored multi-view 3D face reconstruction models, which can handle various viewing angles due to their angle-agnostic nature. However, such models typically require a diverse and representative dataset for training and may be more prone to crossovers and mode switching, leading to poor performance in scenarios with significant occlusions. This paper presents a novel 3D face alignment and reconstruction approach called SADRNet, which utilizes a simple and robust architecture to achieve both local and non-local face alignment without relying on diverse training datasets. Furthermore, SADRNet includes two unique modes to address data with 90-degree angle changes and incorporates a self-alignment mechanism and a dual face regression network to enhance robustness in the presence of local deformations and facial occlusions. Experimentation across diverse datasets shows that the proposed method excels in both front and profile views, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods by significant margins. When applied to a challenging facial expression and 3D face reconstruction dataset, SADRNet achieves comparable performance to leading models while being more computationally efficient.

A significant fluctuation in an inflationary cosmological era can create a "bubble" of space where inflation doesn't stop, potentially giving rise to primordial black holes. Such fluctuations are more likely to form in certain types of inflationary models, specifically those where a particular kind of cosmic disturbance is subject to a critical threshold. A team of researchers has now examined two types of inflationary models, based on the "alpha-attractor" theory, in both its original and modified form, in order to determine the kinds of perturbations they produce and the kinds of bubbles they could form. In the original alpha-attractor model, even the tiniest perturbations can cause a bubble to form, which would be too small to create black holes. In contrast, the modified version can form black holes only if the perturbations are significant enough to cause multiple bubbles to form within a certain distance from each other. If this condition is met, it could potentially explain the missing mass in the universe, known as dark matter.

Researchers examined marked ordered trees with the ability to designate and distinguish 'deepest' vertices, using a combinatorial approach to analyze and interpret the identified properties through exponential generating functions. A key discovery revealed that when the deepest vertex is marked, there is a clear and consistent pattern in which the coefficient of $x_{1} \ldots x_{k}$ in the exponential generating function corresponds to specific structured permutations, referredly known as double right-decompositions of the initial object $1_{k}$. Additionally, further studies on trees without designating the deepest vertex revealed that the exponential generating function can be expressed as a product of two established functions, offering an insightful comparison to the previous scenario.

This research seeks to examine the capabilities of Informed OCR (iOCR) in accurately
identifying total vote counts listed on California's 2020 state ballot affidavits
under both normal and manipulated conditions, with the ultimate goal of exploring
limits and constraints of iOCR in maintaining election integrity through the optical
identification of altered vote tabulation documents.

In recent years, overfitting in linear models has been reinterpreted due to the discovery of a strong link with generalization ability. It has been found that models experiencing benign overfitting are typically characterized by a small gap between their training and test data loss. In the case of time series data, overfitting has been shown to occur in models with a specific structure that account for both current and past observations. However, the relationship between model parameterization and the distance between training and test data loss has not been well understood. This study investigates the effects of model parameterization on time series data models and reveals that there is an optimal range of feature retention depths where models exhibit benign overfitting behavior. It has also been found that models with a certain level of feature overlap do not generally result in the desired behavior, and those with minimal feature overlap exhibit similar performance to standard cross-validation methods. Moreover, this study shows that the optimal range of feature retention depths decreases as the distance between training and test data loss increases, and models that result in a large distance between training and test data loss are often associated with good generalization ability even in the absence of over-parameterization. In the absence of cross-validation, models can be designed that result in a desired range of the distance between training and test data loss simply by adjusting the model's parameterization, and such designs can be combined with existing regularization techniques to enhance the performance of linear models on time series data.

A key aspect of decentralized energy grids lies in the management of local energy storage, which enables households to consume less energy during peak periods in exchange for compensation. However, determining the optimal amount of storage for individual households is a complex mathematical problem, especially when considering uncertainty about future prices and consumption. In this research, we develop a standardized framework to value storage in a way that accounts for both price uncertainty and consumption patterns. By utilizing a stochastic fluid dynamics approach, the method can be applied to various storage technologies, such as batteries, and helps identify whether it's beneficial to have storage, as well as the ideal amount, in scenarios with both daily and seasonal price fluctuations. Furthermore, we create and test an algorithm to calculate these values using a small set of consumption and price data, which can be scaled up for larger datasets with more advanced machine learning methods.

A global circulation model that considers the effects of friction, heat, and atmospheric pressure has been applied to various planetary conditions, simulating atmospheric circulation patterns on other worlds. When applied to Earth's temperature and atmospheric characteristics, the model successfully recreates the atmospheric circulation observed at the surface, showing that the Hadley circulation covers the majority of the equator and expands towards the poles with increasing planetary heat balance. However, when the model is modified to prioritize the conservation of heat over the conservation of angular momentum, it predicts a slower atmospheric rotation speed, an expanded Hadley circulation, and multiple circulation cells that reach further towards the poles. When the model is modified to prioritize the conservation of angular momentum over the conservation of heat, under conditions of low rotation speeds and high temperatures, it predicts extremely fast atmospheric rotation speeds, a narrow Hadley circulation, and multiple circulation cells that are confined to the equatorial region. When the model is further altered to account for the varying height of atmospheric pressure levels, it shows that the atmospheric pressure at the surface is affected by the atmospheric pressure at higher altitudes, which in turn is influenced by the atmospheric circulation pattern, rather than being influenced by the rotation speed and temperature as previously assumed.

Large-scale classification on ImageNet is often viewed as a means to evaluate the
performance of deep learning models. With over 1.5 million images spanning 21,841
classes, it presents significant challenges in model training, particularly when
addressing multi-classification problems. In this work, we explore the connection
between deep learning architectures and the number of classification classes.
We demonstrate that a simple wide residual connection can effectively handle
extreme class imbalance and efficiently handle large numbers of classification
classes. By applying this architecture in an unrestricted training setting on
ImageNet, we achieve a new record of 6.96% top-1 error and 39.32% top-5 error
on the validation set. Our results are accompanied by a dataset analysis,
including an examination of the current labeling standards and an exploration
of the relationship between classification classes and model performance. Our code
has been made available for public use.

Researchers who utilize silicon donor spin have reached a record for coherence time and are close to achieving universal quantum gate functionality. To advance beyond this limit, understanding the behavior of multiple donors and implementing coulomb-driven operations are necessary. In the context of Coulomb-driven operations between two distant donors, our calculations demonstrate that the use of a particular charge state control pulse can effectively mediate the exchange of spin between two silent donors, with minimal impact on the overall system's stability, despite the complexity of their positional and electrical coupling. By accounting for the influence of lattice vibrations, our simulations show that the functional lifetime of these operations can be increased to over 100 microseconds. Our research provides a detailed analysis of the necessary conditions to perform this operation, utilizing effective mass theory to incorporate the effects of valley and orbital coupling. The findings are applicable to planar double gate and quantum dot gate implementations.

Our investigation focused on determining the conductivity of a specific arrangement of HgTe quantum wells at their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal. By applying the $k\cdot p$ method in a three-dimensional model and calculating the conductivity using the Boltzmann transport theory, we compared our results to existing studies using a two-dimensional model.  Our research revealed that the conductivity in the $\Gamma$ direction is anisotropic and varies based on the orientation of the conductivity tensor.  We also examined the conductivity along the $\Gamma$-X direction in a two-dimensional arrangement and found that it closely matches the conductivity in a one-dimensional model, where the conductivity is influenced by the overlap of the heavy-hole and light-hole bands.  To make our calculations more realistic, we incorporated non-equilibrium situations and investigated the conductivity in both the $\Gamma$ direction and along the $\Gamma$-X direction under various temperature and doping conditions.  Our results confirmed that the conductivity in the $\Gamma$ direction and along the $\Gamma$-X direction can be explained by a one-dimensional and a two-dimensional model, respectively.  To simulate an ultra-thin HgTe quantum well, we used a two-dimensional model and calculated the conductivity in the $\Gamma$-X direction, which also corresponds to the conductivity in a one-dimensional arrangement, where the conductivity is influenced by the overlap of the heavy-hole and light-hole bands.  Our results are consistent with existing studies using a one-dimensional model,

Recent developments in 5G systems, specifically with Dynamic TDD (Time Division Duplexing), have introduced challenges related to modeling and managing radio resources. One significant issue is the lack of a unified framework that can adapt to the changing needs of different models and cells within a 5G network. This lack of integration can result in significant performance losses and limitations in the dynamic scheduling of TDD bandwidth. This research addresses these challenges by presenting a new approach to managing D2D links, as well as a set of models that include small cells, combined models, and a 5G D2D link model. The proposed method, called GTMS (Game-Theoretic Model Scheduling), utilizes non-cooperative game theory to determine optimal scheduling and resource allocation in 5G networks, with a focus on combined models and 5G D2D links. The research includes comprehensive simulation results, demonstrating significant performance improvements of up to 24% in the GTMS model when compared to conventional methods, with the potential to further enhance performance in real-world implementations.

In this note, a specific type of Hamiltonian Neural Network (HNN) with a particular architecture is explored to determine its capabilities in regards to differentiating functions. It is demonstrated that this HNN system can successfully replicate the process of calculating derivatives through the Hamiltonian dynamics principle. A link is established between this HNN and a related neural network known as a residual neural network, providing a new perspective on RRNs. Furthermore, an analysis into the conditions under which a function can be learned as part of a Hamiltonian system is conducted, including a discussion on the constraints and the dimension of the Hamiltonian. A novel derivation is presented for a specific Hamiltonian, along with a related Hamiltonian Neural Network, which can be used to efficiently calculate the derivatives of a class of functions with the Hamiltonian dynamics principle. This is particularly useful in regards to the computation of the gradients of loss functions, which is a key issue in the training of HNNs. This is addressed through a simple modification to the Hamiltonian, along with an associated increase in the dimension, which is shown to result in the desired gradients being part of the Hamiltonian currents. This in turn allows for the learning of the Hamiltonian, which is equivalent to the learning of the derivatives of the functions in question. This is a key finding that provides a framework for the learning of the derivatives of functions through the Hamiltonian dynamics principle, which can be applied to a wide range of situations. Artificial neural networks are subject to fluctuations during training, and their performance can significantly change over time. To address this issue, a dynamic model is proposed that accounts for performance variations. When models change rapidly, the proposed dynamic model ensures positive progress, and when they change slowly, it guarantees convergence. A numerical example demonstrates the proposed method's effectiveness, and it's applied to a problem from genetics where it successfully converges to the optimal solution.

Recently developed invariants, specifically the refined topological invariant introduced in arXiv:2012.12307, have shown great promise in providing insights into the volume hypothesis. The mentioned invariants, which are based on a combination of spectral network and shearings of Pfaffian functions, have demonstrated remarkable behavior in line with the volume hypothesis, particularly in the context of scalar products of Jucys-Murphy elements and their relation to volume. In this study, novel invariants are introduced that can be defined using spectral networks on the torus with volume hypotheses behavior, offering an analytical framework for the previously mentioned invariants. Moreover, these invariants can be linked to the invariants based on the Harpe-Zagier and Ito invariants, bridging the gap between them and the invariants related to volume. In addition to these findings, a formula is derived for the invariants of the Borromean rings, which serves as a critical test case for the proposed method.

The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  One well-known approach to achieving this aims to match a word's context with its definition, yet this method can be hindered by the scarcity of available glosses for many words.  To address this challenge, we propose an innovative technique, Context-gloss Enhancement for WSD (CEE4W), which leverages a word's neighboring terms to generate a context that includes a gloss, thereby enriching the available semantic information for disambiguation.  To support our method, we gathered a unique set of data featuring word contexts along with their corresponding semantic definitions, not discovered elsewhere in literature.  According to the experimental results, CEE4W achieved notable improvements over existing methods when applied to multiple word sense disambiguation datasets.

This study derives a family of relaxed integral representations of Geller's reciprocal gamma function, which involves a combination of weakly singular kernels and a logarithmic function. The proposed expressions include the reciprocal gamma function as a solution to a regularized integral equation, where the operator is defined using the Gauss convolution and has a compact resolvent. Additionally, the paper shows that the reciprocal gamma function can be obtained by regularizing the Gauss-Weierstrass integral operator applied to the logarithmic function. The study also establishes the convergence of a series of integral representations that yield the reciprocal gamma function and includes numerical examples of the series.

To identify the production of top quarks in proton-nucleus collisions at LHC energies, a study selects events that contain one or more jets originating from b-quark decays, produced in association with a lepton and a missing transverse momentum. The research uses 2016 proton-lead data, resulting in approximately 162 inverse picobarns of integrated luminosity. Production cross-sections for top quarks are determined using a Bayesian approach and multiple methods are employed to validate the results, including separating events based on centrality and transverse momentum of forward particles. The measured cross-sections for top quark production in proton-lead collisions are 44.3 ± 2.4 (stat.) ± 10.3 (syst.) ± 2.0 (lum.) ± 1.2 (PDF) ± 1.1 (theo.) pb for the l+jets channel and 44.6 ± 7.2 (stat.) ± 8.0 (syst.) ± 1.4 (lum.) ± 0.7 (PDF) ± 0.6 (theo.) pb for the l+missing transverse momentum channel. The results are consistent with theoretical predictions based on parton distribution functions and nuclear effects, and also with the production of top quarks in lead-proton collisions when reversing the collision direction.

Many contemporary systems execute natural language inputs on top of structured data, specifically executing SQL queries on top of database tables.  Models in this category are known as Text-to-SQL models.  Research in this area focuses on models that interpret natural language inputs on top of untrained databases, known as outdoor settings.  A significant challenge in this area is modeling the semantic meaning of natural language inputs in a way that aligns with the schema of the underlying data.  Another challenge is accounting for database columns that are irrelevant to the current task.  A new model called Semantic Type Prediction Network (STRN) addresses these challenges by predicting the semantic types of database columns based on natural language inputs and underlying data.  This model enhances the performance of existing models, particularly on harder tasks with fewer labeled examples.  An analysis of parameters and components in STRN highlights its ability to capture important features like entity recognition and reduces the impact of irrelevant database columns through parameter sparsity.  An additional challenge in this area is modeling the semantic meaning of natural language inputs across different domains.  A new approach called straddling models enhances the performance of models on harder tasks with fewer labeled examples.  An evaluation of straddling models on larger, more challenging datasets is also presented.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of network data, focusing on graph-structured and time-series data. It outlines the primary challenges encountered when applying differential privacy to such data, specifically in regards to statistical accuracy, computation feasibility, and achieved privacy levels. It also explores the various methods employed to tackle private machine learning on graph-structured and time-series data, highlights the theoretical guarantees provided by these methods, and presents a comprehensive analysis of the available literature, along with an examination of notable applications and results obtained. Furthermore, it presents an innovative scheme for privately training complex models on dynamic time-series data and discusses future research avenues and challenges in the field.

The Euclid mission, focusing on the cosmos' synergetic exploration with a 0.25 square degree visual survey, will provide a substantial foundation for future telescopic projects. To make the most of its findings, Euclid's imaging data, incorporating near-infrared spectral analysis, will be critical. This paper outlines the potential Euclid legacy to have on the study of the universe, highlighting areas it will influence and the potential they hold for future discoveries. These domains include the investigation of the cosmos' chemical makeup, the formation of galaxies through various ages, the assembly of galaxies in mass and number, the evolution of planetary systems, and the analysis of the Milky Way.

Researchers have a different approach in mind for possibly achieving large-scale coherent quantum effects in Bose gases, focusing on a phase-space Fock dynamics rather than a semi-classical one. To explore this possibility, a new quantum hydrodynamic framework is presented that describes interacting Bose gases within a random phase approximation and incorporates a phase-space representation of field operators, thus ensuring the dynamics respects fundamental quantization constraints. By tailoring parameters in the model, researchers can transition from a semi-classical to a phase-space description, and in the latter scenario, they find that a specific non-equilibrium hydrodynamic scenario leads to a crossover from a semi-classical to a genuinely quantum regime, characterized by the formation of quanta and ultimately, a state of soliton species that can persist indefinitely.

Consider a sequence of independent and identically distributed natural numbers, each representing the frequency of a symbol in a given text, where the text itself is drawn from a fixed corpus with a specified structure and contains an increasing number of symbols. The asymptotic behavior of a related stochastic process is examined as the total number of symbol frequencies examined increases without bound. Theoretical evidence for a law of large numbers and a large deviation principle for this process has been presented, incorporating principles from the theory of languages and finite-state machines to model the text's structure. The large deviation principle has been shown to hold in both its rate-functional and rate-compact forms, with the rate-functional associated with the ergodic measure that the process converges to being dependent on this text's structure.

We define a new concept of surface minimization within a specific homotopy class in an extrinsically convex subspace, which we call a surface of minimal homotopic type. Next, we establish that any surface of minimal homotopic type in a homotopy class defined by two distinct points within an intrinsically convex subspace automatically becomes the minimum energy state, which is equivalent to being geodesic. Furthermore, we prove that in an intrinsically convex subspace, surfaces of minimal homotopic type are completely smooth and have no singularities. Additionally, we establish that in a space with curvature zero, surfaces of minimal homotopic type are always surfaces of minimal energy, although they may contain sharp edges rather than just being singularity-free.

Recent studies on the 64Ni nucleus with a low-spin structure have provided significant insights into the role of the monopole component of the isospin-dependent interaction, particularly its impact on nuclear shape and symmetry mixing. Although 64Ni was initially reported to exhibit a deformed ground state, subsequent experiments revealed a prolate ground state and multiple positive-parity excited states with 0+ to 8+ configurations, shaped by the interplay between the monopole component of the isospin-dependent interaction and the neutron N=28 shell closure. By combining experimental information with theoretical predictions from the GDR and SDPF-M3Y interactions, as well as ab initio calculations using the FPD16 force, it has been possible to clarify the origins of the low-spin structure and shape coexistence in 64Ni. The data-analytic approach has been complemented by ab initio predictions from the FPD16 interaction, which have been successfully applied to the 64Ni nucleus for the first time. The results indicate that the combination of the isospin-dependent Wigner force and the N=28 shell closure gives rise to the low-spin structure and shape coexistence in 64Ni, a feature that has also been observed in 42,44,46,48Ca and 54Mg. The role of the monopole component of the isospin-dependent interaction in driving shape coexistence in 64Ni has been further confirmed by the successful application of an effective

Machine learning models, particularly neural networks, suffer from two major challenges during hyperparameter tuning: identifying optimal parameters and stabilizing the results. We argue that a common issue in NLP tasks is exacerbated by the variance introduced by random initialization, outperforming the majority of previous attempts to address hyperparameter tuning variance. To reduce this variance, we propose an alternative to k-fold CV, namely the use of the (J-K) cross-validation method, which separates the data into (J) subsets for parameter estimation and (K) subsets for model evaluation. Our results indicate that the (7-3) CV, which divides the data into 4 equal parts for estimating parameters and 1 part for evaluation, yields consistent and superior performance to the majority of other methods tested, including the k-fold CV, leaving one part for estimation and multiple parts for evaluation. We recommend a simple and efficient strategy to reduce the variance when tuning NLP models, which involves dividing the training data into an odd number of parts (J), with an odd number of parts (K) designated for model evaluation, to minimize the variance introduced by random initialization and facilitate hyperparameter tuning.

Deep neural networks with instructor-added auxiliary structures have been successfully applied in knowledge learning, leading to improved performance and robustness, and have been utilized across various tasks such as classification, detection, and generation. This survey paper reviews the current state of instructor--student architectures, discussing their variations, influential factors, and potential pitfalls. Furthermore, the paper explores the connection between instructor--student models and existing training techniques, identifying areas of application and limitations. With over 90 surveyed papers, this work aims to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding the principles and practices of instructor--student models, and looks towards the future of this field by outlining promising areas of study, such as transfer learning, robustness, and fairness.

We've developed a new efficient algorithm for calculating the exact mode of a graphical model under various constraints and finding the optimal assignment that maximizes a given scoring function while satisfying those constraints. This method leverages a novel concise function representation, termed 'brief functions,' which serve as a pattern matching library for our algorithm's purpose. By exploiting this representation, our algorithm systematically explores the space of possible assignments by using substitution operations on brief functions, which provides a means of tracking valid and scoring functions. As a result, only relevant information is examined and scored functions are explored in a data-driven manner, leading to significant performance enhancements. When compared to existing state-of-the-art algorithms for graphical models, our method exhibits significant improvements in both speed and efficiency, with some instances processed up to 100 times faster.

In a precise measurement involving an ultracold strontium-87 gas, we detected the influence of photon recoil on the absorption of a single laser beam as it moves through the gas cloud. By conducting absorption measurements along the direction of the beam's propagation, we observed its deflection and determined the accuracy of our measurement to be 0.0003 times the natural width of the absorption line. We also investigated the effects of photon recoil on the distribution of the absorption peak and found that it differs from both Boltzmann and Maxwell distributions. Utilizing this system, we were able to demonstrate the application of a recent theoretical prediction, showing that the absorption peak's mean squared width can be used to determine the energy of a two-photon interaction up to ten times more precisely than other methods. We achieved an uncertainty of 2.7 kilohertz in the calculation of the two-photon energy, which is equivalent to an interaction time of one millisecond or an average separation between interacting atoms of 20 micrometers.

For suspensions of non-interactive particles that change viscosity suddenly, 
as seen in shear thickening, the relationship between shear rate and viscosity 
can be described using a single parameter, the stress at which viscosity changes. 
Researchers found that for a specific type of shear thickening, visited in 
both laboratory and real-world conditions, this change in viscosity follows 
a consistent pattern across a vast range of scales, from the size of individual 
grains to the size of large buildings.

Recently, a new algebraic structure called the Racah algebra has been identified and found to be a fundamental component in the centralizer of the quantum group $\mathfrak{U}_q(\mathfrak{b}_2)$ acting on the $n$-fold tensor product of the Hilbert space associated with the standard irreducible representation, effectively giving rise to the algebra $Z_n(\mathfrak{b}_2)$. In the specific case where $q=1$, the Racah algebra simplifies to the form $Z_n(\mathfrfr{sl}_2)$, which is demonstrated to be equivalent to the centralizer of the quantum group $\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ acting on the $n$-fold tensor product of the Hilbert space associated with the standard irreducible representation. Notably, the appearance of the Racah algebra as $Z_n(\mathfr{sl}_2)$ in the case of $q=1$ marks the first recorded instance in literature of this algebra in the context of the centralizer of the quantum group $\mathfrak{U}(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$, which is part of a larger chain of algebras that make up the full Fock space and is obtained via an inductive process. This process involves establishing a Hilbert-Poincar\'e series that serves as a distinguishing characteristic for the $n$th tensor power of the

An area of Web search that has not been extensively studied concerns the effects of search engines' default result displays having more than one page of links, leading users to overlook a substantial number of relevant web pages. This research paper explores this phenomenon by examining how the standard Web search result presentation influences users' interactions with a controlled database of search results. It was discovered that, on average, users tend to examine only a small fraction of all the displayed entries, with many ignoring ninety percent of the available results. It's also found that limiting users to their initial search results page causes them to miss at least a third of all relevant web pages, with this figure being at least twice as high in cases where the number of relevant pages is greater. It's worth noting that these results hold constant when user's initial queries are taken into consideration. It's also discovered that users' behavior can be significantly altered for their benefit by changing the default Web search result display to display all the relevant web pages for a given query. It's recommended that search engines provide an option for users to view a more comprehensive list of search results, with one such proposal being to display up to ten entries per results page, with hyperlinks that allow users to navigate between pages of results with ease.

We're exploring the possibilities of a muon collider with an energy of 2 TeV, capable of delivering two focused beams of muons in both directions, and examining its capabilities in particle physics research. By investing $4 billion in the initial construction and $200 million annually for operations, such a facility could identify new particles and forces, shed light on dark matter, reveal hidden aspects of Higgs physics, and determine whether the Higgs boson holds mass. Notably, this collider could operate in three modes: with two beams moving in the same direction, in opposite directions, and with a beam of muons and an incoming high-energy proton stream. By doing so, it could achieve remarkable accuracy in determining the mass of the Higgs boson and explore scenarios of which it might be a composite of two particles. Furthermore, we outline the theoretical underpinnings of colliding muon streams, discuss potential detectors, and compare it with other proposed facilities.

Fast and accurate four-dimensional (4D) T2-weighted imaging is crucial for clinical applications, particularly for abdominal scans that require low respiratory sampling periods. We present a novel approach using multiple breath-hold images, sorted and reconstructed using advanced techniques such as high-resolution radial ordering and compressed sensing, to create 4D images that are both quick and accurate. We further developed an optimized sequence with free breathing capabilities and comparable image quality to traditional approaches, using quantitative metrics such as SNR, contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR), and uniformity. Inflammatory bowel disease outcomes also showed no significant difference when compared to conventional methods. We evaluated our sequence at multiple speed levels and found that operating at 2.3 x 64-exchange coils and 5 mm body matrix resulted in the best trade-off between image quality and acquisition speed. We applied this sequence to actual patient data, demonstrating its potential for various abdominal scans, including pelvic regions with longer respiratory periods.

Recent advancements in paired-permutation testing on graphs have led to the development of methods that precisely pinpoint the location of statistical differences, offering a visual representation of data contrasts. In contrast to traditional permutation-based techniques, these methods generate accurate predictions by employing two complementary permutation tests that are designed to work in tandem. Our work builds upon this progress by an automatic strategy that leverages automated machine learning to choose the most suitable paired-permutation testing method, coupled with the use of two complementary permutation tests to facilitate precise prediction of data contrasts. We have implemented this method as part of the statistical computing library Raccoon, available under the permissive Apache-2 License. Notably, our method has been successfully applied in the context of the PairedPermutationTesting workshop, held in 2021, as exemplified by figure 1, which illustrates the prediction of contrasts made in the PairedPermutationTesting dataset.
