A comprehensive dataset of freight rates, shipping quantities, new and used container ship prices has been assembled from 1966 to 2009, incorporating two prominent indices: the World Container Shipping Freight Rate Index put together by Tsai, and the Container Shipping Quantity Index constructed from various sources. Initially, a subdataset based on Tsai's formula was used to establish the relationship between freight rates and shipping quantities through multiple linear regression analysis. However, due to concerns about multicollinearity, two alternative methods were explored: ridge regression and principal component regression. When incorporating more recent data and following an examination of freight rate and shipping quantity time series, an attempt was made to model these sequences using an ARIMA process.

We define loom areas for a collection of rays moving at equal angles, which includes the example of Grigoriev's loom related to the Coxeter group. We then establish a connection between loom areas and veering triangulations associated with the rays, and investigate the combinatorial properties of these triangulations. By analyzing 2D loom areas, we can determine the associated combinatorial data and demonstrate that it matches the format specified by Guéris, Rivard, and Thibault. Furthermore, we show that the 2D loom areas that form a rhombus correspond to a specific subclass of Yarmola's triangulations. We also explore loom areas in higher-dimensional spaces, with the result that the associated combinatorial data forms a polyhedron whose faces correspond to the faces of a hyperbolic Coxeter group defined by an array. We prove this result in the context of a particular loom area in three-dimensional space, with the result extending to higher-dimensional spaces, and we conjecture that this result holds for all loom areas in any dimension.

Recently, stock value prediction has been a significant area of interest, with the advent of machine learning models that can forecast future stock prices with a high degree of accuracy. In this paper, a novel ensemble model is presented, combining the strengths of BERT and GAN to predict the daily closing prices of Apple stocks listed on the NASDAQ exchange. By utilizing historical stock price data, the model is trained to accurately forecast the next day's closing price. To evaluate the performance of the proposed model, it is compared with a range of established techniques, including ARIMA, LSTNet, and DCRNN, in a daily prediction task. The results show that the ensemble model yields a lower RMSE of 0.6359 and a higher R2-score of 0.9341 compared to the benchmark methods.

In this work, we investigate the capabilities of future $e^+e^+($TeV)$-$ colliders to detect beyond-Standard Model (BSM) Higgs interactions through double Higgs production in the low-luminosity running period. We consider various BSM Higgs interactions, including lepton couplings, additional scalar particles, and vector boson scalar operators. We examine how well these interactions can be identified at three different energy levels (250 GeV, 300 GeV, and 350 Ge CKM). We concentrate on the low-energy regime, utilizing an Effective Field Theory (EFT) framework. We carry out comprehensive studies of double Higgs production in the $\ZZH$ channel, the most promising signature for Higgs physics at these colliders. We account for beam polarization effects and radiative corrections to jet energies. We find that at 250 GeV, the Higgs resonance becomes inaccessible due to beam-gas background. In the $\ZZH$ channel, we find that at 250 GeV, the EFT Higgs coupling modification limit reaches $\sim 10^{-3}$, while at 300 GeV and 350 GeV it reaches $\sim 0.01$ and $\sim 0.1$ respectively. We also find that at 250 GeV, the double Higgs production cross-section in the $\ZZH$ channel is $\sim 0.1$ fb, while at 300 GeV and 350

We investigate a specific type of gravity theory in (2+1) dimensions, which is characterized by the absence of a covariant second-order differential equation governing its conservation laws. We develop two independent Lagrangian descriptions for this theory and demonstrate that they are equivalent to the standard topologically massive gravity when taking into account the effects of a conformally invariant source of gravity. We also examine the role of Weyl transformation and its impact on the Lagrangian, in addition to providing a reformulation of the TMG action using the Euler density.

We investigated the drag experienced by a long, thin cylindrical object moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and sugar, submerged in a fluid, as it is pushed across the surface or pulled through the depth of the granular bed. 
We found that when the cylinder is pushed across the surface, its drag decreases as it moves in the direction parallel to its long axis, until it eventually becomes independent of axis orientation at high speeds.
Conversely, when it's pulled through the depth, the cylinder experiences anisotropic drag that remains orientation-dependent, even at high speeds.
We also found that the anisotropic drag experienced in the deep pull case is more pronounced in saturated beds than in dry ones, and that its causes vary between different types of granular materials. 
We developed a theoretical model explaining the orientation-dependent drag experienced in the deep pull case, and our data supports this model. 
The anisotropic drag experienced by the cylinder can lead to non-trivial consequences, such as it moving in a curved path or getting stuck in one direction but not the other.

Our transport model, which includes thermal partons in a quark-gluon plasma and hadronic partons in a cascade model, successfully reproduces experimental results from RHIC such as collective flow, elliptical flow, and two-particle correlations. Utilizing our model's capabilities, we investigate triangular flow in both Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions by comparing simulated data to existing STAR results. Our findings show that our transport model can explain observed patterns of $v_3$ in both cases, and that the extracted freeze-out temperatures are nearly identical at ~120MeV. Notably, our analysis indicates that initial state fluctuations play a crucial role in driving elliptical flow in both small and large systems.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has achieved precise measurements in two areas, namely rare decay processes of bottom quarks and the violation of Abraham-Lorentz electrodynamics, by studying $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2s)$ mesons produced in semileptonic $B$-meson decays. These measurements are crucial for understanding whether the Standard Model's (SM) predictions align with experimental data and have been carried out in two separate studies using 2010-2012 integrated luminosity in $pp$ collisions at 7 TeV and 8 TeV energies, corresponding to 4.5 picobarn and 5.5 picobarn of proton-proton collisions. The studies analyzed over 170,000 $B_s \to J/\psi \gamma$ and 240,000 $B_d \to J/\psi \gamma$ rare decay events, as well as over 110,000 $B_s \to \mu^+ \mu^- $ and 80,000 $B_d \to \mu^+ \mu^- $ rare decay events. The measured branching fractions and decay rates were compared with the SM's predicted values and showed that the SM's predictions for $B_s \to \phi \gamma$ and $B_d \to \phi \gamma$ decays require further investigation to establish parameters, and the estimated upper limits for these decays were found to be $

A critical aspect in developing accurate and reliable numerical methods involves preserving key properties of the original differential equation. Researchers such as Abels (2019), Herty, Muntean, and Sprekler (2019), and the editors of Kwak, Kim, and Jung (2020) have achieved this in various partial differential equations, including transport equations, Burgers' equations, and Euler equations, by employing high-order spatial discretizations and explicit time-stepping schemes. However, preserving the properties through implicit time-stepping methods by solving a linear system for each time-step has been less explored, especially in large-scale simulations where such systems are typically solved using iterative Krylov methods. This study provides a theoretical framework to analyze the preservation of the transport form of a stiff system when using Krylov methods, specifically GMRES, based on the underlying matrix vector product, and certain linear transformations associated with the method. It also includes case studies involving the Euler equations and a general transport equation using implicit time-stepping and Krylov methods solving.

In medical procedures involving non-rigid instruments such as laparoscopes, it is crucial to align pre-operatively created markings on the surface of organs with those visible during surgery. A key challenge arises when the organ's non-rigid deformation is not accounted for, leading to misalignment and potentially harming patients. To address this issue, a method is proposed to perform real-time surface alignment, taking into consideration the non-rigid deformation of organs. The approach begins by aligning two volumes, and then a biomechanical model is used to project the displacement field from one volume onto the other, based on a training dataset from a previous surgery. The model is then applied to the changing state of the organ during surgery, as detected through a deformable registration of surface points. The proposed algorithm is tested on real data obtained from a laparoscopic surgery, using a haptic feedback system, and the results show that it is possible to perform accurate alignment of organs during surgery with non-rigid instruments, and a video of the experiment is included in the supplementary materials.

Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Traditional methods for estimating scene flow rely heavily on photographs that depict the same objects in different animated states, often employing direct comparison techniques such as optical flow estimation. In contrast, metric learning approaches attempt to position points in low-dimensional spaces in a way that reflects their distance in the three-dimensional space. Prior self-supervised metric learning methods for estimating scene flow typically utilize points from the same image as reference points, often selecting them randomly or based on proximity to each other. In a significant breakthrough, our research demonstrates that using points that are far from each other as reference points in a self-supervised metric learning approach leads to a more accurate flow estimation, with performance exceeding that of the current state-of-the-art method by a notable margin of 5.3%.

In recent years, AI networks, specifically those based on artificial neural systems, have significantly outperformed competitors in a wide range of tasks including image recognition, sound analysis, and language interpretation. However, the growth in size and complexity of these models has created new difficulties in their use in small-scale, energy-constrained devices. Another critical issue with these models, as with any linear least-squares algorithms, is the need for precise matrix operations, which can lead to notable errors in results when performed on matrices with even the slightest deviations from ideal form. Our research aims to address both of these problems and demonstrate how a specific type of neuromorphic technology, known as Random Neural Networks, can accurately classify data while minimizing the necessity for precise matrix operations and keeping the size of the network to a minimum.

Within the framework of the MIT bag model, we investigated the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars under the influence of a strong magnetic field and finite temperature. The distribution of quark densities and electrical charge distribution were determined by numerical solutions to the spin-polarized Strange Quark Matter Equation of State for various temperatures and magnetic fields. We found that in the case of a relativistic degenerate quark gas, the causality condition is satisfied independently of the strength of the magnetic field and temperature. Furthermore, we derived specific formulas for the radius and mass of spin-polarized strange quark stars in the limit where the temperature is negligible compared to the chemical potential. We also determined the maximum mass and radius of static spin-polarized strange quark stars, and found that they are independent of the temperature but dependent on the strong interaction bag constant and the strange quark mass. Notably, the effect of the magnetic field on the radius and mass is negligible when the radius of the star is compared to the magnetic Compton wavelength.

Every perfect matching in a graph can be paired with an edge from its complement, except for possibly one edge, which is part of a Hamiltonian cycle. This fact was initially observed by Haggkvist, Juhnke, Schiermeyer and Warendorf, who used it to develop a 2-factorisation approach for certain types of cubic graphs. This paper delves deeper into the concept by which a pair of disjoint 2-factorisations can be combined to produce a Hamiltonian decomposition, and explores its implications for reducing a Hamiltonian decomposition to edge-colourings. Along the way, it establishes a relationship between the number of factors in a 2-factorisation and the minimum number of colours required in an edge-colouring, which can also be applied to more general types of graphs. Ultimately, this leads to a determination of the minimum number of edge-colourings needed to replicate a Hamiltonian decomposition in a specific class of cubic graphs, which includes a recently-discovered family of Grötzsch lines, as well as another class of cubic graphs constructed using the'switching' technique.

This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for managing system calls in containerized applications. System call policies in containers are typically managed manually by developers, through explicit mount commands to limit system access. However, this approach is often cumbersome, especially for complex, stateful applications with many system calls. In response to these challenges, Timeloops automatically learns system call policies for these containers. It achieves this by inspecting system calls made by applications during a setup period, then enforces the resulting policy throughout the remainder of the program execution. For simple, stateless microservices, existing solutions like Google's gVisor already provide convenient system call policies. But for more intricate applications, Timeloops offers a solution by learning policies in a short period, without requiring source code or extensive modifications. In tests conducted on various containerized applications, Timeloops demonstrated the effectiveness of its approach by successfully learning system call policies for six out of eight tested applications, and failed only because of two denied system call attempts by the other two applications.

Recently, a consensus was reached that incorporating an origin model in probability multi-target assignment with measurement partitioning matching (PMBM) filters leads to better performance, but the most effective method of implementing this model remains unknown. This study investigates two grid-based variants of the origin model, one of which is specifically tailored to better match the PMBM framework, and designates one of these variants as the standard approach for further analysis. In the course of examining both variants, a rule was established to determine when the standard approach should be used, thereby leading to a hybrid method. Furthermore, the study explores the hybrid method's performance in a target tracking scenario with sensor management, and compares it to a standard PMBM filter.

This study examines the internal null controllability of a population dynamics model that includes a degenerate diffusion component and a birth-death process component, as well as a logistic growth component. The model's structure, which includes the degenerate diffusion component and the logistic growth component, is used to establish the global existence and uniqueness of solutions for the associated complete boundary value problem when the control is applied to part of the boundary. The existence of a unique solution to the corresponding adjoint state equation is also established. The study then investigates the internal null controllability of the model by showing that there exists a control that drives the population to zero in a weak sense for a given time period, assuming the population can be controlled to zero in the weak sense for a sufficiently long time period without the degenerate diffusion component. The study also explores the relationship between the model's internal null controllability and the population's decay when the population can be controlled to zero in the weak sense for a sufficiently long time period without the degenerate diffusion component. The study further examines the internal null controllability of a related model with the Neumann boundary condition at the price of restricting the domain to the right-hand side and investigate the asymptotic behavior of the population dynamics model without the degenerate diffusion component.

In soccer, players' decisions become increasingly critical in game-deciding moments, especially when they have opportunities to score or prevent opponents from doing so. To improve these situations, we're exploring the realm of AI, specifically deep reinforcement learning, to create a decision-making framework that can elevate players' choices on the field. We've designed an action selection process using two separate components: one for identifying the best action based on the current game state, and another for adjusting this choice when the referee's call is unexpected, such as awarding a penalty to the opposing team during a counterattack. To test and refine this approach, we've used a simulated environment and applied it to real games, achieving promising results and demonstrating improvements over conventional methods of play.

Crosswell imaging techniques, specifically F-K and F-KI methods, have been widely used to analyze seismic data. However, these methods have limitations when dealing with data that has significant surface wave contamination. A time-domain ESD method was previously proposed to address this issue by considering the evolution of seismic sources over time. Although this method has been successfully applied to real data, its stability and accuracy have been compromised due to its initial design without preconditioning. This paper presents an improved time-domain ESD method that enhances the accuracy of migration images while maintaining the advantages of the original method. The improved algorithm was tested using synthetic data and showed its ability to produce high-quality images with reduced surface wave contamination. Furthermore, this paper discusses an efficient implementation of the time-domain ESD method using multi-threading and SIMD technology.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetric random walk was employed as the mechanism of species dispersal. Two versions of the model were examined: one with a competition-dispersal tradeoff, where more competitive species have poorer dispersal skills, and one without, where the dispersal skill is uniformly distributed among species. In both cases, the dynamics were simulated in a one-dimensional torus with periodic boundary conditions and found to result in either species exclusion or coexistence. The study showed that in the presence of the competition-dispersal tradeoff, the conditions under selection and strong dispersal lead to species coexistence are more stringent, making the model more likely to exhibit species exclusion. Notably, the presence of noise also leads to species coexistence, as it promotes the advection of species towards the other end of the torus, where the conditions are more favorable, even in the absence of the competition-dispersal tradeoff. The study of the noisy model with the competition-dispersal tradeoff found that in the limit as the torus size increases, the model behaves like a piecewise smooth map that exhibits chaos, resulting in the mixing of species and their disappearance from the torus. The study of the model without the competition-dispersal tradeoff found that in the limit as the torus size increases, the model behaves like a piecewise smooth map that includes a quadratic inflection point, leading to the mixing of species and their disappearance from the tor

Recent advancements in integrated data and energy networking technologies have provided new insights, offering a flexible, self-sustaining, and energy-efficient way to operate mobile devices. A key aspect of this development is the presence of D2D communication links, which can facilitate both data and energy transfer between devices. However, managing these connections and transferring energy and data between them is a complex task, especially considering the need for a secure and reliable link, the varying distances between devices, and the limitations of device power transfer capabilities. In this work, a surface-aided integrated data and energy transfer network is proposed, in which a surface node assists in transferring data and energy between devices and helps manage the connections by providing a clear path graph. This surface-aided model allows for the development of an efficient and robust D2D power transfer and communication protocol, based on dual execution time, distance, and power transfer capabilities. By mathematically modelling this protocol as a stochastic optimization problem and utilizing tools from large deviations theory, this work also shows that the protocol can be designed to meet performance requirements under random changes, the worst-case scenario, and can be further optimized to reduce the impact of changes on performance. The validity of these results is shown in simulations conducted with randomly generated scenarios.

The single-point LDV measurement technique is highly effective for determining mean flow characteristics but lacks the capability to conduct 2D turbulence measurements on its own. The lack of a second measurement point is attributed to the inherent need to take cross-correlations between two signals, which are spatially separated by a distance equal to the beam diameter. This limitation can be circumvented by employing a phase-shifting LDV system that measures the phase shift of the signal, allowing for the calculation of the correlation value. As a result, single-point LDV systems can perform 2D measurements even at distant points, without the need for any physical modification. This study presents the results of 2D turbulence measurements conducted using a single-point LDV system at a distant point of 0.2 meters, and compares the calculated 2D Reynolds stress components with those obtained from 1D measurements taken at the same location. The findings indicate that the 2D Reynolds stress components obtained from the single-point LDV system at the distant point are identical to those calculated from the 1D measurements, thus confirming the effectiveness of this system in performing 2D measurements even at considerable distances.

The effectiveness of an aberration-correcting lens in a Transmission Electron Microscope (TEM) is contingent upon the type of electron beam characteristics being analyzed. While it excels with low-density beams, its performance suffers when dealing with high-density beams, limiting its utility in certain studies, particularly with over-integrated biological specimens and programmable phase plates, which rely on beam densities to function. Recent research indicates that a programmable phase plate can correct higher beam densities than previously thought, and studies on biological specimens and an X-ray free electron laser have shown promising results. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that a specific type of programmable phase plate can achieve comparable results to an aberration-correcting lens in electron microscopy, specifically in retrieving high-resolution information from high-density beams, by correcting the electron microscope's spherical aberration when dealing with beam densities of up to 10 times the previously reported values.

We provide detailed analyses of the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a combination of the Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We examine both the conservative and dissipative aspects of this equation, and in the process, we establish bounds on the nonlinear term's strength required for spectral stability. Furthermore, we investigate the orbital stability near a solitary wave, including both scenarios with and without dissipation. Additionally, we offer empirical guidelines for the conditions under which solitary waves emerge and are physically stable based on numerical data.

Let $\Omega$ be a non-commutative algebraic closure of $\mathbb{Q}$ in the algebra $\mathrm{GL}_n(\mathbb{Q}_\tau)$, where $\tau$ is a valuation on $\mathbb{Q}$, whose maximal compact subfield is $\mathbb{Z}_\tau$ for all valuations $\tau$ in a finite set $\Sigma$. Assume that $\Omega$ has a property allowing for the application of a certain theorem from the paper of the first named author and T. Rivoal. Let $K$ be a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}$ with Galois group $\mathrm{G}_K$ and let $\mathrm{H}_K$ be the closed subgroup of $\mathrm{G}_K$ consisting of automorphisms that fix $\Omega$ and extend to $\Omega_K$. Then the theorem stating that any $\sigma \in \mathrm{H}_K$ can be written as $\sigma = \omega_\sigma \mathrm{g}_\sigma^{-1}$, where $\omega_\sigma \in \mathrm{G}_{K,\mathrm{abs}}(\Omega)$ and $\mathrm{g}_\sigma \in \mathrm{G}_{K,\mathrm{abs}}(\mathbb{A}_\Sigma^{\mathrm{f}})$ with archimedean places contained in $\Sigma$, provides a generalization of a theorem by W. Scholl and K. Rubin

To explore the parameter space of a specific scenario where axion-like particles interact with the standard model through a dipole interaction, an analysis of the decays of $B$ mesons is performed, specifically focusing on the process $B \to K \gamma$. To achieve this, a study of the decay modes $B \to K \gamma$ and $B \to K \ell^+\ell^- ($where $\ell$ represents either $e$ or $\mu$\) is necessary. An existing search for $B \to K \ell^+\ell^- ($with $\ell$ representing either $e$ or $\mu$ already provides constraints on this parameter space, particularly for the combination of the dipole moments $(e/\text{GeV})^2$ and $m^2 ($in units of $\text{eV}^2$), especially for the case where $\ell = e$ or $\mu$. To further investigate this scenario, a proposed experiment at the Belle II facility, with the potential to discover $B \to K \ell^+\ell^- ($with $\ell$ representing either $e$ or $\mu$ or place more precise constraints on it, would significantly contribute to the understanding of this scenario by either confirming the existence of $B \to K \ell^+\ell^- ($with $\ell$ representing either $e$ or $\mu$ or establishing a more precise lower limit on its production rate.

Detecting semantic alterations in text is a significant challenge that affects the reliability of information and causes user confusion, potentially leading to safety issues in critical applications. To address this challenge, it is essential to develop highly accurate methods to identify altered text, which, to our knowledge, has not been achieved using machine learning techniques in previous studies. In this work, we assemble a large dataset consisting of pairs of original and altered text, which we utilize to experiment with various features and machine learning models to enhance detection accuracy. Our findings indicate that using a combination of linguistic and semantic features, coupled with a support vector machine (SVM) model, yields the best results among the approaches we examined. Although this method achieves a relatively high F-score of 87%, which indicates a certain level of success, it falls short of meeting the requirements of critical applications. Our analysis highlights the difficulties of detecting semantic alterations and the need for future work to focus on collecting more homogeneous datasets and exploring the use of contextualized language models to improve performance.

Any heavy object rotating rapidly must eventually lose momentum through gravitational radiation, and in the presence of a surrounding dark matter halo, this process can be accelerated by the phenomenon of Kerr-effect, leading to the stabilization of the object's spin. This process can also facilitate the formation of particles with mass, such as axions, via a process known as superradiance, where particles are extracted from the dark matter halo through the object's spin, and this process can also provide a statistical explanation for the absence of certain rotating objects with high spins. By accounting for this process, we can establish an upper limit on the properties of particles with mass that could have been extracted, and in this study, we have calculated these limits for particles with minimal mass interacting with dark matter halos surrounding the rotating objects, and we have also considered the possibility that the objects with high spins are actually composed of particles with mass that have been stably settled in their spin, in which case we have calculated the parameters of these objects, and we have tested our hypotheses using a sample of the most spinning heavy objects in the universe, which have been identified as either massive compact objects or neutron stars with massive compact objects being denoted by the suffix "mc". These objects exhibit varying degrees of spin, and we have analyzed the characteristics of the particles with mass that could have been extracted from their spin, which has allowed us to differentiate between the parameters of the objects with high spins that are composed of axions or other particles with mass,

During brain development, interkinetic nuclear migration refers to the lateral movement of cell nuclei between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue, resulting in the formation of distinct neuronal layers. To investigate the underlying mechanisms of interkinetic nuclear migration, researchers have examined its dynamics using confocal and two-photon time-lapse microscopy in live zebrafish retinas. Our high-resolution imaging data reveal that the random, three-dimensional movements of cell nuclei can be accurately described by a diffusive model, with the direction of movement reversing upon the completion of a nuclear migration cycle. Notably, our findings also indicate that interkinetic nuclear migration occurs at a constant rate in all retinal regions, suggesting a shared mechanism of migration across the retina. Our analysis of nuclear migration patterns in a two-dimensional retinal cupola provides a possible explanation for the formation of curved neuronal layers often observed in the brain. Our study's high-resolution imaging data and mathematical analysis of interkinetic nuclear migration are made publicly available through an interactive website.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, coded acquisition presents both challenges and opportunities. While it simplifies data collection, it complicates reconstruction, requiring additional constraints such as codes and limited color information in image compressed sensing. This paper is focused on coded video recovery, a more specific and related problem. A particular coded aperture structure, called the spatially encoded mask, is explored and an algorithm called codes-free is developed to enhance standard sparse representation-based methods like compressive sensing and dictionary learning. This algorithm can be used with any reconstruction algorithm but is specifically useful when the coded aperture is spatially correlated with the signal, as is often the case with compressed video. Experimental results on both synthetic and real-world data demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm, showing it outperforms standard reconstruction methods using accurate coded aperture estimation, and results with estimated coded aperture obtain similar performance with a factor of ten decrease in SAR in compressed video recovery.

Polar active liquids at equilibrium, characterized by directional particle motion and minimizing curvature, can be challenging to achieve stability in, as the influence of randomness and friction can cause the polarity to break, leading to a vortex phase. A comprehensive study using dynamic renormalization group uncovers the effects of disorder and dimensionality on the phase diagram of this class of systems, revealing that increasing dimensions greater than two and decreasing the rate of particle movement can both lead to a polar phase and the systems' resilience to disorder can be quantified using new criteria.

The growth of artificial intelligence has necessitated the use of data for
training machine learning models, data sharing, and research purposes. The
increase in electronic devices and cloud storage has facilitated the easy
exchange of data. One area that has seen significant progress is document
scanning, which has become an alternative method for sharing and storing
documents. The extraction of information from ID cards has traditionally been
done manually, but with the advent of optical character recognition, this
process can be automated. This project aims to extract the contents of an
Indonesian ID card, known as a KTP, using optical character recognition followed
by natural language processing, which was tested using 50 ID cards with an
accuracy of 87.5%.

Quantum mechanics is characterized by the probability distribution of a system's state, which is described by the square of the magnitude of the wave function. Within the context of harmonic oscillators, a driving force affects the phase space in a sinusoidal manner, leading to a complex Hamiltonian that results in a calculationally manageable Hamiltonian when transformed into a quorum representation. This transformation yields a Gaussian distribution of the quorum variables, facilitating the application of Monte Carlo methods to determine expectation values and the wave function's phase space. A force-driven harmonic oscillator exhibits both coherent and cat state properties, which can be both theoretically and experimentally recognized. As such, this study provides explicit directions for conducting Monte Carlo studies of the time-dependent driven damped harmonic oscillator using a path integral approach.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque that results in a change in rotational velocity, depending on the surface properties and orbital characteristics. By analyzing light curves and orbital data, we determined the rotation rates of three asteroids: 1992 SK (15.84 hours), Geographos (7.46 hours), and Toro (9.97 hours). Calculating the YORP effect for these asteroids over time has made it possible to model their rotational evolution. Based on observed rotation periods and assuming the YORP effect remains constant, we calculated the YORP values as follows: 1992 SK (1.53 deg/century), Geographos (3.23 deg/century), and Toro (1.83 deg/century). Notably, the YORP effect causes the rotation rate of 1992 SK to increase, whereas it decreases for Geographos and Toro. This distinction can be attributed to the YORP's sign, which depends on the ecliptic longitude of the asteroid's perihelion, varying over time and influencing the net torque exerted on the asteroid.
We show that every countable collection of homeomorphisms of a closed surface is not compact with respect to the uniform topology when it is equipped with the Roelcke metric.

In this work, a key advancement is achieved in the field of computable rational expressions. To expand the scope of rational expressions to include over 50 years of research in theoretical computer science, a significant challenge must be met: ensuring that the right Thue system for a given regular language can be determined using an effective algorithm. Until now, it has been widely believed that this challenge cannot be met, thanks to a recent counterexample from the field of formal language theory, which also originated from an earlier result related to Post's problem. To address the challenge at hand, a connection is established between the right Thue systems and a particular form of rational expressions known as monadic rational expressions, for which an established theorem provides a solution to the challenge. To demonstrate the applicability of this result in the context of the Rabin-Scott 1978 problem, additional modifications to the reread algorithm from the same researchers are presented, which enables the direct determination of the right Thue systems for a class of recognizers, specifically those with a specific property, known as the left property. To achieve this, a transformation is applied to the original Thue system, followed by a straightforward application of the reread algorithm, which results in the desired right Thue systems. To illustrate the solution to the Rabin-Scott 1978 problem, a step-by-step example is provided, which includes the original Thue system and the application of the reread algorithm, as well as a comparison

Recent advances in nonlinear dynamics reveal that complex systems with identical components and symmetric connections can exhibit remarkably intricate behavior, characterized by multiple stable states with distinct patterns and connections. We have conducted a comprehensive mathematical and numerical analysis of a nonlinear equation that represents a paradigm of these complex systems. Specifically, we investigated a network of identically coupled identically behaving neurons, all connected in the same manner, and with the same type of connection between the state of the system and external driving forces. Our numerical exploration uncovered a vast array of multistable behaviors in these systems, revealing that, depending on the system's parameters, it can exhibit either a single stable state, multiple stable states with distinct patterns, or patterns connected in a loop. Our goal is to apply this understanding to explain a recently observed phenomenon in a model of the human brain, where multiple attractors with varying patterns and connections were discovered in the brains of individuals with schizophrenia, as well as in simulations of the human brain, where all components of the brain are connected and interact with each other, based on data from functional magnetic resonance imaging.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and cost, a second-order Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) equation has been proposed for use in dynamic programming. However, due to the challenge of efficiently solving the high-dimensional HJI equation, this approach has limitations for large problems. This paper presents a second-order Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation written in a Eulerian formulation and solves the corresponding two-person variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation numerically using a sampling-based method. A control barrier function can be obtained from the solution of this equation, which can be used to prevent a system from entering an unsafe set. This approach has been tested on a simple aircraft and a more complex drone, and the results show that this method can handle large problems and is more efficient than the Eulerian method based on the Hamiltonian-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) equation.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, with some research suggesting it is a linear hierarchy reflecting creature classification, while others propose a more complex structure influenced by factors such as evolutionary history, taxonomic relationships, and cultural perceptions. In an attempt to clarify this, we conducted two experiments using a technique called repeated measures animacy classification, which allows for the analysis of data based on individual subjects' patterns of activity without requiring group data aggregation. We found that at a local level, within the ventral temporal cortex, a linear divide exists, but this does not necessarily validate a straightforward hierarchy when the big picture is considered. Rather, our results show that this approach can avoid conferring an unjustified status of significance on an assumed hierarchy, instead revealing a more nuanced structure that is unique to each individual studied. We also explored the applicability of this method to other brain regions and found that it can be used generally, and our data and analysis code are available online for further examination and interpretation.

The concept of unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at the prime factorization 2*4 is proven to hold efficiently, with no instance of which occurs, and it's also shown that this implies the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros.

We have developed a program logic with quantum relational Hoare predicates to facilitate proofs about programs with quantum operations, relying on a concept we call the "quantum dialect." We have demonstrated the effectiveness of this program logic by using it to formally prove the correctness of two quantum program verifiers: the QProp verifier used in the training regime for Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum computers and the Jazz verifier for quantum integer addition. Additionally, we have established that the "quantum dialect" holds true for these programs.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases can be significantly accelerated by a single highly contagious individual, known as a super-spreader, whose infection rate is exponentially increased for a limited period, either due to a specific event or an individual characteristic. We have examined the effects of super-spreader events in epidemic models and have found that they can lead to the exponential growth of an epidemic, potentially even causing an epidemic to become pandemic if not controlled. The severity of the outcome is influenced by factors including the time period during which the super-spreader's transmission rate is elevated, the rate itself, and the implemented control measures. We have also identified the transmission rate threshold below which an epidemic will die out, even with a super-spreader event. The study's results can be applied to various epidemic scenarios, such as influenza, SARS, MERS, and COVID-19.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the set of bounded linear operators acting on X, referred to as B(X). This paper seeks to explore unique properties related to the operator norm, specifically the behavior of a specific class of functions, called the Nishimori class, which exhibit remarkable symmetry. As part of our analysis, we will derive an important inequality, demonstrate the existence of a circle of operators that satisfy a specific curvature condition, and also investigate the task of minimizing the curvature subject to constraints defined by a set of operators, all while navigating the intricacies of the Nishimori class.

Recent studies suggest a potential bias in RMCDI inferred magnetic field values, specifically with underestimation of weak field components, which could be related to data calibration and has implications for using this method in inferential statistics. Variations in this bias have been observed with different values of noise levels in input data and need to be considered when applying this technique, especially its second-order properties. Two approaches have been explored to reduce this bias, either by adjusting the calibration of RMCDI or the regularisation parameters, and both methods have been found to be effective in reducing the bias, although more research is needed to fully understand its causes and suitable application constraints.

A sign issue in Monte Carlo methods for complex actions has been a persistent challenge, hindering simulations of certain types of many-electron systems at finite temperatures. Our study introduces a complex-valued neural network to project augmented complex actions onto a suitable equivalent form, enabling temperature-dependent simulations of any many-electron system while minimizing the sign issue. Utilizing this setup, we successfully conducted thermal and zero-temperature simulations of the Hubbard model using both exact diagonalization and the continuous time quantum Monte Carlo method. Our results demonstrate that the complex neural network effectively mitigates the sign issue, even in systems with large lattice sizes, and that it can be trained to minimize the impact of the sign issue at both temperatures, and to reduce the basis size in the auxiliary field approach.

Given any non-erasing free monoid homomorphism f, we find that the composition of the map taking the complexity of a word to its image under f, paired with the map that converts a word's complexity to its associated topological entropy, is subadditive when applied to the set of words with a given length. Additionally, when the homomorphism is non-decreasing with respect to the lexical order, this combined map is additive for words of a particular length, and in the case of the free group F_n, a similar result holds for a subset of words with lengths that avoid a specific pattern.

By leveraging previously gained skills and adapting them to unfamiliar domains without additional guidance is a common challenge across various fields of study and real-world applications. This process is referred to as cross-domain generalization. This research focuses on exploring unsupervised cross-domain generalization in the context of conversational AI, specifically within dialogues generated without direct supervision. A key challenge in this area is the lack of a well-defined performance metric to assess cross-domain generalization. To address this challenge, we propose a method to evaluate cross-domain generalization by drawing on both the diversity and representation of generated responses. A major obstacle in this field is the limited availability of high-quality reference datasets to serve as comparison standards for evaluating generated responses. To address this issue, we propose utilizing positive references retrieved from unconditioned conversational data as a comparison benchmark. Furthermore, we propose an unsupervised retrieval-enhanced method to facilitate cross-domain generalization by leveraging the capabilities already developed in specific domains. This method involves conducting a comparison between generated responses and reference dialogues and employs a contrastive learning approach to update the conversational model. We validated this model on two datasets, namely ConvAI2-2020 and TOPICLINK, and the results showed that it is capable of adapting to new domains through cross-domain generalization.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private training of deep learning models is a challenging task due to the need to collect large amounts of private data. This challenge is compounded by the limited number of data typically used for hyperparameter tuning, making it difficult to generalize to the private training setting. In this work, a novel approach is proposed to streamline the process of hyperparameter optimization for the SGD algorithm in the presence of differential privacy. The method in question involves conducting a limited amount of data-driven hyperparameter optimization prior to private training, with the resulting parameters serving as a starting point for further optimization in the private training process. Theoretical guarantees are provided to ensure that this approach yields hyperparameters that satisfy the privacy and accuracy requirements for the private training of deep learning models. Experimental results are presented, demonstrating the efficacy of this approach for the private training of deep learning models on various datasets.

Every permutation that fixes 1 can be expressed as either an even number of transpositions or, alternatively, a product of cycles whose lengths are even numbers, except for one exception where the remaining cycle has a length of 1. This exception is represented by the cycle (1) and can be thought of as a sine or cosine function, specifically where it cycles through 1, a value in the set {0, 2}, or the set {0, 2, 1} when considered under the permutation 12, or the permutation 123 respectively. The study then delves into analyzing the group generated by these basic cycles, examining the relationship with the Coxeter group and determining under what conditions it forms a subgroup. The investigation also covers the scenario where the permutations in question can act on a Boolean algebra, in such an investigation that dates back to a study from 1977 by G. Grubbs.

We applied two independent methods to model the abundance patterns of stars in the Milky Way disk, using data from APOGEE.  Both techniques, which analyzed chemodynamic models of the galaxy's evolution and plateaus in abundance gradients, yielded highly consistent results.  We identified four distinct populations of stars, with similar characteristics:  ancient metal-poor stars, metal-poor stars with recent formation, metal-rich stars with recent formation, and metal-rich stars with long formation histories.  We found that the chemical abundance of elements like carbon, nitrogen, and aluminum can vary significantly within certain populations of stars, even after accounting for factors like age, metallicity, and mass.  These variations may indicate the effects of various processes, such as mass transfer from binary companions, nuclear burning in stellar cores, or element synthesis from supernova explosions.  We also developed a two-parameter equation to describe the abundance patterns of stars in the galaxy, and used it to estimate the contributions of different elements to the formation of the galaxy's disk.  We found that elements like oxygen, silicon, and iron are primarily produced through the explosion of intermediate-mass stars, while elements like carbon, nitrogen, and aluminum are mainly produced through the explosion of massive stars, with some also being synthesized in the galaxy's core.

The rapid dissemination of online rumors during crises poses a significant threat to public safety, health, and infrastructure, among other things. Research on online rumor dynamics typically uses simple models, but there's a lack of consideration for the diverse paths of spread and the variable influences of different factors. This study develops a novel method to examine the spread of online rumors through analysis of search engine trends and social media data, incorporating a influence measurement that accounts for the varied paths of dissemination. By applying this method to online rumors that circulated in China during the initial phase of the COVID-19 pandemic, researchers gained a deeper understanding of the sources, transmission routes, critical periods, and factors contributing to the dissemination of these rumors. The study's findings highlight the role of medical misinformation in the early stages of the pandemic, as well as the significant impact of government responses, public fear, and medical developments on the spread of online rumors.

A new catalog of 1166PN candidates has been created from observations of the Fornax cluster of galaxies, obtained through VLT/MUSE spectroscopy and photometry from the HST, HST+ACS, and VLT/TrOSIS data.  This catalog includes PN morphological classifications for 1346PN features observed in 7 galaxies within the cluster.  An analysis of the luminosity function for the PN populations in 3 spiral galaxies revealed average luminosity weights of 1.32, 1.29, and 1.35, with a PN abundance ratio of 1.01 for all 3 galaxies.  An independent method for calculating the distance to the galaxies in the cluster yielded a mean distance of 18.75 megaparsecs, with a standard error of 0.16 megaparsecs.  This is in agreement with previous estimates based on the surface brightness fluctuations method and the population calibration method.  The accuracy of this new method was tested by calculating the distance to the galaxy NGC 4594 and was found to be 9.67 megaparsecs, with a standard error of 0.24 megaparsecs.  The cluster galaxies were found to be moving away from each other at speeds of up to 80 kilometers per second, with the central galaxies of the cluster moving away from the outer galaxies at the greatest rate.

In network research, periodic streams are common, representing recurring network data patterns, and flow processing applications within these streams are widespread, including scenarios in protocol processing, traffic analysis, and statistical monitoring, among others. Due to the temporal repetition of data in periodic streams, previously developed match-and-select flow processing approaches can be highly effective, and many flow processing applications share similar repeating patterns of operations, such as regular expressions, tree matching, and sorting, that can be efficiently executed on periodic streams with limited memory. To address the needs of periodic streams and flow processing, we present a new flow processing engine called LifeStream that combines match-and-select with periodic stream processing capabilities and provides a structured and reusable program representation to facilitate rapid execution, caching, and reuse of results. In evaluating LifeStream on real-world datasets, it outperforms other flow processing engines by 3 times and achieves near-optimal performance on challenging IP lookup benchmarks, showcasing its effectiveness in tackling complex network applications with minimal overhead.

We investigate a type of curve, called timelike Bertrand curves, in a semi-metric space, and this work aims to explore their key characteristics, presenting both necessary and sufficient conditions for a curve to be considered timelike Bertrand in a semi-metric space. We begin by outlining the fundamental principles and preliminary findings related to these curves in a general context, followed by a specific examination of Bertrand curves within the confines of a semi-metric space. We also establish a connection between these curves and a particular operator, and in the case of a Euclidean space, we recover previously established conditions for a curve to be classified as Bertrand. Furthermore, we provide a clear and concise formula that defines the direction of these curves in a semi-metric space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network can significantly influence its performance, and selecting an optimal loss function is crucial for achieving superior results in classification tasks. Despite its importance, current automated machine learning tools often overlook the possibility of adjusting the default loss function, instead focusing on optimizing other variables such as learning rate, regularisation techniques and hyperparameters associated with dropout. This study investigates the potential benefits and drawbacks of experimenting with different loss functions in order to improve the accuracy of a neural network, and explores the connection between loss functions and the underlying characteristics of data. It also becomes clear that selecting an appropriate loss function can be an important aspect of understanding and representing the characteristics of data, and as such, should be considered an integral component of automated machine learning tools.

This research aims to simulate the mechanical and thermal effects of crystallization in polymer materials using a computational model. When polymer liquids are deformed, crystallization can occur, leading to microstructural changes and subsequent mechanical properties. However, this process also causes heat generation, affecting the temperature and further influencing the crystallization. A coupled thermomechanical model is proposed, incorporating the Arrhenius method to describe temperature dependence and an equation predicting microstructure changes based on deformation rates and temperature. Verification of the model is achieved by comparing simulated results with experimental data on temperature and microstructure, and further applications are demonstrated in a coupled analysis of a drop impact experiment.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the external magnetic field in both nematic and chiral scenarios. Moreover, the orientation of the superconducting order parameter relative to the external magnetic field was found to exhibit non-trivial behavior in both cases. A notable result from this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter's orientation is aligned with the external magnetic field in both nematic and chiral scenarios when the external magnetic field is applied within the $ab$ plane, resulting in a planar distribution of the superconducting order parameter's orientation. In contrast, when the external magnetic field is applied perpendicular to the $ab$ plane, the superconducting order parameter's orientation is angled with respect to the external magnetic field in both nematic and chiral scenarios, leading to an oval-shaped distribution of the superconducting order parameter's orientation. In addition to this analysis, we also investigated the interplay between spin-triplet nematic superconductivity and ferromagnetism in the presence of tetragonal crystal field, which leads to an onset of an oval-shaped distribution of the superconducting order parameter's

Continuous phase modulation offers superior performance over binary modulation formats due to its resistance to carrier frequency errors and phase rotations. Nonetheless, its resistance to phase errors has a disadvantageous impact on its tolerance to symbol timing errors, particularly in scenarios with significant jitter, common in optical communication systems. This restriction applies to differential detection methods, particularly those employing N-dimensional phase-shift keying, which experience a significant decline in performance when timing errors are substantial. This paper focuses on a particular differential detection scheme, namely conventional non-coherent differential detection CPM, and presents an in-depth analysis of its performance in the presence of both carrier frequency errors and timing errors. By conducting an accurate bound-based analysis and simulation results for 4-ary CPM, the paper identifies areas where further improvement can be made to enhance its performance under delay constraints.

Consider a quantum field in a $1+1$ dimensional spacetime with a massless scalar field, expressed in terms of the Weyl semicircle ensemble. The focus is on the positivity of the metric tensor $g_{\mu\nu}$ in the Lorentzian sector of a specific spacetime configuration, known as the "Lorentzian wedge." A crucial aspect of this analysis involves the comparison of the Lorentzian wedge with alternative spacetime metrics derived from specific non-equilibrium sources, including a step function temperature distribution, a moving heat bath, and a moving mirror. The aim of this research is to establish a minimum temperature threshold below which the Lorentzian wedge becomes the most stable spacetime geometry in both local and asymptotic regions. Notably, it was discovered that the Lorentzian wedge outcompetes all other metrics in the asymptotic region at a critical coupling constant of $\gamma_c=1/2$, whereas in the local region, it was found that there is a lower bound of $\gamma_{loc}\simeq0.92$ required for the Lorentzian wedge to prevail over all other metrics. The results obtained in this study can be applied to the theory of linearized gravitational waves. The research into the Lorentzian wedge also yields an estimation of the number of DOF associated with massless scalar fields, which is found to be in the range of $s\approx0.25$ to

Our research focuses on exploring a specific aspect of reasoning where if-then statements are used to convey causal relationships. We've developed a comprehensive atlas that maps these connections in a dataset called ATOMIC, which comprises over 150,000 sentences connecting entities within a given text and external knowledge. We've also created a vast knowledge base with over 300,000 entity relationships derived from ATOMIC and external sources, which we've utilized to construct over 300,000 if-then statements for our machine intelligence to learn from. By leveraging this knowledge, our models have achieved superior performance in tasks like reasoning within the atlas, as well as on the GLUE benchmark. We believe this atlas and the underlying technology can serve as a platform for developing more sophisticated reasoning systems, capable of handling the kind of causal relationships presented in ATOMIC, and we invite the public to explore and learn from it.

Quantum linear algebra methods, such as HHL, hold significant potential to overcome the computational challenges of numerous applications by exploiting vast amounts of sparse data efficiently. However, the practical implementation of HHL is hindered by the need to perform large number of matrix multiplications that result in extremely dense outputs, which cannot be efficiently handled on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum hardware due to limitations in available memory. Our solution addresses this challenge by introducing the concept of "Quantum Portfolio Optimization", a novel application of quantum linear algebra that can be used to efficiently handle the dense outputs of HHL. We demonstrate this concept by modifying the HHL algorithm to solve a complex energy minimization problem, a key component of electronic structure calculations, which results in a significant reduction of quantum memory requirements from 128 qubits to 16 qubits as well as a notable improvement in the execution fidelity. Our findings also highlight the significance of carefully selecting the parameters of the HHL algorithm, specifically the pre-amplication and post-amplication multipliers, in order to achieve a balance between computation and memory demands.

To further enhance the performance of multi-modal training for better speech recognition, we've developed and tested two novel methods: (1) a technique called "interchangeable teacher and student" where the roles of teacher and student models are switched between the text and speech inputs, and (2) a "bidirectional focus" method that allows for both forward and backward attention within the encoder. We've incorporated these techniques into a multi-modal training setup where the models are trained to pay attention to either the text or speech inputs, and the results show significant performance gains of up to 8.15% in WER.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, asymptotically behave like $1$ through $k_n$ in the random metric $\rho_n$, where $\rho_n(i,j) = |\pi_n(i) - \pi_n(j)|$. The rate at which the first positions asymptotically behave this way can be any value greater than $\frac{1}{2}$ and is capable of being less than 1, as it depends on the parameter $\lambda$ derived from the generating function of uniform parking distributions, provided that $\lambda>1$. When $\lambda=1$, we find that the first positions behave this way at rate $\frac{3}{2}$; when $\lambda>1$, the rate is equal to $\frac{\lambda^2+3}{2\lambda}$, as a result of analyzing the combinatorial properties of parking distributions.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly niobium nitride, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction, below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate over Joule heating, thus hindering superconducting state restoration.  By examining the behavior of individual quantum phase slips in nanowires with varying lengths, it became apparent that a particular gate voltage could either facilitate the occurrence of quantum phase slips or shift them to higher voltages, with the effect being length-dependent.  It was discovered that in longer nanowires, a gate-induced potential can either lead to the saturation of quantum phase slips at high conduction voltages or result in the formation of a quantum well, with energies aligned to the threshold of dc conduction.  In contrast, in shorter nanowires, the presence of quantum phase slips was found to be suppressed at high conduction voltages, with the formation of a quantum well dominating the behavior.  It was also observed that in the shortest nanowires, there was a transition from the heated state to coherent quantum phase slips at certain gate voltages, with the transition being related to the nanowire's capacitance and temperature, with the specific values being equivalent to those for which the behavior of single-electron quantum tunneling was previously established.

We've observed significant progress in video prediction, yet a key challenge remains: creating accurate predictions for new views. In this paper, we assemble a dataset with a diverse range of viewing angles and focus on the "new view" video prediction task. We introduce a novel dual-representation framework, featuring two parallel pathways that process spatial information differently. One pathway, based on non-local self-attention, and the other, based on latent space manipulation via variational autoencoders. We leverage a novel perspective on view representation as a latent transformation, which enables our model to generate new views by transforming a base representation. We demonstrate substantial gains in PSNR and SSIM scores on our newly assembled dataset, as well as comparable performance on the widely used YouTube-BB video prediction dataset.

In a recent study, inter-level coupling in a Landau level system was theoretically proved to occur, and it was shown that it results in non-zero Berry curvature and a van Hove singularity in the Chern dispersive, which could give rise to inter- Landau level mixing and the appearance of new inter- Landau level mixed character in the 0th Landau level. All of these features have been experimentally confirmed using spectroscopic measurements conducted on graphene within near-resonant laser illumination.

An exhaustive analysis of spectroscopic properties for $\Omega$ baryons was performed by applying a relativistic quark-diquark model. Calculations took into account the interactions between quarks and their intrinsic properties, and were based on the assumption that the interactions remain unchanged since they primarily result from the electromagnetic interaction. A full exploration of possible quantum states was achieved by employing a Hamiltonian with no upper bounds, and resulted in predicted energy levels that match experimental data, with particular emphasis placed on the relative signs of quark masses and their impact on momentum components. A notable finding emerged during this analysis, where the assumed relationship between quark masses and the energy levels of $\Omega$ baryons was found to be inconsistent with momentum components, and could only be reconciled when the mass difference between u and d quarks was considered as negligible in relation to the mass of the strange quark. A simple and predictable pattern of energy levels was observed and could potentially be verified through future experiments, and a comparison was also drawn with an alternative model where the energy levels of $\Omega$ baryons were explained using non-relativistic quark models.

A key factor in the spread of airborne pathogens is the mixing of individuals within closed environments, and understanding the severity of this impact can be crucial in assessing risks during daily activities, such as using public transportation. Previous studies have examined the effects of varying airflow patterns on the spread of disease in buses, but a well-established model assumes that air is evenly mixed, which we tested and validated by simulating the movement of a single cough cloud within a bus using an unsteady Eulerian model, and it produced results similar to the well-mixed model when including the recirculation of exhaled breath. By applying this model to an urban bus with a ventilation system, we obtained transmission probabilities for a range of distances between an infected individual and nearby passengers, and these probabilities can be used as inputs for compartment models of disease transmission.

Recent studies have focused on magnetic interfaces in spin-orbit coupling (SOC) materials, revealing unique SOC-related phenomena, and have promising applications in SOC-based devices. However, the lack of clear data on the precise nature of interface coupling hinders the development of SOC-based technologies. In this work, we investigated a bilayer made of bismuth strontium candiate (BSC) and cobalt (Co) and determined the long-range spin polarization of Co, which is influenced by the BSC's strong SOC. It was discovered that in BSC/Co bilayers, the spin polarization of Co exhibits a decay length of approximately 0.6 nanometers, and it is oriented both in and out of the plane, depending on the BSC's chemical composition. Furthermore, we found that BSC with a high carrier concentration exhibits enhanced spin polarization of Co due to increased spin accumulation caused by the drag effect. Our findings demonstrate that Co in multilayer structures can exhibit long-range spin polarization influenced by the chemical composition of the BSC interface, and it is expected that this phenomenon will be useful in the design of SOC-based devices utilizing Co.

This paper provides the fundamental framework for the fractional Schrödinger equation within the context of a specific potential "generalized Mie-type potential" in $N$-dimensional space. Theoretical solutions to the energy eigenvalue problem can be achieved using the fractional Schrödinger equation, and it's possible to define the fractional derivative using three different approaches, although the Jumarie type approach will be utilized in this study. By applying this approach, we transform the fractional Schrödinger equation into a solvable form and then obtain expressions for the wave function and energy levels. The paper also compares the results with those obtained using the Riemann-Liouville type approach. The generalized Mie-type potential can be seen as a combination of the fractional inverse square potential and the fractional oscillator potential. The paper provides an exhaustive analysis of the energy levels for this potential, which includes the fractional inverse square potential, the fractional oscillator potential, the Mie-type potential, and the Hulthen potential as special cases. The paper also provides numerical data on the energy levels for the fractional inverse square potential, the fractional oscillator potential, the Mie-type potential, and the Hulthen potential as special cases. The results obtained in this study can be compared with previous works that employed the Riemann-Liouville type approach and other fractionalization methods. The paper also discusses the relationship between the dimensions of the space and the energy levels of the generalized Mie-type potential. The

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. By applying this method to multiple normal distribution datasets, we found that a regularized neural network training procedure, achieved through an innovative technique using the upper bound of the Lipschitz constant, leads to optimal performance when the norm used in training matches the underlying distribution's generating norm. We also observed that this method performs comparably to current techniques when the underlying distribution is normally distributed, but results in a significant performance drop when the underlying distribution is not normally distributed. We attribute this performance decline to overfitting caused by the stringent conditions enforced by the regularized training procedure. We further investigated the effects of the training procedure's stringency on model performance and found that reducing the regularized training procedure's intensity leads to improved performance. We also explored the application of this technique to the task of adversarial training and discovered that it can be used to enhance the robustness of neural networks at a minimal performance cost.

We investigate the production of diboson pairs in the decay of vector leptoquark models at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), specifically with third-generation fermion couplings. This study focuses on the production of W boson pairs, W and Z boson pairs, and Z boson pairs in proton-proton collisions. The analysis utilizes the accurate Next-to-Leading Order (NLO) QCD calculations in combination with Leading Order (LO) parton distribution functions, based on the implementation in the Virtual-Amplitude-Expansion (VVA) framework, which provides a precise description of the collision process. By comparing our results to existing NLO QCD predictions, we demonstrate the significance of non-abelian gauge boson coupling corrections, which can reach as much as 12%. Furthermore, we analyze the contributions of different leptoquark form factors and fermion charges, as well as the impact of NLO QCD corrections on diboson-pair production at the LHC with 13 and 8 TeV center-of-mass energies.

Low-dose CT can be safely replaced with conventional CT due to low residual radiation, but CT-to-PET translation models may experience difficulties when there's a significant discrepancy between training and testing data, including out-of-distribution data, such as extremely low-dose PET. To address this challenge, we present a novel uncertainty-aware multimodal learning framework that incorporates the effects of physics-based noise in training, which results in the development of robust and low-dose PET image reconstruction capabilities, as shown in our research. Utilizing a noise model that simulates Poisson noise and Gibbs sampling, we developed a training process called "stretching," which causes the uncertainty of the model to increase in step with noise levels. As a result, the model becomes capable of reconstructing images at noise levels as high as six times the initial level. According to our experimental data, this framework can successfully reduce PET doses by up to 85x without a drop in image quality, as measured by PSNR, SSIM, and radiologist-assisted clinical scoring. Moreover, the framework generalizes effectively to out-of-distribution data, including low-dose PET images at levels as low as 1.67 MBq per liter, which is considered extremely low.

Recently, significant advancements have been made in coreference resolution through the application of deep learning techniques, however the underlying principles behind these achievements remain poorly understood. In an attempt to shed light on this, an analysis of existing coreference resolution systems was conducted, focusing on their ability to adhere to well-established linguistic principles, specifically centering theory. The study examined six prominent entry in the Coreference Resolution Task: DUC2000, which evaluated systems in accordance with centering theory. The results showed that although current systems excel in numerical scores, they struggle with qualitative assessments based on centering theory. In particular, they fail to meet two crucial conditions: they allow for coreference chains that are not centered (13.6%) and permit unconnected chains (45.6%). In addition, an investigation was made of systems that incorporate syntactic information in an attempt to gain insight into the role of tree structure in relation to coreference chains. The findings revealed a diverse set of associations between the two, with some systems that used syntactic trees incorrectly, leading to worse performance. In an attempt to improve the performance of systems in accordance with centering theory, an simple approach was proposed, involving the selection of chains that are centered, this was applied to the BART system, and resulted in a 0.5 F score improvement, and a 0.3 difference in exact match, when evaluated on the DUC2000 dataset.

Recently, WiFi sensing has become a popular technique for estimating distances, 
object detection and tracking, and other location-aware applications. As a result, 
researchers and developers are showing significant interest in this area, and the 
amount of available data is increasing rapidly. To take advantage of this trend, 
researchers presented a method for training a model to predict distances using WiFi 
signal strength, based on a dataset that includes both measured data and, in this 
case, a small set of training samples and a larger set of estimation samples. The 
algorithm was tested using two datasets, and the results showed that it is capable 
of accurately estimating distances, even in environments with complex structures, 
and that it is more effective than a comparison algorithm, especially when it is 
trained on a small dataset. The code for this project has been made available on 
GitHub.

The beam breakup instability is a critical issue that affects the design of particle accelerators and can lead to a limitation in achieving high beam currents, ultimately constraining achievable effects in experiments, such as probing scattering lengths. Research has been focused on the dynamics of beam interaction and potential design improvements to mitigate the impact of beam breakup instability. A major finding from previous studies established the link between beam line design and the regenerative beam breakup instability, highlighting the significance of identifying the longest straight section in energy recovery linacs to determine the beam breakup wavelength and associated instability threshold. However, an in-depth examination of beam interaction dynamics revealed that the relationship is not universally applicable, as it is influenced by filling patterns and can result in beam breakup wavelengths that do not align with the longest straight section in designs featuring multiple straight sections of varying lengths.
