A theoretical framework has been developed to study beam interaction dynamics and provides the basis for a numerical model used to simulate interactions and predict beam breakup wavelengths in various energy recovery linac designs. A key outcome from this analysis is the guidance that filling patterns can either match or differ from the longest straight section, with specific examples including designs where the beam breakup wavelength matches the longest straight section (e.g., an LERI design with a filling pattern of 2.16 meters) or differs from it (e.g., an IRIS design with a filling pattern of 1.5 meters).

Using the BFKT formalism, we expanded the one-loop amplitude for two gluons in N=4 SYM theory, expressing it through a set of elementary building blocks - two gluon central-emission vertices and a pair of gluon "mermaid" diagrams with two collinear gluons. We calculated the one-loop amplitude in two different approaches: directly from the one-loop amplitude and by reconstructing it from the pre-defined building blocks. We found that the one-loop amplitude for two gluons in N=4 SYM theory equals one half the sum of the square of the color-ordered two-gluon amplitude and the reconstructed amplitude from the pair of "mermaid" diagrams. We also validated our results by analyzing the one-loop amplitude for two gluons in N=4 SYM theory in the limit of large rapidity separation, where it equals one half the sum of the square of the BES one-loop amplitude.

Theories explaining the behavior of stretched polymer brushes have provided valuable insights into the properties of these surfaces and have been applied in various contexts, including biomimetic, biological, and technological fields. Full and partial exclusion zones surrounding grafted polymers have been extensively examined in cylindrical and spherical arrangements, with the latter including annealed and quenched versions of surface chains. In this study, we have developed a computational model to simulate strong, molten polymer brushes in variously shaped arrangements and have confirmed that the property of excluded volume applies universally, with exact thresholds for different shapes confirmed as follows: with regards to the width of the excluded zone in cylindrical arrangements, it is necessary that the degree of stretching exceed 3.2, in spherical arrangements a value of 6 is required, and values of 4.5, 5, and 6.5 are necessary for triangular, square, and pentagonal arrangements respectively.

A recent superstructure, called the "trimmed metric dimension", was introduced in a previous work, building on the foundation of the metric dimension. This parameter counts the minimum number required to determine all distances in a graph. In the process of exploring trimmed variants, we discovered connections to existing metrics and established bounds for this new measure. Specifically, we found that the trimmed version is equal to half the circumference of a graph, when the circumference is even, and we also showed it can be either the ceiling of half the circumference or the circumference itself, if the circumference is odd. Furthermore, we found that the trimmed dimension of a graph is greater than or equal to its metric dimension, and in the process of proving this, we established an upper bound for the trimmed dimension in terms of vertex cover, which is in turn related to other measures of a graph's complexity.

Researchers have applied machine learning techniques to analyze all-sky maps of gamma radiation using the Fermi-LAT telescope. By utilizing random forests, an enhanced map of the variable sky has been created by identifying sources and removing transient ones. This method's effectiveness was tested by applying it to data from 3 year observations of the blazar Mrk 501, which are correlated with contemporaneous UV and X-ray data from the Telescop e Ground Imager and the X-ray Telescope. The results show that the machine learning analysis can accurately forecast the variability of Mrk 501 based on the FSRQ characteristics of the blazar and account for variations in the gamma radiation detected by the Fermi-LAT telescope. It also reveals that the spectrum of the variable radiation remains consistent with the power-law distribution of the blazar.

In the context of scheduling tasks for monarchies, where tasks can be executed by any member and their execution affects the selection of the next leader, we define two types of monarchical structures: those in which the future leaders are known from the beginning (fixed) and those in which the future leaders are not known until the actual leader is chosen (dynamic). We have established the mathematical frameworks for both fixed and dynamic monarchies and have optimized various objectives for these structures. For the case of task execution times being distinct and the goal of minimizing the latest finish time, we have shown that the monarchical structure in which the future leaders are known is more efficient than those in which the future leaders are not known until the actual leader is chosen. On the other hand, for the case of task execution times being identical and the goal of scheduling to minimize the latest finish time, we have an instance in which the monarchical structure in which the future leaders are not known until the actual leader is chosen can result in a much better latest finish time compared to those in which the future leaders are known. We have also explored the relationship between monarchical structures and other scheduling problems and have the instance in which the future leaders being known is equivalent to the case of scheduling jobs on two identical machines.

We searched archival images from the Pan-STARRS1 survey to locate binary asteroid candidates by employing a technique called "astrometric photometry". This method involves analyzing images for a specific object in multiple colors, with a particular technique called "image subtraction", to pinpoint objects that have varied significantly across different images of the same object taken in different bands. We used a statistical tool called "Keldysh's criterion" to determine the most suitable band combinations that would yield the positions of binary asteroids with the greatest orbital separation, and employed a computer program to analyze the positions of binary asteroids in the $x$ and $y$ directions by applying the parameters of their elliptical orbits. We developed an algorithm to identify the most reliable binary asteroid candidates based on their orbital characteristics and astrometric measurements, and carried out thorough searches for binary asteroids in three different ways, covering the entire survey, as well as specific regions around bright asteroids with small orbital periods and within the inner solar system. We ended up analyzing 103,600 images from the survey, and identified 245 binary asteroid candidates with a projected separation of at least 1000 km, with an estimated accuracy of 90%. We also found that the most frequent binary asteroid candidates occur in the asteroid families (340, 10, and 15), with an estimated frequency of 13% on the asteroid (145) Pepita, and an estimated frequency of 25% on the asteroid (704) ACADemia.

This research focuses on modeling and estimating a partially linear regression where a variable from a network enters the model in a linear fashion, while controlling for endogeneity. It also explores the possibility of incorporating network peer effects into the model. It is essential to note that identifying this model requires specific conditions, namely that the network variable enters the model in a way that does not depend on the error term, and that the regression function for the variable of primary interest is strictly decreasing or increasing. It is also crucial to note that even with these conditions met, the model still cannot be identified using only a single cross-sectional dataset. However, we provide parametric and semi-parametric estimation methods for the parameters of interest, as well as their standard errors. It is also possible to test the significance of the network peer effects and to estimate the distribution of the influence weights. Notably, we apply this model to estimate the effects of network influences on the adoption of a treatment, as well as to investigate issues related to endogeneity and selection into a network. Additionally, we find that the model accurately accounts for the structure of the network, provided that the network is sufficiently dense.

This research paper derives novel versions of Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. By applying these derived formulas, we can express the application of the Variable-Order fractional derivative to a function that has been subjected to the Variable-Order fractional integral in terms of the initial and end points of the variable beta. Similarly, we can also obtain modified versions of Taylor's series expansion and the Euler-Lagrange fractional variational principle using these rules.

We've developed a novel approach to guiding players in conversational role-playing games through a theory-of-mind-inspired framework, combining the Intention Dynamics model to capture intentions and a GPT-3 encoder to represent game states. In a controlled environment using transcripts from actual Dungeons and Dragons games, we've shown that our approach can: (1) accurately identify player intentions by 83%, (2) effectively predict subsequent player actions with a 1.4x increase in likelihood, (3) demonstrate improved player engagement by 12%, (2) generate coherent and engaging story elements as judged by a 20% improvement in a crowd-sourced evaluation, and (3) apply to both beginner and experienced players with a 21% difference in evaluation score. By learning to classify intents and a theory-of-mind components in Dungeons and Dragons, our model has also generalizable applications in other domains that rely on intent and mental state prediction, such as customer service chatbots.

Recently developed topological models can distinguish twisted protein structures based on knot types, and now a study has shown that the geometry of knotted proteins can be used to identify selected bending paths along which protein chains are transformed from one twisted structure to another, without changing the knot type. This approach has been applied to examine the possible transformation paths for 144 knotted proteins with specific types of twists, including protein structures that have a trefoil knot and a twist that cannot be easily unfolded, as well as those with a figure-eight knot and a specific type of twisted structure. Notably, the study found that only a small number of possible bending paths are selected and preferred over others, and these preferred paths tend to involve the same type of twisted structure, suggesting that the preferred paths may be influenced by the geometry of the protein structure. Additionally, the study found that the preferred paths for a trefoil knot are more complex than those for a figure-eight knot, and also found that only a small number of preferred paths are used by different knotted proteins, implying that the same bending path may be used by multiple protein structures, and this idea is supported by the fact that preferred paths are more similar to each other than the protein structures themselves, and this is especially evident when comparing the preferred paths used by different types of twisted structures, and also when comparing the preferred paths to random protein structures, and further analysis has shown that the preferred paths may be influenced by the charge distribution and other characteristics of the protein structure,

Let $\omega$ be a symplectic form on the real vector space $V$.  The symplectic mapping category group associated with $\omega$, denoted as $\Gamma_{\omega}(V)$, consists of the set of equipped with a category structure, and its underlying component is defined as the group generated by smooth mappings from $V$ to itself, where the group operation is given by a certain kind of composition of mappings.  This paper investigates the structure of $\Gamma_{\omega}(V)$ when $V$ is given as the blowup of a torus with one dimension, and it also includes a discussion on how $\Gamma_{\omega}(V)$ behaves under a change of coordinates.

A modified Nambu-Goldstone theorem holds in both relativistic and nonrelativistic systems with spontaneous symmetry breaking, where the assumption of a symmetry group being represented by an abstract algebra is dropped. Instead, a relationship between the number of massless Nambu-Goldstone bosons and the dimensionality of the symmetry group's Lie algebra, as well as the reality of the matrix of the symmetry group's generators squared, is established. In the nonrelativistic limit, this version of the theorem can be applied to both Lorentz-invariant and Lorentz-breaking systems. A consistent Faddeev-Skhoderean quantization can be achieved when these conditions are met. A discussion on the Wess-Zumino term and the $\theta$-angle parameterization also arises from the context of this theorem's derivation.

Our proposed method, Discriminative Counterfactual Semantics Explorer (DISCO), leverages the capabilities of large-scale language models to accurately differentiate actual language patterns from counterfactual ones by learning from classification tasks. We employ a binary classification framework to train a model that distinguishes between genuine and altered phrasal distributions. The resulting model effectively captures the underlying semantics of language, including probabilities associated with counterfactual distributions. We demonstrate DISCO's effectiveness by utilizing trained models to extract essential information from counterfactual distributions, which leads to a 9.5% improvement in our primary evaluation metric compared to a strong baseline.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene has shown promising results, enabling the growth of high-quality films without a direct interface, which can be crucial for reducing defects and improving device performance. However, the exact mechanisms governing epitaxial relationships on graphene remain poorly understood, largely being attributed to the interplay between graphene and a substrate interface. Our study on the epitaxial growth of GdAgHeusler films on graphene/sapphire investigated the effects of deposition temperature, film thickness, and substrate misorientation on epitaxial relationships. We observed a transition from a 30-degree rotated superstructure related to surface roughening to films grown through van der Waals interaction on graphene, which can be controlled by deposition temperature and film thickness. Our findings are supported by computational modeling highlighting the significance of surface interactions and local curvature of the graphene sheet in determining epitaxial relationships. Our work demonstrates the potential for precise control over epitaxial relationships through film preparation and highlights the importance of considering surface and interface physics when designing remote epitaxial growth processes.

A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the dimension of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes as well as the determination of their kernel, thereby providing a clearer understanding of these codes and facilitating the development of error-correcting decoding algorithms for the $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes and their gray images.

Multi-label classification poses the challenge of identifying not one, but several relevant labels for a given data point. It is often difficult to obtain and manage a dataset with correctly assigned multiple labels for each example, especially when collecting annotated data is already a labor-intensive process. In this work, we explore the idea that many instances labeled with a single positive class actually represent multi-label relationships. Therefore, we propose a method to extract the likely associated labels for each instance, effectively converting single-label annotations into a multi-label framework. The proposed technique leverages an existing organized structure, such as a pre-existing hierarchical or co-occurrence graph, to guide the prediction task. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on several datasets, including those with a natural, hierarchical structure, by comparing it to existing methods and a simple baseline technique. The resulting algorithm is efficient, easy to implement, and can be used to enhance the performance of existing multi-label classification models by incorporating a second layer of learning.

The GNS construction links the category of observables in a C*-algebra to the category of Hilbert spaces and linear operators, through a correspondence that involves states. We show that when this connection is refined to a 2-categorical level, it forms a coherent structure that includes the Weyl algebra as the underlying object for a specific 2-isomorphism, resulting from the composition of the inverse of the GNS representation and the canonical inclusion into the C*-algebra of linear operators. We also establish that when the underlying state is symmetric, this 2-categorical structure can be naturally extended to the compact operators, and demonstrate that in this case, the 2-categorical connection corresponds to the standard Frobeneius algebra structure.

The origin of gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting extremely high energy gamma-rays remains a mystery.  Two leading explanations for this phenomenon are the collapse of massive stars and the dissolution of nearby star clusters.  However, studies have shown that many of these galaxies have young stars that are not part of any galaxy cluster, which could be contributing gamma-rays through their magnetic fields.  A new theoretical model suggests that gamma-rays could be produced when fast-moving cosmic particles collide with magnetic fields surrounding young stars in galaxies.  This model has been applied to three galaxies and shows that gamma-rays could be explained by this mechanism, with certain conditions such as the presence of a specific molecular gas component being key factors in its success.  Furthermore, this model can also be used to determine the number of young stars in these galaxies, which in the case of the three studied galaxies are found to be in the hundreds, and are capable of producing gamma-rays even after millions of years, provided they are located in areas with low magnetic restrictions.

Early detection of heart conditions such as cardiomyopathies can be critical in preventing sudden death, but current methods that rely on electrocardiograms may not always get it right. Doctors often listen to heart sounds with the help of a stethoscope to make these diagnoses, but this method too has its limitations, and an automated solution could greatly improve outcomes. To this end, researchers have been exploring ways to analyze heart sounds using various signal processing techniques, but with poor signal quality, as is often the case, it can be very difficult to accurately identify certain sounds, even for the most advanced machines. To reflect this, scientists have been using computational models that simulate the kinds of noise and distortion encountered when recording heart sounds, and in this study, the researchers added a new level of complexity to these models by making them more realistic, and then used these enhanced models to train a machine learning algorithm to accurately classify heart sounds with the kinds of noise and distortion encountered in clinical settings. And in a significant breakthrough, the study shows that it is possible to improve the accuracy of these machine learning algorithms not just by collecting more heart sound data, but also by improving the quality of the recording equipment, and that is a key finding with important implications for the design of better stethoscopes and recording systems.

The proliferation of wearable devices and machine learning-based health monitoring has generated vast amounts of data, leading to opportunities and challenges. With data localized on the devices, there's no direct way to perform centralised machine learning, and models trained on one day may become obsolete within a few days. To address these issues, a novel Federated Transfer Learning framework, FedHealth, is proposed for enhancing the accuracy of machine learning models on wearable devices. FedHealth collaboratively trains models between devices while considering their distinct data sources, allows for temporal updates using new sensor readings, and leverages knowledge transfer to accommodate changes in models and data. To demonstrate the efficacy of FedHealth, an application is developed for predicting users' physical and mental health status. Experimental evaluations of FedHealth on real-world datasets reveal its superiority over existing methods.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations. An important connection between two renowned methods, Genetic Algorithm and Utility Theory, was discovered, demonstrating how Utility Theory can be viewed as a particular case of a multi-objective optimization using Genetic Algorithm. An existing study's results showing that utility functions with polynomial structures can mimic the effects of additional moment inclusion was also leveraged to provide further insights into the relationship between these methods.

The growing complexity of software systems necessitates the automation of critical tasks in software development and maintenance. The community at large, including end-users, application users, and programmers, interacts with these systems through command-line interfaces, graphical user interfaces, or API calls, extracting information and reconfiguring systems in response to data updates, system changes, and new requirements.
However, writing and maintaining software automation scripts can be time-consuming and difficult, with potential side effects like broken links, outdated data, and faulty functionality.
This work explores the possibilities of fully or partially automating various aspects of software systems, without the need for access to source code, using simple and efficient matching logic.
The approach is demonstrated through a specific application, namely the automation of SAP software, with the potential for generalization to other systems and scenarios.

This study focuses on a complex control problem where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly. Our goal is to explore how these abrupt changes affect the optimal control strategy, particularly when the state dynamics involve delays. Our main achievement is to demonstrate the existence of an optimal policy that involves switching times, not just times of change in the costs, when the state dynamics are smooth and there are no obstacles. Additionally, we provide a characterization of the value function, especially when there are no delays. Furthermore, when the state dynamics involve obstacles, we show that the value function is the minimum of the values obtained when the state is on either side of the obstacle, with the costs on the two sides being able to change suddenly. When the state dynamics involve sudden changes and not smooth transitions, we provide an alternative characterization of the value function.

Even leptoquark production can be identified through events featuring same-sign or opposite-sign dileptons, depending on the quark charge. In contrast, odd leptoquark production always results in same-sign dileptons. Even leptoquark production can be either even or odd, whereas odd leptoquark production is consistently odd. Even leptoquark production can be either scalar or vector, whereas the vector leptoquark production is always odd. In the standard model, even and odd leptoquark production rates are examined, along with the impact of even and odd leptoquark couplings on production rates. Even and odd leptoquark production rates in QCD can be expressed using even and odd leptoquark coupling factors. These factors can be used to examine even and odd leptoquark production rates in the high-energy limit. Even and odd leptoquark production rates in the LHC were examined using the ATLAS and CMS detectors. We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies from the HERA Galaxies Survey with line widths available for two fine structure lines of atomic carbon, C I at 492, 809 GHz, which were matched in frequency and angular size to data from ATLAS3D, GASRINGS, and PHIBS observations, with line widths being compared to gas temperature estimates derived from various C I line ratios, with results indicating that gas temperatures are generally lower than line widths, with an average difference of about 1 sigma, with variations influenced by galaxy properties including stellar mass, star formation rate, and luminosity, with no noticeable effect from gas line widths, with implications for the significance of a phenomenon observed in this study, in which line widths are found to be greater than the thermal velocity dispersion in about 20% of the sample, with possible explanations including the presence of a warm outflow component, with potential utility in identifying such features and with further research needed to fully understand the results and with the study conducted using a simple model with assumptions including that the line widths are symmetrical with no net velocity shift.

In the sequence reconstruction issue, it is assumed that a random subset of strings from a given set is created using a specific distance metric, and the task is to determine the original set of strings. This problem has been studied under the Hamming distance in previous research, but only for the context of binary strings. The sequence reconstruction issue can also be applied to permutations, but in the binary context of the Hamming distance, it requires additional conditions such as the number of strings in the subset exceeding half of the total permutations divided by two to the power of the distance limit. The issue of reconstructing sequences has been addressed for the Hamming distance in previous research, but only for the context of binary permutations. A new approach has been found to solve the sequence reconstruction issue for non-binary permutations using the Hamming distance without the need for extra conditions. The required number of strings in the subset that can be used to determine the original set of strings has been established as (d+2)(d+1)/2, where the distance limit is denoted by d. The sequence reconstruction issue for the Hamming distance can be difficult to solve in some cases, and such difficulties can be avoided by using a more powerful distance metric. The sequence reconstruction issue has applications in fields like statistics, mathematics, and biology. Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries of which there are expected to be thousands within PTA observation range. These binaries move in elliptical orbits, emitting gravitational waves at specific frequencies related to their orbital period and eccentricity, and will eventually merge, emitting a persistent chirp signal similar to that of a binary neutron star or binary black hole. By analyzing the combinations of orbital frequency harmonics, researchers can identify the motion of the binaries and recover their parameters with an approach recently developed. A new method is introduced for creating PTA data streams from individual detectors by analyzing the effects of these binaries on Earth-based PTA observations. This involves calculating the time delays experienced by gravitational waves as they travel through Earth and are affected by its mass distribution and gravitational delay maps. A new code, called $GWD$\_\{TA}\_, is also introduced which efficiently generates PTA data streams and is an improvement on existing approaches. By testing this code and previous versions, it became clear that existing codes faced significant computational limitations and were not accurate enough for current PTA data. In contrast, $GWD$\_{TA}\_ is capable of handling a much larger number of binaries and is more than 100 times more efficient than previous codes while being accurate to the level of post-Newtonian parameters for PTA observations. We establish a connection between the Asymptotic Extended Partially Intercaped Exchange (ASEP) velocity process and the current observations in the Asymptotic Extended Partially Intercaped Exchange (ASEP) model. By utilizing a natural change of measure, we apply moment method techniques to show that the ASEP velocity process is asymptotically equivalent to a natural discrete velocity process, whose validity can be proven more directly. When the ASEP model includes non-negative weight assignments on the lattice sites, we demonstrate that the resulting process converges to a continuous velocity process with specific characteristics.

Mathematical models have consistently provided critical insights for public health officials during the current COVID-19 pandemic, offering valuable data for evaluating policy effectiveness and predicting epidemic trajectories. We have carried out an extensive review of key models, including ordinary differential equations, individual-based simulations, and hybrid approaches, which have been applied to various aspects of the pandemic, such as vaccine distribution and mask-wearing policies, hotel quarantine measures, and holiday travel impacts. Our analysis highlights the strengths and limitations of each model and simulation tool, along with the methods used to tackle challenges and uncertainties, such as estimating key parameters and accounting for global connections. We also examine the role of collaboration and open communication between modellers, and the public release of data and models, which has facilitated the development of accurate and effective models. We conclude by discussing the key lessons learned from modeling the pandemic, along with the remaining challenges and future research directions, such as incorporating individual responses into models and developing predictive tools for identifying and mitigating potential surges in transmission.

We have theoretically examined the possibility of converting spinless atoms into molecules using a specific arrangement of laser beams, which would result in atom-molecule conversion through a recombination process involving three particles. This process is certain to occur when a specific combination of two particle interactions takes place, which take the form of a collision between two spinless atoms and one "polarized" atom or an interaction between a molecule and two "polarized" atoms. Notably, this proposal can be applied to convert spinless Bose-Fermi atom pairs into molecules, which is particularly relevant for systems of spinless Bose gases, as any molecules formed through other processes would likely have a different parity than the original atoms, leading to instability. This proposed method allows for the formation of molecules through a controlled process that occurs at a slow rate, which could result in the breakdown of molecule-atom pairs into smaller units, effectively transferring spin, as well as transferring parity, through photon-matter interactions. This could potentially lead to the transfer of angular momentum in various forms, which could be observed in both theoretical and experimental studies.

Recently, DNA storage has gained interest for securing and long-term data storage due to the inherent properties of DNA, such as durability, heritability of data and superior resistance to cyber attacks compared to conventional storage methods. Prior studies have focused on developing methods for encoding and decoding data in DNA, while more advanced capabilities such as managing complex data structures and updating stored information have not been explored. In this research, we develop an innovative method for efficiently creating a hierarchy of data that can be stored in DNA, including support for tree-based data structures and we demonstrate its effectiveness by storing a hash table in DNA. Furthermore, we have also designed a protocol for updating stored information in DNA, which can be accomplished via a decoding and re-encoding process of the stored data. As a proof of concept, we successfully stored multiple types of data in DNA, including a hash table consisting of 16,000 entries, reaching a storage density of 0.02 base megabytes for every megabyte of information.

Precise and efficient flood risk management depends heavily on having access to a swift and dependable method for computing discharge values in rivers and streams. Presently, solutions based on the shallow water equations, particularly the 2D version, are used for this purpose, but they have limitations when it comes to speed due to their complex nature. This paper introduces a novel method for solving the 2D shallow water equations, characterized by a deconvolutional neural network that provides discharge values near existing water levels, but it lacks a traditional solver. To validate the model, results from the Kaskadia flood event and the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami were used as input, and the discharge values obtained from the solver were found to be accurate when compared to measured values from river gauges.

Recent smartphone cameras have gained the ability to shoot in high-dynamic-range (HDR) format, yet there's limited research on HDR image processing for continuous shooting, a common smartphone photography technique. In continuous shooting, an HDR photograph is created by combining multiple photos taken at varying exposure levels, but there's no clear guidance on how to set the optimal number of included images and their corresponding exposure levels. This research proposes a straightforward method to determine the ideal number of images and their optimal exposure levels for HDR combination and presents a simple HDR image processing system using exposure estimation and image fusion techniques. The proposed method has been tested using a smartphone capable of shooting in HDR format and the results show that this method can effectively reduce HDR image processing time while producing higher-quality images compared to existing techniques.

Causal deep learning is a recent approach that aims to make deep learning more robust by incorporating causal assumptions into the learning process. This method has been shown to improve the performance and generalizability of deep learning models, and has been applied to various tasks including regression, classification, and missing data recovery. However, the field of causal deep learning is still relatively young and has a limited number of studies related to it, particularly in regards to its potential pitfalls and limitations. In an effort to advance the field, we investigate three critical issues related to causal deep learning: when it is unnecessary, when it is misleading, and when it fails to converge. We provide a mathematical framework for studying these issues, and offer a number of theoretical and empirical results related to them. Our research also leads to the development of new algorithms and the discovery of hidden conditions for convergence in existing methods of causal deep learning. We hope that our work will contribute to a better understanding of the potential risks of causal deep learning and will pave the way for the development of more effective and general strategies of model learning.

In 2004, Mironov and the paper's co-author established the relationship between certain topological properties of a manifold being divisible by a certain number, and the ability to construct specific types of maps from that manifold to another manifold with certain characteristics. This connection was expressed through the application of a specific mathematical principle, known as the b-principle, which has been consistently demonstrated to be crucial in resolving a broad range of problems related to the presence of certain embedded patterns within other, more complex structures. The paper to be discussed in this section will delve into the specifics of how the b-principle was utilized to resolve a notable and challenging problem of geometric topology known as the Mumford Conjecture. The analysis will involve an in-depth examination of the conjecture itself, the techniques that were developed to tackle it, and the connection between the b-principle and the methods employed, as well as the role that the resolution of the Mumford Conjecture played in the application of the b-principle to a broad class of problems known as the embedding problems. The analysis will also touch on the limitations of the b-principle, specifically in regards to the ability to construct embedding problems when the target manifold has a complex structure, and the possibilities that this presents for further advancing the b-principle. Understanding the behavior of cardiac tissue mechanics is crucial for accurate modeling of the heart, which can be achieved by applying mathematical modeling consisting of partial differential equations (PDEs). However, solving these PDEs yields a massive system of algebraic equations, specifically a linear system of up to 10^7 elements in cardiac mechanics applications. To efficiently solve this large system, multilevel preconditioners have gained popularity in recent years. This study compares two distinct methods for constructing multilevel preconditioners in cardiac mechanics: one utilizing an explicit approach and another with an implicit construction. An examination of both strategies reveals their strengths and weaknesses under different simulation settings, particularly when varying mesh size, solver iteration limits, and boundary conditions. Furthermore, this research investigates the connection between one-dimensional cardiac tissue models and their multilevel preconditioners, showing that a specific configuration can lead to a significant reduction in solve time for one-dimensional models by as much as 3 times. An openly available software framework allows users to replicate the study's results.

Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. This model can simulate the behavior of particles in turbulent fluids and random electric fields. We developed the anomalous diffusion equation that applies to this specific scenario, using a new approach that combines fractional Brownian motion and a time-changing diffusion characteristic. This equation can also be represented in a non-Markovian form, offering insights into the distribution of diffusion characteristics. We tested and validated our results through numerical simulations, where our predictions were compared to experimental data obtained from tracking individual particles in turbulent fluids.

A novel mathematical framework, known as mode interaction theory, has been
developed to describe both fundamental interactions and Kerr nonlinear effects
between an arbitrary device's eigenmodes and external fields, including light.
This theory, initially proposed by one of the authors in 2018, has been expanded
upon its original structure and incorporates the influence of Kerr nonlinearity
and higher-order effects, as well as interactions with external fields beyond
electromagnetic scenarios. The mode interaction theory has been successfully
applied to a variety of geometries, including circular microarrays, optical
microstrings, and photonic crystal cavities, and has been shown to provide a
precise and efficient means of computing the linear mode coupling coefficients
and Kerr nonlinear phenomena, such as mode locking, thresholdless optical
switching, and microcombs. In addition, the theory has been expanded to include
higher-order effects, scattering, and mode coupling, and has been integrated
with numerical tools, such as the finite-difference time-domain method and
three-dimensional FDTD simulations. The theory has been validated through
comparisons of its predictions with experimental and numerical data, and has
been applied to design novel geometries, such as racetrack optical microstrings,
and circular microarrays with embedded metalized defects, to achieve efficient
mode coupling and controlled Kerr nonlinear phenomena. The mode interaction
theory has been made available online as a user-friendly tool for both educational
and design purposes.

To enhance the resolution of vast, intricate fluid flows resulting from chaotic turbulence, a novel approach is proposed, utilizing a highly sophisticated technique from deep learning to create an ultra-high-resolution reconstruction from a low-resolution image sequence obtained through Kolmogorov's direct numerical simulation at a Reynolds number of 200,000. A specially designed high-resolution reference was utilized as a golden standard to evaluate the proposed technique's accuracy in three-dimensional flow reconstructions, as well as the proposed technique's ability to train models for two-dimensional plane flows without supplying the neural network with any spatial information. A novel technique was also introduced to calculate the Reynolds number's influence on the flow's dynamics by training the model on low-resolution images featuring varying Reynolds numbers. To validate the proposed technique, a novel metric called the multi-scale structural similarity coefficient was developed to evaluate the reconstructed images at different spatial scales, as well as their temporal stability. To further examine the proposed technique's capabilities, a range of flow images were reconstructed at a much higher resolution, as well as a check of the proposed technique's ability to return to the original low-resolution flow dynamics. To achieve this, the proposed technique was modified to include a bypass connection, resulting in the return to the original flow dynamics when the resolution was decreased again. For complex tasks that require multiple skills, a lifelong learning approach is desired, where the agent can master one ability and then apply it to a different, often unrelated, capability, without starting from scratch. In this setting, evaluating the method and comparing it to other techniques becomes a challenging and time-consuming process. To facilitate the evaluation process and streamline the comparison for lifelong learning methods, we present a new evaluation framework, called L2Explorer, which enables the evaluation of lifelong learning algorithms on a wide range of platforms, including multiple challenging problems that involve both physical interactions and complex data inputs. We demonstrate the versatility of L2Explorer by incorporating 7 publicly available benchmarks into the framework, spanning various domains such as robotics, simulation, and video games, and showcasing a key innovation of the framework, the ability to seamlessly extend it to new environments with minimal effort. We believe that the L2Explorer framework will be highly beneficial for the research community by providing an accessible platform for the evaluation, comparison, and credit accumulation analysis of lifelong learning algorithms, and the chance to engage in friendly competitions and share knowledge.

Understanding and monitoring complex processes are crucial steps in managing and maintaining process-based systems. Declaring processes as fully specified lead to better visibility and enable the detection of deviations at their source. An approach has been developed to explore such processes and detect deviations, it also includes a strategy for navigating the process and a method for determining suitable paths, the result is an algorithm for declaring processes and a protocol for navigation, the protocol can be implemented using process and stream-based technologies.

This research paper introduces a new category, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$-extended Chow groups ($\mathcal{D}$-ech), which includes $\mathcal{D}$-algebraic cycles as a subgroup and is well-equipped to house the K\"ahler Euler image under a specific mapping. Furthermore, we establish that the $\mathcal{D}$-ech group of a projective manifold is analytically isomorphic to its de Rham cohomology through the Euler image of the natural inclusion. Notably, this result can be obtained using the properties of the K\"ahler Euler image alone without relying on the algebraic cycle interpretation.

The mass of a galaxy's central sink of gas and stars and the rate at which it forms stars are related in a way that depends on the mass of the galaxy, with this relationship differing in the bulge, the disk, or an active galactic nucleus. The mass of a galaxy's central sink of gas and stars and the rate at which it forms stars are related in a way that depends on whether the mass of the galaxy falls above or below a certain threshold, with this threshold also affecting the rate at which it forms stars. Notably, research using supermassive black holes that contain fallen star material and are found in the centers of galaxies has shown that the rate at which it forms stars is related in a way that can be influenced by whether an active galactic nucleus is present or not.
