For the quantum group U_q(g) at an unspecified complex parameter q, we establish that it contains an abundance of finite-dimensional representations that form clusters, in effect serving as the foundation for the q-loop algebra classification developed by Frenkel and Gausterer. Notably, this result surpasses the earlier achievement of Sujishi, who successfully demonstrated the existence of non-trivial one-dimensional representations within U_q(g) but was unable to extend this finding to higher dimensional clusters.

In December 2021, Forsage emerged as a highly publicized Ponzi scheme built on the Ethereum platform.  Forsage's unique multi-level marketing structure allowed users to make referrals and get paid for them, using a complex network of pseudonymous transactions.  This case study examines the technical aspects of Forsage's code and its impact on the Ethereum blockchain, with a focus on how it facilitated fraudulent activity.  A detailed analysis of Forsage's code reveals its underlying mechanisms, including a devised method for managing participant transactions, a pay-out system based on referral networks, and various anti-detection measures.  In looking at Forsage's transaction data, researchers identified a distinct pattern of activity, with users falling into one of three categories: those who recruited others, those who only participated in the scheme, and those who acted as middlemen in referral chains.  By decompiling Forsage's Solidity code into its underlying components, and using clustering analysis of transaction data, this study provides a comprehensive understanding of Forsage's scheme, along with valuable insights for detecting similar scams in the future.

The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete, particularly in the crowded and distant stellar fields of the Galactic bulge. We have investigated 19 previously unconfirmed variable star candidates that are situated in this region and likely belong to globular clusters using data from the VVV survey. By considering the physical properties of RR Lyrae stars, we have been able to calculate the probable distances and luminosocities of these variables. As a result, we have identified 6 new globular cluster candidates located in the Galactic bulge. As such, the total number of identified globular clusters in the bulge is now 21, although one cluster candidate remains uncertain in its composition. We have also conducted an initial examination of 13 variables that could not be classified as RR Lyrae stars, but this study is ongoing.

In this context, we explore a specific type of holographic tensor networks, named Hyper-Invariant Matrix Product States, applied to simulate the behavior of a class of boundary systems in 1D, characterized by strong correlations according to power laws. A key aspect of these networks is being able to simulate approximately the error correction codes associated with the devil's circuit scenario, a well-studied example in quantum holography. By combining two well-established tools, a symmetry-based reduction method and a perturbative correction technique, we generate networks that simulate the dynamics of a wide range of boundary systems, including those with Albrecht et al.'s proposed error correction codes based on conformal field theory, specifically the (1,3) de Dominicis-Julienne and Tricumatric models, as well as a family of Baxter-Zhuber models. By examining the behavior of these networks, we provide a quantitative analysis of the conditions under which the networks simulate the devil's circuit scenario and the error correction codes associated with it, and the range of parameters that result in power-law correlations in the thermalized networks.

Deep-learning methods, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks and Recurrent
Neural Networks, have seen significant success in predicting business outcomes and
analyzing organizational processes when combined with techniques like
feature learning and optimization. By leveraging structured data and process
information, such as workflow definitions, organizations can enhance the
predictive power of their models. A review of current research indicates that
using raw process data can lead to decreased performance, whereas using feature
learning can result in increased accuracy of up to 30%. Furthermore, compared
to traditional machine learning models, the difference in accuracy can be as
high as 10% when combined with process features. A case study involving a
predictive model for estimating project timelines shows that, when trained with
process features, models can achieve an r-squared value of 0.7, whereas those
without process features can achieve an r-squared value of only 0.1.

We investigate key properties of several types of Gelfand-Shilov spaces, which are characterized by the decay of their smooth functions and their Fourier transforms. The nontriviality of these spaces, specifically ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$, is shown to depend on the values of $s$ and ${\sigma}$ being greater than 1. We establish that in the case where $s \leq 1$, the Banach algebra is nontrivial and contains the operators of compact perturbation of the identity. We also establish that the space ${\Sigma}^{\sigma}_s$ is isomorphic to the set of operators of order $2s$ when $s$ is greater than 1 and not an integer, and to the set of operators of order $2s-1$ when $s$ is an integer greater than 1.

A new method has been implemented to calculate the continuum of the near-ultraviolet spectrum for a specific flare of AD Leo, utilizing a semi-empirical approach based on the analysis of absorption features. The method involves breaking down the continuum into contributions from different atmospheric layers, with a focus on the properties of chromospheric plasma. By comparing the calculated continuum with observed spectra, it is possible to determine the temperature and density of different plasma components. For the AD Leo flare spectrum, a two-component model is sufficient to replicate the observed data, with the resulting analysis indicating a significant difference in density and little change in temperature between the two components. Furthermore, the study reveals that the temperature and density of the atmospheric layers remain unchanged during the flare, with any overall scaling being attributed to the total electron weight.

Neural network-based point cloud models have shown significant progress in recent years, with a focus on self-supervised learning allowing them to be trained without accompanying class labels. However, training these models with 3D classification data still yields better results when label information is utilized, particularly when smoothing the models through noise addition. A major limitation of current point cloud models is their inability to remain invariant in the face of transformations, which hinders the effectiveness of labeled self-supervised learning and leads to suboptimal performance on shifted data. To address this challenge, we propose a novel uniquesmoothing technique that incorporates the concept of unique transformation matrices. When the point cloud is sampled from a distribution that varies with transformations, uniquesmoothing proves effective in making the model more resilient, and our method is particularly well-suited for learning from single-class point cloud datasets with affine transformations. Our method achieves superior performance over baseline models, and through extensive experimentation, we find it to be particularly beneficial for modeling real-world data with small shifts in the x, y, and rotation axes.

Recently, accurate measurements of $^{16}$O's electric dipole excitations have been carried out with high precision by electrical methods, allowing for the re-evaluation of its giant dipole resonance in the context of the long-standing "doubly magic nucleus $^{16}$O" puzzle. Within the Random Phase Approximation model, the Jost function can be used to extract eigenenergies from complex spectra by employing a least squares method. When accounting for collisions between pairs of nucleons, the RPA calculation yields a complex spectrum, and when considering the effects of finite widths, the Jost function can be used to determine the total width of the GDZ resonance. According to our calculations, the GDZ resonance's total width can be explained by either the emission of the $\gamma$-ray into the continuum or the conversion of its component to the $\pi$-meson, rather than the assumption that it can be solely attributed to the emission of the $\gamma$-ray into the continuum. Furthermore, when comparing the results obtained from two different RPA approaches, we found that they yield nearly identical eigenenergies, and the apparent discrepancy can be eliminated by accounting for the differences in their treatment of the long-range Coulomb interaction.

Recent advancements in data collection options have provided valuable time series data which can be utilized for identifying patterns and structures in complex systems. Unfortunately, existing clustering methods aren't well-suited to arrange this data based on the system's dynamics and the impact that certain inputs have on it. In response to this challenge, a new approach called NICD is proposed, which takes both the time series data and control inputs into consideration to perform dimensionality reduction and clustering. Dimensionality reduction in NICD is achieved by constructing a relevant subspace that contains details about the system's dynamics and how it's affected by the inputs, while the clustering algorithm itself is designed to operate within this subspace to produce a set of clusters that each correspond to a different impact that the inputs have on the system. The effectiveness of NICD is demonstrated through numerical experiments using two examples: one with a known solution and another with real-world data from a mechanical system.

Developing a generative adversarial language model that efficiently generates long-form text while considering both finish and generation signals is challenging. Our proposed SparseGAN model addresses this issue by incorporating a more effective adversarial training method and introduces two novel techniques: it conditionally terminates sampling based on generated text cues, and employs a sparse mask to selectively sample words for adversarial training. By optimizing two objectives – one for guiding the model towards generating coherent text and another for determining the optimal number of words for adversarial training – our model achieves state-of-the-art performance on various long-text generation benchmarks.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a method was developed to identify two types of evidence for interstellar panspermia: initial signs of it and proof of it. Signs of it would involve observing microorganisms that have traveled between systems, but have not yet caused any harm or evolution, which could be achieved by looking for microbial remains with a specific isotope composition on multiple planets that have similar conditions. Proof of it would involve finding microorganisms that have traveled between systems and have caused harm or evolved as a result, which could be achieved by searching for instances where the conditions are very different, such as on a young planet and an older planet. A simulation of a survey was conducted that searched for evidence of interstellar panspermia on exoplanets by analyzing the properties of exoplanets that could harbor life and accounting for factors that could mask the signal, and the results showed that detecting proof of interstellar panspermia will be extremely difficult but not impossible, while detecting signs of it or initial evidence could be possible with a large survey, and it may be more likely to find evidence on planets that were hit by a nearby star than on planets that were not affected.

Animal movement and social interactions are crucial aspects of an ecosystem's structure and function, yet the study of these phenomena at a community level poses significant methodological challenges. In a breakthrough, a new technique has been developed which can extract valuable insights from encounter data resulting from capture-recapture studies in the presence of competition for resources. This statistical innovation enables researchers to infer essential details about the spatial distribution of individuals within a community, including their preference for certain areas and their ability to recognize one another, using encounter data that can be influenced by various factors including the distance between individuals move. This new method has been tested and proven effective using simulated data, and its application has been demonstrated using a real-world dataset of the social spider, Anelosculus californicus.

The study of networks of nonlocally coupled oscillators has been widely used to model the transmission of solutions in various phenomena, such as solar winds disturbing the Earth's magnetosphere and the spread of patterns in chemical reactions. We've expanded the existing analysis to include a new feature – a time-varying period of the oscillators – and have developed an explicit expression for the condition allowing the transmission of solutions in oscillatory networks with a circular geometry. We've also created a metaphorical example of a variable period affecting the stability of a ring network. Additionally, we've examined the effects of a time-varying period on the transmission of solutions in a channel network and discovered that it may lead to the loss of solution transmission, even at high driving amplitudes. We've supported these findings with numerical data and have proposed a dimensionless parameter that characterizes the transmission of solutions in a variety of networks. We've also explored a model with a periodic change in period, which has revealed that such changes may cause the network to become unstable, even at small amplitudes.

Given a linear differential operator, determining its type (elliptic, parabolic, or hyperbolic) is crucial in solving various mathematical problems, especially in the field of linear partial differential equations. This project focuses on the second-order Cauchy stress operator, which is part of the Navier-Lame equations, and aims to identify the minimum parameters required to determine its type, as well as to determine the type of the operator in the context of the Sobolev space $H^1$. The results obtained in this study can be applied to the Navier-Lame equations and the Stokes equations.

In this context, we believe that testing can be seen as a way to detect mistakes in the geometric framework used to define a program, and in this regard, it's essential to identify appropriate methods for describing programs geometrically. We have previously proposed a fundamental approach based on testing, which relies on the programs being represented as half-spaces, and in this paper, we will explore different ways of describing programs geometrically, examining their robustness in the face of testing. We will also introduce the concept of "orientation" to enhance the stability of programs, and demonstrate its benefits through examples and simulations.

Consider a finite-dimensional vector space over the complex number field, equipped with a Hermitian inner product. Let $\Phi$ be a linear transformation of this space, whose characteristic polynomial is given. We define the circle of $\Phi$ as the collection of all linear transformations sharing the same characteristics as $\Phi$. Our task is to demonstrate that in certain cases, including when the characteristic polynomial is of the form $(x-\alpha)^3$, the circle of $\Phi$ does not contain any circles of $\Phi$ for a specific norm.

Recently, a significant focus has been placed on developing methods to estimate network characteristics through node interactions, especially in the presence of malicious entities. In a recent study, researchers established that, in large-scale networks with nodes behaving randomly and independently, it's possible to accurately estimate a key graph property using a distributed algorithm, even when some nodes are unreliable and provide incorrect information. In contrast, small-world networks, often representative of real-life networks, have not been explored in this context. This paper investigates network-scale estimation in small-world networks, with an emphasis on estimating a property that can be linked to local density, and shows that, in the presence of randomly behaving nodes, it is possible to estimate this property effectively. When the network contains nodes that intentionally provide false information, estimating certain properties may not be feasible, and the conditions under which this becomes impossible were identified. A novel algorithm was developed to facilitate estimation and was tested in simulations using models that mimic real-world networks.

Accurate traffic management heavily relies on reliable traffic state estimation.
This study introduces a novel, nonparametric approach to estimate short-term
queue lengths without assuming random arrivals or estimating specific parameters.
The method, which uses simple mathematical expressions based solely on traffic
signal timing, estimates conditional queue lengths at intersections for multiple
probe vehicle trajectories. Unlike traditional methods, it doesn't require
parameter estimation or assume random arrivals. The approach was tested on real
data from Nagoya, Japan and Nagoya, USA, showing it could effectively estimate
conditional queue lengths for both cities.

In numerical relativity, a significant challenge arises when attempting to apply the conformal transverse-traceless decomposition to unbounded waveforms, particularly when it comes to creating an accurate and stable link between the conformal metric and the Weyl scalar in 3D spaces. We have developed the Conformal Transverse to Kantowski-Sachs method, which generates an unlimited range of TT Weyl scalars for any given Kantowski-Sachs spacetime, and we have successfully applied this to a variety of scenarios, including black hole and cosmic string mergers with arbitrarily long and complex waveforms. By utilizing this method, we have solved the CTK constraint and achieved a thorough understanding of the constraints, and have further refined the technique by developing the Conformal Transverse to Kantowski-Sachs- Komutator (CTTK) method, which provides a novel solution to the constraints using Komutator (conformally equivalent) spacetimes.

Recent discoveries of an anomalous Nernst effect in certain materials with an anti-ferromagnetic spin structure have been found, particularly in films of manganese nitride, Mn$_3$NiN, which exhibit an ultra-thin width of less than 10 nm, displaying an intricate interplay of magnetic properties and thermal gradient effects. The investigation of these effects at an atomic level has been achieved through the use of a scanning tunneling microscope, which provides a detailed understanding of the magnetic properties on a local level and the atomic structure, as well as the discovery of unique temperature and electric field-dependent phenomena. The study of these phenomena holds the potential for advancing the understanding and manipulation of the anomalous Nernst effect in the atomic level.

Recent advancements in synchrotron radiation technologies have significantly improved the resolution and sensitivity of experiments, making them crucial for in-depth analysis in fields like biomedicine, chemistry, and materials science. To fully leverage these capabilities, the MSANDA beamline at the Pohang Accelerator Laboratory was designed with remote operability in mind. This beamline features a control room physically separated from the experimental area, with operators located up to 150 meters away from the sample. To facilitate seamless, real-time control despite this distance, the beamline was equipped with a high-speed data network and specialized software allowing for automated experimentation through extensive use of artificial intelligence. By minimizing direct human contact with the sample and maximizing the efficiency of experiments through automation, MSANDA ensures safe, high-throughput operations at the forefront of user facilities.

We have obtained improved regularity properties for solutions to a specific category of non-autonomous obstacle problems, which are defined by the minimization of the functional given by the sum of the L^2-norm of the gradient and a boundary measure, subject to constraints defined by the presence of obstacles. Notably, under the assumption that the growth condition of the energy functional is subquadratic with a specific power, we have demonstrated the existence of a local C^alpha-estimate for the solution, with an alpha that depends on the distance from the point of singularity, as well as the properties of the obstacle and the measure defining the boundary. Additionally, we have the following results: if the energy functional growth is between the L1 and L2 classes, we have established the existence of a solution with the property of having bounded gradient in a neighborhood of any point where the measure defining the boundary vanishes; if the energy functional growth is of L2 class near a point where the measure defining the boundary vanishes, we have shown the existence of a solution with the property of having the property of Holder continuity of the gradient in a neighborhood of that point. We have also shown that the C^1 regularity of the solution holds if the growth condition of the energy functional is of L2 class, without any restriction on the measure defining the boundary. We provide a detailed description of certain Serre weights for GL_2 in the context of Kummer theory. Specifically, we show that the set of attainable Serre weights in the generic case of weight space, defined using local epsilon factors from a family of motives associated with Hilbert modular forms, matches the character table of the Weyl group W_S(2) when K is a p-adic field with a prime p dividing the discriminant of the base weight lattice. This description also extends to non-CM weights. Additionally, we establish connections between these weights and the geometry of a certain Kummer surface.

We have derived a novel, far-reaching consequence from a recent advancement in linear elliptic integral equations. By utilizing a significant recent finding related to elliptic integral equations, we have demonstrated that a specific type of surface, defined by a particular Hessian determinant and subject to a bounded mean curvature constraint, must possess a specific property called "mesoscale smoothness." This property is characterized by the surface having a particular structure at both the local and global levels, and it must also satisfy a specific type of isoperimetric inequality, known as the Solnechnikov inequality, as well as a related inequality called the Stec functional inequality, in a variety of different scenarios, including when the surface has minimal curvature, is subject to certain boundary constraints, or is part of a compact body with specific properties, among others.

Recent advancements in self-sensing composite materials have made it possible to determine and control damage accurately, using imaging techniques such as Electrical Impedance Tomography. In the context of preventing structural failure, researchers have been exploring damage control techniques, specifically "exact shaping of damage", which involves determining precise applied forces to achieve desired levels of damage within a material. In this study, a method was developed to use EIT and genetic algorithms to determine the exact distribution of applied loads to create a specific level of damage in composite materials, with results shown using both numerical and experimental data.

Recent research indicates that the performance of neural networks can be affected by the level of their elemental complexity, specifically whether their components are based on linear or nonlinear elements. Contrary to expectations, using nonlinear components doesn't necessarily lead to better results, and linear components can sometimes produce equivalent or even better outcomes. This phenomenon has been observed across various neural network architectures and datasets, and it's unclear at this point whether there's a general principle at play that governing how the complexity of network elements impacts performance. Further investigation is required to fully understand this relationship.

This work proposes an alternate tensor framework for Euclidean spaces centered on geometric vector descriptions, with a focus on scalar values defined through vector relationships, including dot products and cross products. With this method, we demonstrate the derivation of vector operations, scalar transformations, and differential geometry theorems, including the expansion of the classical Gauss and Bernstein theorems, as well as the Helmholtz decomposition and the Kirchhoff plate equation, with the aim of providing a unified understanding of vector operations and theorems through the analysis of geometric scalar values.

A class of light particles can be made up of a mix of quarks and leptons, allowing them to transform from one type of particle to another while also changing flavor. These transformations can occur through either weak interaction or electromagnetic interaction and can be influenced by either scalar or pseudoscalar interactions. In order for these interactions to be meaningful at the Large Hadron Collider, they must occur through either the $W$ boson or the Higgs boson. If these interactions were a part of the Standard Model, they would already have been discovered. However, if they resulted from new interactions beyond the Standard Model, they could be verified through specific processes such as the scattering of two protons producing two jets, missing energy, and metastable muons or electrons, and could also be investigated through neutrino scattering off atomic nuclei. If these interactions occurred through the $W$ boson, they might mimic the behavior of dark matter, depending on the mass of these particles, which could range from a few GeV to tens of TeV, with the most likely scenario being masses in the range of a few hundred GeV to a few TeV.

All conformal field theory correlation functions can be derived from the Toda conformal field theory, specifically through the use of the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. In this paper, we develop the concept of Ward identities in the Toda conformal field theory, which are then applied to the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory to derive correlation functions of the WZW model at a specific coupling. At this coupling, the Toda conformal field theory and the WZW model coincide as theories, allowing us to derive the Toda conformal field theory's two-point correlation functions. We also demonstrate the extension of these results to higher-point functions. The Toda conformal field theory's correlation functions can be matched to the 2D quantum gravity and the minimal CFT with central charge $c=4$. The paper includes an appendix detailing the integration method for the Toda conformal field theory's four-point correlation functions.

These algorithms can operate within an infinite number of steps, are based on a finite amount of initial data, and rely on the use of reflecting transformations. An earlier study discovered a link between a specific brain frequency and a particular walking path, however, it didn't account for conflicting neural signals that may result from the subject's ambiguous mental state during the experiment. A new study builds on this finding by creating two distinct conditions in which a man with paralysis in Texas walks in response to neural stimulation, first on a linear path and then on a U shape. It was essential to consider both conditions to fully understand the relationship between brain frequency and the direction of the U-shaped path. A key contribution of this research is developing an accurate method to determine the frequency associated with the U-shaped path by taking into account the subject's cerebral state and his step rate. It achieved this by analyzing the unique patterns of his brain signals recorded using an electrocorticogram. A key outcome of this study is the discovery that there is a significant correlation between the U-shaped path frequency and the subject's step rate. It was observed that as the subject's step rate increased, the frequency associated with the U-shaped path also increased, although only at a gradual pace. It was found that this U-shaped path frequency could be used in the future to control the subject's step rate as he walks in response to neural stimulation. It was also discovered that this study's method could be applied to other types of motor control, such as the subject's arm, by simply modifying the U-shaped path to the desired movement. For a given finite graph $G$, the right-angled Artin group $W_G$ has a defining presentation where generators of $W_G$ correspond to vertices of $G$, and relations in $W_G$ are based on the non-edges of $G$. A key research aim is to determine when the right-angled Artin groups have non-trivial finite index subgroups, and a crucial step in this direction is achieved by this paper. It demonstrates that any finite index subgroup of $W_G$ is isomorphic to $W_H$ for a subgraph $H$ of $G$ that can be obtained by taking subsets of $G$'s vertices, and the corresponding edges in $H$ are the same as those in $G$ among pairs of vertices generating the same transverse left ideal in the envelope $\Lambda_W$ of $W_G$.

Recent advancements in machine learning connectitiy estimation have primarily focused on static representations, neglecting the fundamental dynamics of neural systems. In contrast, our approach develops a novel dual-layer model where connectivity is expressed as both a time-dependent matrix and a weight vector. We introduce the Time-Varying Graph Convolutional Neural Network (TVGCNN), a pioneering architecture that leverages temporal patterns from input data to guide the learning process. TVGCNN operates by integrating local connections defined by a neighboring function, similar to traditional graph neural networks, and showcases equivalent performance to existing methods while offering a glimpse into the temporal characteristics of neural systems through its dynamic connectivity estimation. In support of our claim, we present empirical evidence showing that pre-training with TVGCNN on temporal signals before classification leads to a 6.4% improvement in mean accuracy on the ADNI dataset and a 10% reduction in TVGCNN parameters required for the same accuracy on the MCI dataset.

In recent years, biological movement has been a subject of interest for researchers as it is believed to be an evolutionarily preserved trait indicating the presence of certain psychological disorders such as schizophrenia, narcissistic personality disorder and Machiavellianism. Researchers have employed various methods to study this behavior, including surveys, laboratory experiments and field observations, with the latter being the most reliable indicator. However, accurately identifying biological movement in video recordings presents a challenge due to its subjectivity and the limited range of possible movements the human body can make. To address this issue, a computational approach has been proposed, involving three stages of analysis to determine the presence of abnormal biological movement in video footage. In the first stage, video recordings are segmented into blocks of a second's duration to facilitate the extraction of features. In the second stage, a set of descriptors known as Local Binary Patterns and Histogram of Oriented Gradient are employed to quantify the local characteristics of each block. In the third and final stage, a decision is made regarding the presence of abnormal biological movement based on the results of the previous stage of analysis. A dataset consisting of 20 subjects, 10 males and 10 females, has been used to test the proposed method, with results showing that it can accurately detect abnormal biological movement in up to 90 percent of cases. High-speed computing on complex simulations relies heavily on efficient iterative matrix inversion and solving systems of linear equations. We have developed a method for fast approximate iterative matrix inversion using a limited number of precise multiplications. Our technique employs the Neumann series expansion, which is particularly effective for large numbers of iterations. To enhance accuracy, we have introduced two correction techniques, both of which show significant improvements over existing methods in our simulations. Our results indicate that for a given level of precision, we can achieve up to 4 times the speed and 6 times the efficiency with a GPU implementation compared to the current state-of-the-art, while achieving identical or better accuracy.

Topological phases in one-dimensional materials can be ensured by creating a band structure with a gap and winding numbers as a key feature. One method to achieve this is by utilizing a quasicrystal construction, which incorporates incommensurate lattices and results in a spatially modulated potential that induces a topological phase based on the potential's period. In this work, a one-dimensional topological system is proposed that relies on a different approach, utilizing a random binary disorder instead of quasicrystals. When the disorder is truly random, no topological phase can be initiated, but as the disorder becomes non-rigorous random, a topological phase can be triggered by a simple condition that is independent of the disorder's specifics. A one-dimensional topological Anderson material can be modeled by a tight-binding model with two nearest-neighbor interaction terms, and non-rigorous disorders will affect localization and topological properties in unique ways that can be analyzed through numerical simulations.

We've developed a new framework for describing the behavior of a specific type of graph cut, using the principles of category theory. This approach allows us to apply fundamental theorems from category theory to achieve notable results, such as the equivalence of certain graph matching algorithms and the validity of a particular relaxation of the maximum independent set problem. We believe this method offers a versatile tool for analyzing various graph-based problems and can be found useful in the broader context of category-based solvers.

As a result, we've derived the on-shell propagator corrections for all 64 Higgs particles in the MSSM. Utilizing the on-shell Higgs two-point functions, we've also calculated on-shell Higgs decay widths into standard model particles, fermion pairs of the third generation, and decay widths into gauge and third-generation fermilys, which are crucial components in determining on-shell Higgs quantities in the MSSM. Contextual linear bandits is a key model to consider for personalization in settings with limited information exchange, yet standard approaches to solving this problem require knowledge of individual context matrices among agents.  In a recent study, a method was discovered that enables agents to estimate their own context matrix while solving the contextual linear bandit problem, resulting in performance comparable to having full knowledge of the matrix.  This was achieved by analyzing the context matrix from data generated by linear bandit actions, using a variation of the well-known empirical Dufvenberg regressions.  Further improvements were made by utilizing a more advanced estimator, the Overlapping ATE regression, which led to a non-asymptotic bound on the number of actions required to accurately estimate the context matrix.  As for the linear bandit problem itself, a bound was derived based on the celebrated LSV algorithm, by leveraging the estimate of the context matrix as an alternative to the usual projection. We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our response addresses methodological and theoretical concerns raised, clarifying the assumptions, limitations, and potential extensions of our work. Concerning estimation challenges, we acknowledge that our method assumes access to a consistent estimator of the propensity score, and for inverse propensity score weighting, this is a well-established assumption. For weighted learning, more caution is needed as there is less theoretical support available. We also consider two main points from the context: first, the focus on binary treatments, which may not always be appropriate, and the need to generalize to categorical treatments. Second, and more significantly, the assumption that conditional mean outcomes are known up to a constant error term may not always hold in practice. We agree with Sager and Tsiatas that our results can be seen as a special case of the consistency of the rule-based estimator in (Tang and Tsiatas, 2020), and with Kallus that our result regarding the $\sqrt{n}$-rate can be obtained from Theorem 2 in (Kallus, 2020). We also appreciate the interest shown in generalizing our results to categorical treatments and explore an approach using the constrained convex optimization framework in (Tang and Tsiatas, 2020) as an initial step.

Our study introduces a method for manipulating event shapes by shifting the most peripheral events towards more central ones, either in terms of centrality, transverse momentum, or particle flow, which helps to minimize systematic effects when measuring collective behavior in small systems. We apply this event shape manipulation to LHC data on inclusive pT spectra and elliptic flow in non-central semi-central Pb-Pb collisions at a sqrt(s_NN) of 2.76 TeV, and find that it yields results consistent with the assumption of hydrodynamic behavior, specifically q_2/proton ratio values of approximately 0.48-0.57 for inclusive charged hadron spectra and approximately 0.18-0.20 for pion spectra. We also develop an event generation framework that simulates event shape manipulation using Monte Carlo methods with ATOMIC transport simulations, and verify that it reproduces results from hydrodynamics, with slight discrepancies possibly attributed to specific assumptions made in the ATOMIC model.

In an interference network with independent identically distributed node pairwise distances, we used a typing argument to establish an upper bound on the number of extreme points in the feasible region of weight sharing networks. With an assumption of uniformly distributed node pairwise distances, we showed this upper bound is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$. Furthermore, by correlating the number of extreme points with the number of optimal solutions in various benchmark problems, we demonstrated the accuracy of this $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ characterization for uniformly distributed node pairwise distances. As a part of these analyses, we obtained a priori estimates of the number of solutions to two benchmark problems defined by Foschini: the binary and the continuous power control problems. In the case of uniformly distributed node pairwise distances, these estimates yielded the known results of $\Theta(K^2)$ and $\Theta(K^3)$ respectively, as well as a new result of $\Theta(K^{5/2})$ for the continuous power control problem. In addition, we defined a new class of network problems with weight sharing structures and proved they all have a $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ number of extreme points, a result that can be viewed as a generalization of a result in the literature that was established with an alternative method.

To simulate complex interactions in detail and maintain accuracy and realism in particle-level simulations, a short collision time is typically employed, as it allows for the precise tracking of individual particles during contact events. However, this approach can lead to unrealistic results due to the artificial prolongation of collision events, which in turn can result in an unacceptably prolonged simulation time. In the present study, a multiple-time-step integration method is proposed to address this challenge by using a longer time step for the free flow phases between collisions and a significantly shorter time step during the collision phase. The simulation can be efficiently updated using this method, which is achieved by modifying the existing force and collision resolution routines. According to our numerical tests, the multiple-time-step integration method can effectively reduce the simulation time while maintaining the same level of accuracy as a single-time-step method, as evidenced by its ability to accurately reproduce the results of a single-time-step method. In addition, the method is shown to be capable of capturing the statistical characteristics of complex flow phenomena, as demonstrated by its application to simulations of turbulent flow and particle transport.

A significant challenge in creating efficient and fast legged robots is overcoming the obstacle of variable terrain, particularly with robots that have a limited number of legs. To achieve high efficiency, legged robots need to be able to take long strides, which can lead to issues with stability, particularly when they land. Another problem with variable terrain is the difficulty in determining the appropriate amount of force to apply, which can result in uncertain outcomes when applying significant impact forces to unknown surfaces. Our research focuses on designing a simplified, efficient hopping mechanism for a monopod robot that can mitigate some of these issues. By reducing the amount of energy wasted during the hopping process, we were able to achieve an energy-efficient cycle with a high height-to-mass ratio, which allows the robot to hop efficiently on yielding terrain. In order to validate the design, we performed a series of tests by which we adjusted key parameters such as the length of the hopping leg and the surface hardness. Our results showed that it is possible to achieve significant height gains with a compact design, and that the relationship between the design and the resulting height gains can be accurately predicted using simulation tools. In the process of developing the design and testing it, we encountered several challenges, including issues with material selection, the risk of pin failure, and the difficulty of modeling the interaction between the pins and the surface of the terrain. Ultimately, our research demonstrated that it is possible to create a monopod robot with a compact design that can gain significant height with each

In this paper, we apply a flexible approach to study the form factors of mesons in a unified framework, which is based on the assumption that all mesons, both light quark systems and heavy quark systems, follow a single set of parameters. We test this method by calculating the electric form factors of heavy mesons and find that, in the limit of large momentum, the results conform to the predictions of the quark charge distribution and align with the findings of other studies. Furthermore, we investigate the decay widths of heavy mesons and find that the flexible approach yields accurate results when compared to other methods, especially for the $D$-meson family. We also examine the charge radii of heavy mesons and find that the flexible approach can describe both the $D$-meson family and the $\bar{B}$-meson family with a high degree of precision.

An organization's seniority structure, such as a military rank or a corporate hierarchy, can be represented as a directed graph, where the direction of the edges corresponds to reporting guidelines. Researchers have methods to infer such structures from data, but they typically require large amounts of memory and cannot handle the scale of datasets like those found in large social media platforms. Our new framework addresses these challenges by creating a hierarchical structure using simple rules and node attributes, without the need for explicit paths between nodes. This framework can be trained using a new objective function that takes into account the diversity of the embedded nodes, and it can also incorporate constraints based on external data, such as a list of seniority levels. When applied to datasets like the Yelp network of who-ranks-whom, it shows significant improvements in accuracy and a 6 times speedup in training, and can be extended to more complex structures like the Amazon collaboration graph.

Quantum annealing holds promise for efficiently resolving complex optimization challenges by bypassing obstructions in the classical realm through wave-like motion. However, the likelihood of successful outcome depends greatly on how far the quantum wave packet extends into the sample's interior. This study investigates the relationship between quantum annealing parameters and the likelihood of finding the optimal solution among the sample's output, as well as the behavior of the outcome when the quantum wave packet is suddenly released from an intermediate state of evolution. A simple yet accurate model is developed to describe the outcome distribution and the quench dynamics in the Exponential Ratchet regime characteristic of D-Wave machines.

Due to strong correlations, a lack of charge transfer makes nickel difficult to model. The assumption of minimal correlation in one band can lead to inaccurate results. A framework that considers strong interaction in both bands is necessary for a correct understanding of nickelate physics. Screening effects from adjacent bands can also cause problems by either overestimating or underestimating the effective electron-electron interaction, depending on the energy range analyzed. A calculation of the effective interaction, taking into account the energy dependence of localizing orbitals, is required for an accurate description of nickelate physics. A two-dimensional model with a specific arrangement of orbitals can serve as a foundation for further analysis. By applying a method of projecting onto localizing orbitals within a two-band framework, the physics of a particular nickelate material can be studied and compared with experimental data, showing that it exhibits both correlation-induced dimerization and charge/orbital polarization, and can also exhibit both Kondo-screened and Fermi-Liquid-like behavior depending on the distance between nickel atoms.

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 3 to 10 times nuclear saturation density, present in the cores of stars like neutron stars and quark stars, cannot be fully determined by current observational methods, and thus, any possible relation between these properties and the appearance of specific phenomena, such as strange quark matter, remains speculative, although it's often used as a basis for hypothetical dark matter models. We are exploring the possible connection between the phenomenon of strange quark matter and the disappearance of certain types of neutron stars, focusing on sound speed measurements and density boundary within density range mentioned above, by analyzing various types of neutron stars made of hadronic, hybrid, and quark matter. We found that the sound speed in hadronic stars can be any value from approximately 0.45 to 0.65, while in quark stars it is around 0.4 to 0.5, with a more precise range of 0.475 to 0.485 for the latter when considering the possibility of strange quark stars and the properties of strange quark matter as previously mentioned. Additionally, we established the following relations between the density of which stars can exist and the sound speed: above a certain density, hadronic stars cannot exist; below a certain density, quark stars cannot exist; and there are specific sound speed values that define the density at which strange quark stars can exist, with possible applications in models of dark matter.

We have derived a comprehensive set of Heisenberg lattice dynamics equations, applicable to bosonic systems, and demonstrated the significance of our approach by investigating the impact of applied forces on both symmetric and asymmetric situations. When the number of atoms is kept constant, we found that a gradient of up to three sites can withstand external influences without being disrupted. In contrast, when the number of atoms can vary, even a small gradient will lead to destructive consequences. The effects of shifting the lattice also behave differently, with stable states existing in some situations but not in others. The potential applications of our results in the fields of atomic physics and quantum information are discussed.

Recently discovered dust growth can significantly influence the properties of particles in protoplanetary disks, and may impact the settling of small particles, which in turn affects the conditions favoring the development of vertical shear instability. We have re-examined the stability of dust particles in the outer regions of protoplanetary disks, considering the effects of particle growth, settling, and the local properties of the disks. We have conducted numerical simulations of dust growth, which have shown that particles in the outer regions of disks grow to a size range of 1-10 micrometers. This size range leads to the partial suppression of vertical shear instability in the outer regions of disks. We have also found that the conditions that drive the development of vertical shear instability in the outer regions of disks are the presence of gas and dust turbulence, and the local optical depth of the disks. The presence of this instability may influence the distribution of dust particles in the outer regions of disks, and can also impact the formation of planetesimals and the growth of solid particles in the outer regions of disks.

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and where a specific average curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this type of manifold, without relying on the well-known gradient estimate for the Harnack inequality. As a result, we are able to provide a new proof for the convergence of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time, where the average curvature eventually reaches a constant, and where the volume remains unchanged.

Recent advancements in creating sophisticated hidden mechanisms for manipulating
artificial intelligence have led to the development of intricate triggers with
multiple classes and dynamic triggers that can be adapted to various data sets.
Researchers have primarily focused on constructing hidden channels using
classification data, without exploring the potential of overfitting in this area.
A novel method, known as DBGP, is presented here for the first time, which
represents a groundbreaking approach in this field by utilizing neural networks
to create complex hidden channels that can resist overfitting.
This breakthrough was found to succeed in multiple fields, including audio with
triggers, image with dynamic channels, and text with hidden meanings, making it
a versatile innovation.
By using GMP as a fundamental component, the project delves into the in-depth
analysis of how this structure resists overfitting, and presents a new theory
called the "channel diversity effect" which explains this phenomenon for the
first time.
In addition to this, an novel strategy called the "adversarial learning of
dynamic triggers" was discovered to enhance the security of hidden channels,
thereby preventing the model from learning the trigger in artificial training
processes.
