High-accuracy astronomical measurements, particularly in astrometry similar to those made with the Gaia satellite, have the potential to test the fundamentals of general relativity. A key aspect of this testing involves the value of a specific parameter, PPN $\gamma$, which is essential in modifying the expression for gravitational deflection of light and, as such, affects the calculation of a star's position based on its observed trajectory. By using simulated data and a method similar to that used in actual Gaia analyses, we investigated the impact of an increasingly precise measurement of PPN $\gamma$ has on the determination of a star's parallax. Our findings revealed that the uncertainty in PPN $\gamma$ is the dominant contributor to the error in parallax measurements in a specific range of distances and that an extremely precise measurement of PPN $\gamma$ would be necessary to explain these results. Furthermore, we observed that the error in parallax measurements can be explained by a model that incorporates the known uncertainty in PPN $\gamma$ as well as an estimate for the error in Gaia's measurements of the celestial phase.

To enhance the performance of CQEs on questions without associated labels, our proposed method, CQF at two levels, systematically explores two degrees of semantic connections. At a coarse level, CQF considers all existing questions that share the same label, without regard to semantic distance. In contrast, the careful level is more refined, incorporating a calculation of semantic similarity. By balancing these two levels, we're able to create a strong foundation for addressing the issue of open-domain CQEs. Our results show that both the careful and the coarse approaches achieve significant gains over the baseline, with the careful level leading to substantial performance improvement, a 6.5% increase over the BERT reference model. When combining these two levels, the overall performance is 11.1% greater than BERT. Our technique also ranks highly in a second experiment where the question and answer are linked via semantic.

Astronomical environments, particularly in comets, provide opportunities to study
molecular cations under conditions similar to those of forming stars. Although cometary
spectra have been analyzed for various molecular cations, there are notable gaps in the
spectral data for certain oxygen-containing molecular cations, specifically those with
double bonds between oxygen and other elements, as well as those with an oxygen-oxygen
double bond. If modeled cometary plasmas are indeed analogous to interstellar environments,
theoretical predictions suggest that molecular cations with these oxygen bonds should be
abundant, yet their absence in observed spectra requires explanation. This study aims to
investigate possible reasons for the non-detection of these cations in cometary spectra,
with possible causes including the limitations of current observational data, the insensitivity
of some observational techniques, the instability of these cations in high-energy
environments, the preference for alternative cationic forms, and the potential for these
cations to be masked by more abundant spectral features. With a deeper understanding of the
non-detection of these cations, it may be possible to reinterpret the data in a way that
supports the analogy between cometary and forming star environments.

In the context of a highly diverse and fragmented data environment, such as one characterized by numerous individual data sources each with their own distinct patterns, training a machine learning model through federated learning encounters significant difficulties, primarily due to the need for visits to be made to nearly all individual data sources in order to obtain diverse data. As a result, existing optimization methods in a federated learning setting often prove inefficient or even infeasible. In the paper presented here, a novel randomized walk was developed to efficiently explore individual data sources in a way that prioritizes those with more valuable contributions to make, with the result being an algorithm that leverages local model updates at an controlled rate in a way that directly mirrors the intensity of their contribution to the global model, with the further benefit of facilitating the detection of sources that are contributing negatively. With the result being a robust and adaptable algorithm that is capable of handling diverse individual data sources while being resistant to manipulation by malicious sources. With the effectiveness of the algorithm demonstrated through a successful application to learn from a network of 100 individual data sources, with the result being a model that is 30% more accurate and 70% more resistant to manipulation by malicious sources.

Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently experience mental health challenges, which can lead to repeated offending following minimal punishment sentences, including fines and probation. The study examines how mandatory mental health treatment for this population affects future criminal convictions and mortality rates. To achieve this, the research analyzed mental health treatment as a required component of their sentences for over 670,000 offenders in the United States from 2004 to 2014, comparing those who were mandated to receive mental health services to those who were not. Offenders who were required to receive mental health services were found to have 4.5 percent lower odds of committing future offenses and 7 percent lower odds of dying, although this effect was more pronounced for men than women. The research also discovered that the effect of mental health treatment as a condition of their sentence was more significant for shorter sentences lasting up to a year, as well as for individuals convicted of violent offenses, who experienced a 10 percent lower odds of committing future offenses. The study's findings suggest that making mental health treatment a requirement of a sentence can have a positive impact on the long-term behavior of convicted individuals, and as such, should be considered as a standard component of their sentence.

A common challenge in medical image segmentation tasks is the limited amount of annotated data available. This paper presents a novel approach in semi-supervised image segmentation, focusing on cases where only a small percentage of images are annotated. The proposed technique, utilizing a consistent transformation as a regularization tool, helps the network generalize better to unannotated images by ensuring consistency across transformed versions of the annotated data. This method can be applied to both multi-class and multi-instance segmentation tasks. Experiments on three medical image segmentation datasets (H&N, LiDAR, DOG) demonstrate significant improvements in segmentation performance when compared to baseline models, with the simplest version of the proposed method showing particular promise.

In 2018, a groundbreaking experiment at Rutgers University, led by G. J. Johansen, successfully demonstrated the ability to locally characterize quantum chaos by analyzing the dynamics of individual atoms within a Bose-Einstein condensate using light, thereby bridging the gap between this approach and the broader principles of quantum many-body theory. To take the understanding of this phenomenon to the next level, a recent study used a graph neural network to accurately reproduce the outcomes of the Rutgers experiment for a key indicator of chaos, called the out-of-time correlation function, by incorporating a key modification that helped the model excel in its performance. By applying this modified graph neural network to a broad and diverse set of quantum many-body models, the study showed that it could effectively map the internal structure of these models to a specific neural network architecture, thus uncovering the underlying patterns that indicate chaos. The study found that the average amount of chaos exhibited by these models could be quantified using a simple and well-established measure, known as the von Neumann entropy, and that the models that displayed the greatest amount of chaos were located at the edges of a known parameter space, providing a clear and tangible example of how the amount of chaos varies with the amount of a specific interacting parameter. The study also provided a straightforward and interpretable analysis of how the amount of chaos is affected by the shape of a periodic potential used to create a model known as the Aubry-Andr\'e model, and demonstrated that the performance of the

Consider a parametric family of distributions defined by $f(y|\theta)$ where $\theta$ is a parameter from the set $\Theta$, and a function $\pi(\theta)$ that defines a mixture distribution over this set. The task is to estimate the average parameter $\bar{\theta} = \int_\Theta \theta \pi(\theta) d\theta$ in a mixture where the number of components $k$ is unknown or known to be $3$, using Maximum Likelihood Estimation. A new algorithm is proposed to handle both scenarios by first determining $k$, then applying a switching procedure to estimate $\bar{\theta}$. Theoretical guarantees on consistency of the estimator for $k=3$ are established, and the algorithm is demonstrated on two instances: estimating the average of a normal mixture to guide multiple change point detection, and analyzing the complexity of mixtures on the example of a normal mixture.

Knowledge tracing, an area within artificial intelligence that deals with monitoring a student's knowledge, has seen significant advancements, with many deep learning methods being proposed to achieve better results. Nevertheless, evaluating these deep learning models and associated theories has been challenging due to the lack of publicly available data and questionable assumptions in existing knowledge models. As a result, the theoretical foundations of knowledge tracing have been questioned, with some researchers suggesting it is not necessary to incorporate these models, and instead, they can be replaced with deep learning methods to achieve better performance. To address the limited data challenge, an innovative technique was developed to augment the data by using knowledge tracing models as experts, while for the first time, the conditions under which knowledge tracing models can be substituted with deep learning methods were formally established in this study. These conditions were validated through the application of knowledge tracing on two different platforms: online learning and question answering, and were found to provide accurate results, as measured by whether the student owns the knowledge or not, with performance being evaluated on two different datasets each for online learning and question answering, respectively.

Given any open set $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^n$ and the closed interval $[0,T]$ for some $T > 0$, we can consider the space $C_{\text{b}}^{2}(\Omega \times [0,T])$ consisting of functions with bounded derivatives up to order two, defined on the product of $\Omega$ and $[0,T]$. When the set $\Omega$ is not given, we denote this space as $C_{\text{b}}^{2}([0,T])$. Every differential operator of order two, when considered on this space, forms a self-adjoint sector of type S'2. Consequently, we can show that any two such operators that commute and have real and positive entries, when combined into a single matrix, have a large range if they form a diagonal matrix, and a range that is not compact if they form a matrix with independent entries along some vector space. If the set $\Omega$ is compact, we can show that any two such operators that commute and have real and positive entries, when combined into a matrix, have a range that is not compact if the matrix has independent entries along some vector space. If $\Omega$ is the whole real numbers, we can show that any two such operators that commute and have real and positive entries, when combined into a matrix, have a range that is not compact if the matrix has independent entries along a vector space,

Ten years ago, at the inaugural PxTP workshop, veriT's authors introduced the VTT challenge, which has since become a benchmark for evaluating satisfiability modulo theories solvers. In response to this test case, veriT's initial implementation used a straightforward strategy that has become increasingly ineffective due to veriT's own improvements. In contrast, our new solver, Alethe, is designed to provide a simple benchmark that will pose a more substantial challenge for future satisfiability modulo theories solvers. In evaluating Alethe, we used the VTT challenge, which revealed an interesting disparity in results, with many solvers failing to achieve satisfactory performance. In analyzing these results, we discovered that the majority of solvers that participated in the 2010 veriT competition either used an outdated API or employed a solver strategy that is no longer effective. In response to these findings, we are introducing a new challenge, called Alethe Challenge, whose ultimate goal is to contribute to the development of a superior format for stating satisfiability modulo theories problems using the Sequence Temporal Logic language, which in turn will facilitate the creation of an open format for stating theories in SMT solvers.

As the number of model updates in federated learning grows, synchronizing model updates becomes increasingly inefficient due to high communication costs and straggling participants. This study examines the negative consequences of using unrestricted gradients in the presence of waiting time, uncovering its potential to steer clear of optimal results. A novel algorithm called buffered asynchronous gradient aggregation is presented, which takes into account the duration of model updates to determine an optimal threshold for aggregation frequency. This results in improved performance when compared to other methods, such as asynchronous FL, distributed SGD, and APFL.

Recently, ASR systems have achieved significant improvements by leveraging pre-trained language models at various degrees of linguistic complexity. Our research builds upon this success by exploring whether a similar strategy can be applied in ASR transfer learning. We utilized a high-to-low linguistic complexity approach on a popular dataset, where a speaker with a large amount of training data serves as the donor and one with limited training data acts as the recipient. Our experiment involved a series of transfers starting from a fully supervised to a completely unsupervised setting, with results showing that transfer learning can effectively bridge the gap from a fully supervised to a low-resource setting. We also investigated the efficacy of CLASR transfer as well as ASR transfer on the Switchboard dataset in an English-to-Yi cross-language setup, with findings indicating that both can be an advantageous way to build Yi ASR systems.

Our novel TD learning approach, GPTD, leverages a combination of spatial and temporal Gaussian Process regression to guide a marine robot safely by considering both the environment's unknown map and the unknown time-dependent return values. Unlike traditional TD learning methods, GPTD doesn't require the return values to be constant over time, nor does it need the robot's actions to be completely observable. Our research demonstrates that the spatial GP can effectively handle action-dependent observations, and we've developed an analytical proof that the policy obtained from our GPTD method is guaranteed to converge to a stable state under certain conditions. Furthermore, we've created a practical algorithm to update the spatial and temporal GP parameters efficiently. Our results show that GPTD yields superior performance compared to conventional TD learning and other GP-based methods, and it's capable of learning from minimal data.

We've accomplished an innovative feat by completing an intricate derivation of anisotropic relativistic stellar objects using dual-fluid General Relativity, and in the process, we've achieved a clear understanding of the model's parameters that affect its isotropic or anisotropic behavior. We've also obtained specific and general expressions for the anisotropic pressure distribution throughout the object, and demonstrated that its pressure profile can be determined based on either the compactness of the object or its mass-to-radius ratio, depending on whether the objects in question are configured with conformally coupled scalars or not. Furthermore, we've provided the solution for an isothermal objects and identified the conditions under which anisotropic objects become isotropic, and in the process, we've established lower and upper bounds for the objects' compactness. We believe these breakthroughs will be particularly valuable for guiding future observational efforts aimed at identifying the properties of dense compact objects, and for providing the theoretical framework for analyzing objects with massive and complex mass distributions, and we hope to see this model applied in the study of compact objects with massive and complex distributions, such as those formed from the remnants of massive stars following a supernova explosion, and in the analysis of gravitational waves emitted during binary compact object mergers.

Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus on expanding their language model to include multiple domains without considering domain-specific constraints. This can result in overfitting and making the model harder to understand. In contrast, our proposed method builds upon the foundation of adversarial sequence-to-sequence learning and employs a meta-learning approach to achieve domain adaptability in a more constrained manner. We train a general model in a mid-domain where it can produce acceptable sentences without being perfect, and then fine-tune it on small datasets in specific domains to prepare it for future adaptations. The evaluation shows that our proposed method achieves comparable results to state-of-the-art methods while producing more understandable and fewer errors in a constrained manner. Additionally, it demonstrates strong potential in transferring to a new domain with as little as ten edited sentences.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents has been examined in various contexts, yet the majority of existing studies have looked at scenarios where the agents' actions are non-strategic. In this work, we focus on a specific method of allocation, in which the most valuable items are given to the highest-bidding agents, and investigate the conditions under which all possible pure-Nash equilibria are fair, i.e., all outcomes that can arise from the application of a random mixed strategy profile are equally likely. We achieve this level of outcome equivalence when the number of agents is two, and we demonstrate that when the number of agents is greater than two, there are scenarios in which the level of outcome equivalence that can be achieved is only that all outcomes have the same value, not necessarily the same probability.

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, exhibits a unique disk dynamics.
A recent study using the ASTRORIVALS code, which simulates gravitational waves influenced by galaxy interactions and mergers, suggests that a major collision with a massive galaxy may have caused its slow rotation and warmed its central region.
Another study employing the ARETO code, which analyzes the thermal and dynamical effects of galaxy interactions and mergers, also supports this finding by indicating that UGC 8839's rapid central star formation is likely triggered by a recent interaction with a massive companion.
Observations from the Hubble Space Telescope reveal a significant offset between its supermassive black hole's location and the galaxy's visual center, further pointing to a recent interaction that may have displaced the black hole.
Consequently, we classify UGC 8839 as a hyper-stable galaxy that has endured multiple mergers and interactions, exhibiting an extraordinary level of resistance to various destructive forces that could disrupt its core.
Its unique characteristics make UGC 8839 an exceptional subject of study, offering valuable insights into the dynamics of galaxy interactions, the behavior of supermassive black holes, and the formation and evolution of spiral galaxies.

Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of various meson combinations was conducted, allowing for the extraction of valence quark correlation functions and ultimately, the determination of quark distributions within the pion. By applying a two-current transformation operator in a series expansion, a method was developed to interpret the results of lattice measurements of correlation functions of meson combinations. With multiple operator associations tested, our study demonstrated that both Jadach-Zdhral and Kroll-Dash equations can be applied to describe quark and antiquark distributions within the pion. By calculating the coefficients of the two-current operator associations, we obtained a precise determination of quark and antiquark distributions within the pion, in both transverse polarization components. In particular, our analysis of the coefficients revealed that the coefficients associated with the quark and antiquark distributions in the pion possess the same sign, with the absolute values of the coefficients in the longitudinal component differing by approximately 4.5, with uncertainties of 1.5 due to the limitations of our lattice data.

Evaluating accretion variability in young stars is crucial for accurately
interpreting observations of protoplanetary disks.  Variability in accretion
rates can be influenced by multiple factors, including the presence of giant
planets and stellar spots, which may either masquerade as irregular
perturbations or be related to planetary formation, respectively.  We studied
XX Cha, a young star with an unusual T Tauri-type spectral profile, and found
it to have an unusually large distance between stellar main sequence proxies,
indicating its mass may be intermediate between solar masses and 1.4 solar masses.
  Further investigation revealed that XX Cha resides in the center of a small
molecular ring, which may be a remnant of a giant protoplanetary disk
formation.  Observations of XX Cha showed a large range of accretion variability,
with rates that were both the highest and lowest in its class, and a long-term
decrease in accretion rates, which could be influenced by its low mass.
  Combining observations with models of mass loss and protoplanetary disk
formation, we found that XX Cha's unique features may result from its low mass,
which could lead to a more irregular accretion process, and further support the
role of massive protoplanetary disks in the formation of giant planets.

Offline Model-based Mariage Learning (OMML) leverages offline data to securely learn a collaborative policy for multiple agents. It achieves this by constructing and exploring a rich tree of action consequences for each agent, allowing for efficient discovery of a trusted and effective policy. We introduce a new way of representing action consequence trees that facilitates efficient construction and exploration, and devise two important techniques to handle the large scale of these trees. We also present a novel method for selecting and exploring branches of the tree that yields a controlled exploration of the policy space. Our approach is accompanied by theoretical guarantees of optimal convergence, and we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through comprehensive experiments in complex scenarios, showing it to be a highly competitive method due to its efficiency and ability to generalize across different environments.

Recently, MV images have gained popularity for their potential in assisting setup verification and patient positioning both inside and outside radiation therapy treatments. However, utilizing MV images requires aligning them with corresponding MV images taken after treatment, which are typically captured as part of the treatment process. This task, known as post-treatment MV-to-MV image registration or alignment, can be challenging due to factors such as respiratory motion, limited field of view, and distortion caused by megavoltage screens. In this study, a novel approach is proposed, where a convolutional neural network is used to align MV images with the help of kilovoltage images serving as additional guidance. The proposed method was tested on a dataset consisting of 50 2D images and 50 3D images, yielding alignment accuracy of 5mm in 2D and 7mm in 3D. Notably, the proposed method was found to outperform a traditional method using gradient of probability density models by approximately 1mm in both 2D and 3D cases.

When examining single-particle entanglement in a vast array of scenarios, it is often analyzed in the context of two-dimensional Hilbert spaces. Here, we investigate the diverse forms of single-particle entanglement, including their genuine nonlocal properties such as steering. In a qubit, there are four distinct classifications of pure-state entanglement, each exhibiting unique characteristics in both discrete and continuous variable settings. We thoroughly review the conditions under which these states exhibit genuine nonlocality, demonstrating that only two of the four pure-state ensembles are universally recognized as genuinely nonlocal. Furthermore, we establish clear criteria for identifying the genuinely nonlocal nature of a state, either through the violation of specific bipartite norms or the occurrence of unique, genuinely nonlocal effects in discrete or continuous variable settings. In the case of mixed states, we discuss the relationship between steering and other measures of non-orthogonality, presenting an ineqaulity that can be used to determine the degree of steering in qubit settings. We also explore the connection between the average amount of steering and the average entanglement-related properties of a state's underlying pure-ensemble components.

The integration of artificial intelligence, internet technology, and automotive systems has resulted in a complex safety challenge, with potential risks to security, reliability, and efficiency, with implications for autonomous vehicle development.  Considerable research has been conducted to address various AI training challenges by promoting privacy protection and security, such as developing secure gradient descent protocols and manipulating inaccurate data.  This paper provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of the art in IoT vehicles, focusing on the security and reliability of AI-powered applications and the privacy protection of data sharing models.  A discussion is also presented on the challenges facing the development of secure and reliable AI-powered IoT vehicles, along with potential solutions and future research directions.  This work is the result of a previous literature review on FedLearn and IoT vehicles, with the original work published in IET CYBER at 2023 and the extended version published in IEEE TCC at 2023.

V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose two-year observing period course has been studied using the 0.6-2.0 GeV range of the Fermi Gamma-Ray Space Telescope.  This study reveals that V392 Persei initially displayed unusual behavior in 2018, with its energy levels peaking at levels 10 to 30 times greater than typical nova eruptions.  After this peak, the object's energy gradually decreased until it reached a level comparable with that of other novae.  Further research into this object was facilitated by optical observations from the AAVSO International Database, H-alpha spectroscopy from the Southern African Large Telescope, and X-ray data from the Chandra X-ray Observatory.  According to this data, V392 Persei's 2018 behavior can be attributed to a two-staged eruption, with its energy levels first increasing during the gamma-ray phase and then decreasing during the nebular phase.  Additionally, analysis of this object's pre-eruptive and post-eruptive phases revealed that it was in a state of reduced activity compared to other dwarf novae, with a possible disc configuration that may have contributed to its unique behavior.  Furthermore, this research provides insights into the possible mechanisms that powered this remarkable object's energy, with its pre-eruptive phase possibly being influenced by a super-soft X-ray source and a possible interaction between

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding method leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to create a compact codebook and reduces information exchange between base station and mobile terminal.

A type of nonequilibrium transport known as surface current has been given significant attention in recent years, particularly in two-dimensional systems where it was found to exhibit sturdy resistance-free behavior, even in the presence of disorder. In this study, we expand on surface current beyond two-dimensional realms by conducting an in-depth analysis of the nonequilibrium transport properties in three-dimensional Hofstadter models. We perform numerical computations, combining discrete differential approximation and exact diagonalization methods, and discover that in the limit of strong magnetic fields, a robust resistance-free surface current emerges in Weyl and fcc lattice types, including in situations with tilts and in the presence of next-nearest-neighbor interactions. Notably, we find that a specific honeycomb Hofstadter model can mimic the behavior of a well-known one-dimensional model, demonstrating that surface current can be viewed as a three-dimensional version of the Kondo lattice model.

One of the key assumptions in general relativity is that an isolated, rotating, and expanding object must inevitably collapse due to its own gravitational force. This concept has been challenged by the stability of rotating, expanding objects in Einstein's theory of relativity, specifically where the energy-momentum tensor satisfies a specific causality condition. In (2) it was demonstrated that a Lorentzian energy-momentum tensor leads to the enforcement of the geodesic equation in relativistic hydrodynamics, resulting in the autonomy of fluid particles in a expanding and rotating scenario. 

By applying a Lorentzian energy-momentum tensor, we investigate the stability of rotating and expanding objects in a vacuum surrounding, using the method of (2) in conjunction with an approximate solution for the hydrodynamics of an isolated and rotating object in general relativity. We find that this type of object can only survive if its rate of expansion does not exceed a certain limit, defined as (1 - 1/√3) times the speed of light, or if it is not too massive or if it does not have significant angular momentum. 

We also investigate the effects of a surrounding Bondi fluid on the stability of an isolated and expanding object. We find that if the rate of mass loss of this surrounding fluid does not exceed (1/4)(1 - 1/√3) times the rate of expansion, it will not affect the autonomy of fluid particles in the expanding object.

We analyzed the formation of nuclear star clusters at the hearts of giant galaxies and concluded that the central mass concentrations should contain remnants from the first stars formed in the universe. These remnants, comprising either neutron stars or black holes made from the collapsed cores of the earliest stars, would likely be found in close proximity to each other, leading to the formation of pulsars and their associated globular-like clusters with small radii. 

Noticing that these clusters with small radii are missing from the Milky Way's cluster inventory, we searched for them by applying a new algorithm to the Kuijken parametrization of the luminosity functions of the galaxy's globular clusters. 

Following this identification process, we located 13 such clusters with radii less than 3.5pc, and calculated the merger rates of pulsar binaries that formed within these clusters. 

Preliminary estimates suggest that the detection sensitivity of LIGO I and Virgo, particularly LIGO I, should be sufficient to detect the signals from these binaries. 

Further investigation is necessary to refine the merger rate calculations and determine the contribution of these clusters to the overall population of pulsar binaries detectable by LIGO I and Virgo.

In this work, we investigate the security enhancements of a wireless system that uses dual hop OFDM technology, specifically with an AF relay node, to form an end-to-end communication path. To optimize the performance, we need to determine the optimal values for two key parameters: the power transmitted by the relay node and the power received by the destination node. To this end, we established an equation that expresses the eavesdropper's received signal power in terms of the transmitted signal power, taking into account the characteristics of the fading channels. To maximize the difference in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) between the intended recipients and the eavesdropper, we proposed an algorithm that employs a binary search to find the optimal power transmission power at the relay node for given fading channel conditions. To further improve the system's security, we investigated ways to manipulate the SNR of the eavesdropper's received signal by adjusting the delay and Doppler spread of the wireless channel. To this end, we formulated an equation that expresses the SNR of the eavesdropper in terms of the delay and Doppler spread, and demonstrated that increasing the delay spread and decreasing the Doppler spread can both enhance the system's security. To maximize the difference in SNR between the intended recipients and the eavesdropper, we proposed an algorithm that employs an iterative method to find the optimal delay and Doppler spread for a given scenario. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, which seriously hampers the testing of sophisticated virtual agents.
A novel framework, TextWorldExpress, is presented here, capable of simulating two popular text-based games at an incredible rate of one million actions per second, which can be achieved using a single high-end GPU.
TextWorldExpress also includes a range of tools to help researchers quickly transition their current setups to the new framework, with minimal modifications required.

Deep learning models, specifically long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, have achieved high accuracy in video identification tasks but are limited by their computational cost and memory requirements. To address this challenge, a novel LSTM architecture and a corresponding custom hardware design are proposed to increase energy efficiency while maintaining high identification recognition rates. The new LSTM design features a compact structure with fewer parameters and includes a hierarchical Tucker tensor decomposition of the weight matrices. To further enhance performance, a custom hardware platform is designed, incorporating multiple novel features such as: (1) a hierarchical memory access scheme, (2) a tensor decomposition-based computation method, (3) a novel fusion technique for skip connections, and (4) a custom LSTM core with improved performance. The proposed LSTM architecture was verified to achieve a 6-fold decrease in energy consumption and a 4-fold decrease in memory requirements compared to a generic LSTM implementation, with an accompanying increase in accuracy of 2.5% in video identification tasks when compared to a generic LSTM.

The convex hull criterion plays a significant role in identifying the ground state of a system in certain situations, particularly when applied to holographic conformal field theories. It ensures that the closest point to the ground state, using the Hamltonian as a distance metric, is part of the original convex hull of ground state operators. If the system is in a state of thermodynamic equilibrium, this condition is met. It remains unclear whether this condition is a fundamental requirement or a consequence of a specific setup. However, studies have shown that even when ground state operators are not in a state of thermodynamic equilibrium, the condition still holds, indicating it might be a fundamental property. Notably, an examination of a specific scenario, involving a system at finite temperature in an AdS-Schwarzschild black hole background, shows that even when the system is not in a state of thermodynamic equilibrium, the condition is met, although it is not a necessary requirement as it can be satisfied in other ways.

Given a Noetherian local ring (R, m) and an (R,m)-module of finite length, we define the tight Hilbert function as the difference between the Hilbert function of R/m and the Hilbert function of R/m applied to F-invariant subsets of R. Our primary goal is to examine the relationship between this function and R's F-regular properties, specifically by demonstrating its connection to the volume of R and establishing that it achieves a specific value in relation to the dimension of R when R is equidimensional and F-regular.

An important aspect of auxiliary services such as electricity demand response and supply response is the ability to quickly respond to changes in supply and demand. However, research has shown that some firms may overstate their capabilities in order to gain preferential treatment in procurement processes. This behavior causes issues because of the high costs associated with training and the risk of penalties for failing to meet expectations. This paper proposes a model to accurately estimate the number of auxiliary services that can be effectively deployed by different types of firms, taking into account their behavior and the associated costs. It also examines the impact of auxiliary services on the dynamics of power generation and consumption, and provides policy recommendations to improve the design of procurement processes. Key findings suggest that only partially truthful firms are likely to participate in auxiliary services, and that the number of auxiliary services that can be deployed is influenced by the cost of lying as well as the probability of penalties for failing to meet expectations. It is also shown that the cost of lying is the most significant factor in determining the number of auxiliary services that can be deployed, and that increasing this cost can lead to an overall decrease in the number of auxiliary services deployed, although it may also increase the risk of insufficient response in the event of an emergency. It is recommended to design procurement processes in a way that accurately reflects the costs associated with training and the risk of penalties for failing to meet expectations, and to consider implementing policies that encourage the development of auxiliary services and punish firms for overstateing their capabilities. We examine a specific type of complex polynomial mappings, those that leave prime numbers unchanged under repeated application, to better understand their properties and behavior. We establish guidelines to distinguish such polynomials and investigate the relationship between these guidelines and the presence of specific polynomial factors. Additionally, we explore the implications for these polynomials resulting from prime number-related constraints and analyze their invariant properties under composition.

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm waves in both hemispheres. The formation of summertime polar vortices is a crucial aspect of Saturn's atmospheric behavior but has been observed only in Earth's southern hemisphere. Our study uses the Mars Express OMEGA instrument and the NASA's Cassini CIRS to analyze the distribution of a specific atmospheric constituent, methane, and temperature in Saturn's northern stratosphere during the summer solstice. The vortices in Saturn's northern hemisphere have a weaker signal of methane and a specific temperature pattern that can be used to identify them. The vortices in Saturn's northern hemisphere form in the summer, and the temperature pattern varies with longitude, indicating that the entire hemisphere is affected by the vortices' formation. The emergence of the northern hemisphere's summertime polar vortices is associated with large warm waves that form a hexagon-shaped pattern and are caused by the planetary wave's instability, leading to the formation of the vortices through the interaction of the stratospheric and atmospheric waves.

This work investigates solutions to the focusing nonlinear Schrödinger equation outside a convex boundary, specifically where the solution's energy exceeds a certain threshold. It is observed that any solution with energy near this threshold will eventually become arbitrarily large in both the time and space domains within the confines of the convex boundary. It is also shown that solutions with energy below this threshold will either dissipate over time or become confined to a smaller area within the boundary. It is worth noting that research on this topic is ongoing, and the cases involving a boundary with sharp corners or the Schrödinger equation written in a different form have not been fully explored.

We provide a novel proof that local characteristic-zero, semi-parametric embeddings for a polynomial variety defined over the integers have an equivalent form to local positive-characteristic reductions of the variety for nearly all prime numbers.

We create a linearization functor for full linearization along a given section, applying it to graded bundles of a specific type. We establish that every graded bundle can be obtained by a successive process of linearization along a section. We also investigate the order of differentiation required to return to the initial setup from a given bundle, defining it as the minimum number of linearizations needed. We then examine the properties and invariants of this order, demonstrating its connection to the Euler characteristic of the underlying manifold and providing a lower bound for its value.

This informal note begins by illustrating some technical concepts, which include the re-normalization of orbital integrals from algebraic geometry and the application of certain technical properties related to compact groups. These properties were initially established by C. Mozo as a direct corollary of the results found in A. Connes', M. Shulman's, and E. H. Wigner's work. We also discuss some specific examples and related proofs.

The dynamics of atomic and molecular bonds within nuclei can be examined by studying the scattering of high-energy electrons off nuclei, a process known as electron-nucleus scattering. Although this research was initially theoretical, it has become possible with the advancement of high-intensity, monochromatic electron and heavy ion sources, as well as advanced detectors. The study proposes an alternative method to achieve this research goal, utilizing high-intensity, coherent x-ray pulses to scatter off nuclei and measuring the change in atomic and molecular bond lengths, which can be extracted from the scattering pattern. A proposed experiment at the x-ray free electron laser Amplitude and Contrast Source, using a 13C molecule as an example, is presented and the potential for retrieving molecular stage information from the scattering data is demonstrated through a simulation of the experiment using a complex nuclear wave function.

We have developed a novel mixed finite element method to model single-phase Darcy flow within a highly heterogeneous porous medium that includes fractures. This approach enables the use of a broad range of effective permeability values to represent the variable porosity, even when the porosity is discontinuous, without the need for the usual assumption of its continuity, thus accurately capturing the behavior of fractures. A key innovation of this method is the introduction of a new type of polynomial space, specifically amitratic space, which allows for the representation of data with varying levels of smoothness, thus facilitating the efficient numerical solution of this type of problem. We have developed and proven the convergence of a hybrid-primal mixed finite element method that uses the a priori choice of a broad range of effective permeability values, as well as a more challenging test case solved using a two-way a posteriori error estimation to steer the use of varying effective permeability values. Our numerical results demonstrate the accuracy and flexibility of this method, showcasing its ability to handle a wide range of fracture conductivities, including those with non-smooth effective permeability values, as well as its capacity to accurately model the behavior of complex flow problems by controlling the approximation of the pressure gradient.

When employing Bayes factors to distinguish between hypotheses, their stability is crucial as it can be heavily influenced by the specifics of the calculation method. We examined the impact of three key factors on Bayes factor estimates: Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) estimation, normalisation, and model selection. Our study utilized the popular affine-conjugate MCMC algorithm and found that the length of the burn-in period, the number of posterior samples, and the method of calculating the second-level normalisation have a significant impact on Bayes factor estimates. Furthermore, we found that the average of the logged Bayes factors yields more accurate results than the logged average of the Bayes factors. Our analysis was applied to the well-known Navratilova and Sederberg (2017) letter classification data, using a model that includes both holistic and analytic processing components.

In our analysis of Twitter posts containing "by contrast" and similar comparative
expressions, we identified various semantic patterns, including both contrastive
and non-contrastive uses. Our study shows that many previous assumptions
about the inherent oppositional nature of these expressions are inaccurate.
Rather, their meaning is influenced by the context in which they are employed.
We have constructed a rule-based system to automate the examination of the
semantic implications of discourse markers, including those that indicate
contrast, and have utilized this tool to investigate the diverse meanings ascribed
to "by contrast" and comparable expressions, including its potential contrastive
and noncontrastive interpretations, across different genres of text, and
within the specific context of Twitter posts. Our research in this regard has
been applied to Twitter data, where we have analyzed the expressed intentions
behind the use of these expressions, and have made the tool, known as DiscSense
available to the public for further study and extension.

We conduct a comprehensive landscape analysis of a particular matrix optimization problem under a generator that produces specific rank matrices, utilizing a geodesic convexity concept. By creating a framework based on convex subsets along geodesic lines, we establish the existence of a unique optimal solution at which the objective function has its minimum value, achieving this result with a focus on the Riemannian perspective. A subsequent theorem reveals that a specific class of matrix optimization problems, which include matrix mean shift and matrix regression, can be treated as optimizing a function over the generated matrices that result in a geodesic convex set when the loss function is quadratic. A dimensionality reduction approach and a local gradient descent algorithm are also presented as methods for handling large-scale matrix optimization problems. Our findings are validated through simulations and real-world applications, covering matrix regression, matrix mean shift, and a decomposition problem known as CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP).

A graph is considered bipartite if it can be divided into two distinct groups with no connections within each group, and it's classified as cubic when each of its vertices has exactly three connections. A coloring of a graph is defined by designating a specific number of shades for its vertices and applying an edge-coloring algorithm based on Gruyter's principles, resulting in an edge-coloring when each connection between two vertices uses a different shade than the connection between the two vertices it connects. It has been previously suggested that a bipartite cubic graph requires a minimum of six shades in an edge-coloring, but our research reveals that a bipartite cubic graph called the Lucas cubic graph requires only five shades in an edge-coloring, thus disproving the earlier statement.

We employed coevolutionary genetic algorithms in a range of Cournot models to replicate players' learning and adaptation in a dynamic environment, as well as the emergence of Nash equilibria through coevolutionary processes. Through simulations, we clarified how production strategies evolve and converge to a stable state of Nash equilibrium. We also investigated the impact of various parameters on the speed of convergence and the accuracy of learning in a range of scenarios, including a significant decrease in convergence time when using paired comparison as a selection method, as well as an examination of how production convergence is affected by noise levels in a range of situations. Furthermore, we compared the effectiveness of GAGA and genetic algorithms in a range of scenarios, including an instance where GAGA failed to reach a Nash equilibrium while the genetic algorithm succeeded. In addition to these results, we explored the emergence of Nash equilibria in an environment with an exogenously changing supply curve and production convergence in an incomplete information Cournot model, providing initial evidence for the presence of multiple Nash equilibria and partially opportunistic behavior.

Consider a weighted directed graph, denoted as $\mathcal{D}$, and the edge ideal associated with it, labeled as $I(\mathcal{D})$. A result shows that the symbolic and typical power lengths of $I(\mathcal{D})$ coincide, with a value equal to the number of oriented cycles in $\mathcal{D}$. This finding extends a previous consequence related to path directed graphs.

Deep learning models like convolutional neural networks (CNNs) can withstand minor errors that occur during training, and these models are also resistant to certain types of hardware faults, such as stuck or faulty memory. To further enhance CNNs' resilience, we've developed a method called activation range supervision (ARS) that helps reduce the impact of stuck faults. ARS works by limiting the output range of each layer to a specific range that's in line with the expected input to the next layer, based on training data. Using a CNN that's trained for image classification, we found that ARS can reduce the effect of stuck faults by up to 3 orders of magnitude. To demonstrate CNNs' resistance to faults in actual hardware, we conducted experiments using memory with stuck faults, simulated on an application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) and a field-programmable gate array (FPGA). To further validate our results, we compared our approach with another method called approximate neural networks (ANNs). To analyze the spatial distribution of faults in real hardware, we performed a scan of a CNN implemented on an FPGA and an ASIC, and an evaluation of our approach's potential for hardware designs. To make ARS feasible for large-scale CNNs, we developed a method to efficiently compute the output range of each layer, based on a simple yet accurate approximation, and demonstrated the effectiveness of this method with a CNN that's trained for natural language processing. Building upon the foundation of the Bagger-Capeletti-Siegelbacov-Witten superconformal field theory, a one-parameter family of Jordanian twists was introduced in [1, 2]. Here we demonstrate that this  one-parameter family of Jordanian twists constitutes a part of a more comprehensive set of twists that can be obtained through the application of a parent Jordanian twist to the Yangian algebra, for the specific case of gl(K). This identification reveals that the one-parameter family of Jordanian twists is, in fact, equivalent to a particular ordering of the U$_{\mathfrak{s}}$(sln(K)) algebra, where $\mathfrak{s}$ denotes a shift in the index, ultimately leading to the reconstruction of the one-parameter family of Jordanian twists in the U$_{\mathfrak{s}}$(sln(K)) limit as the U$_{\mathfrak{s}}$(sln(K)) algebra approaches the Yangian algebras for the case of gl(K).

Recently, there has been a growing interest in modeling cross-lingual semantic spaces. Researchers have been successful in achieving this goal at the individual word level, but it remains a challenge to identify the common semantic area that underlies multiple languages. This challenge can be addressed by clustering words within a single language to define intra-lingual semantics and then mapping these clusters across languages to define the inter-lingual semantics. In this work, a novel method is presented to construct the inter-lingual semantics by first training a cluster-consistent multilingual word embedding without parameter sharing, which ensures that words with the same semantic label have the same embedding across languages. This embedding serves as a proxy to identify the common semantic area that underlies multiple languages and can be further analyzed to gain insights into the structure of the inter-lingual semantics. To support our method, an additional task is designed to predict the semantic label of individual words within this model, which enables the inter-lingual semantics to be decoded and compared to existing approaches using three different evaluation metrics.

Xe-Xe collisions at the high energy of 5.44 TeV provide a rich data set for studying rare processes and hard-to-detect particles, such as $K^0_s$, $\Lambda$, $\bar{\Lambda}$, and $\phi$, especially in the forward region where the ALICE detector has unique capabilities. The production of these particles in different rapidity regions can be examined to identify local charge asymmetry and c\bar{c} pair production, as well as to study rare $\phi$ meson production and $\Lambda$ and $\bar{\Lambda}$ hyperon production in high-energy collisions. The research focuses on determining the charge asymmetry, polar angle distributions, and mid-rapidity densities of these particles in Xe-Xe collisions. The results show that the production of $K^0_s$, $\Lambda$, $\bar{\Lambda}$, and $\phi$ mesons is found to be proportional to the number of participating nucleons and collision centrality, with charges asymmetries of 0.1-0.3 and rare $\phi$/p\bar{p} ratios of 0.15-0.25, respectively. The findings are comparable to those obtained in LHC Pb-Pb collisions and are expected to be similar to those in future LHC p-Pb collisions with the LHCb detector, with the potential for detecting rare processes like $\Lambda \to p \gamma$ and $\phi \to e^

In late October 2019, violent demonstrations and societal unrest gripped Chile, leading to widespread loss of life and property.  A team of researchers from Chile and the United States developed a mathematical model to represent the spread of protest-related mortality rates across the country's 346 communes.  This paper presents an alternative formulation of the earlier model, with the added feature of a non-local term in the equations.  Numerical solutions to the modified model can provide insights into the patterns of communal mortality rates and the role of the non-local term in the context of the 2019 Chilean protests.

This research focuses on resolving a specific type of regular expression constraint that is more advanced than standard regular expression constraints, yet has been poorly addressed in existing literature. We have developed a new approach to solve over finite wordsets using regular expression constraints with the following additional features: the ability to express both the existence and non-existence of a substring, which we have found to be equivalent to the problem of negative patterns over finite words. We have also established the relationship between regular expression constraints and negative patterns, showing they are interchangeable, and have established the complexity of constraints, as well as the relationship between constraints and patterns, which can be used to solve problems related to negative patterns.

Accurate positioning in various applications such as robotics, surveillance video analysis, and augmented reality is crucial. In outdoor environments with multiple mapping options like GPS with varying accuracy and Inertial Measurement Units with drift issues, a reliable and robust localization technique is essential. Our proposed method, EMA-VIO, leverages a visual-inertial odometry with an external memory attention mechanism to achieve efficient and accurate localization. To account for the external memory's computational cost, we implemented a dynamic updating mechanism to limit the memory's modification to only the relevant frames. By minimizing the movement estimation between frames with an attention-based mechanism, we significantly reduced the number of required measurements on the external memory by an order of ten. Our results show that EMA-VIO achieves a 95th percentile error of 3.79 meters in a public VIO dataset and 2.01 meters in a custom dataset, outperforming the current state-of-the-art methods by at least one meter.

A novel concept, quadratic Berry curvature, has been intensely studied and its applications explored, however the potential of a more advanced phenomenon, cubic Berry curvature, remains unmined. This study delves into the properties of a novel class of materials, which it terms "square-root Weyl materials", by taking a theoretical approach to combine multiple Weyl points into a single entity. Using theoretical modeling, we discovered a specific solid-state realization where a particular lattice structure based on a kagome band forms a "Weyl semimetal" when a certain parameter is altered, resulting in a topological phase transition from a three-dimensional Weyl semimetal to a chiral bulk phase. Moreover, this study demonstrates that both the "square-root Weyl points" and "octapoint" node can be created in a two-dimensional material, referred to as square-root Weyl material, whose unique properties can be managed through an external electric field.

This paper proposes a numerical scheme to solve the electrical impedance tomography's inverse problem, which is to recover impedance data from partial Cauchy data of the Maxwell's equations, using the quasi-reversibility method. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the inverse problem can be achieved under the assumption that the recovered data belongs to a specific Holder class. A quasi-reversibility numerical model is established and the convergence of its solution to the desired data is proven, along with an error estimate. This estimate shows the solution's smoothness is linked to the mesh size, which affects the accuracy of the recovered data. A finite element discretization of the quasi-reversibility problem is then presented and the convergence of the algorithm is numerically demonstrated for various examples.

In the context of multiple agents or systems that gather and analyze data, knowing which, why, and how to combine their individual knowledge bases is crucial. A key challenge in knowledge amalgamation is selecting and incorporating relevant information from other agents, which can be difficult when there are many possible sources and only some contain valuable information, making the process inefficient. To address this, we present a novel approach, called Federated Selective Collection (FSC), which identifies the most useful information from other agents and incorporates it into the current knowledge base while considering limitations such as communication costs and security constraints. We demonstrate the effectiveness of FSC by comparing it to existing methods in several scenarios, including those with biased or incomplete data, and show that FSC outperforms these methods in terms of the accuracy of combined knowledge.

We analyze the Mordell-Weil rank of elliptic curves in quartic extensions of rational numbers, focusing on those defined by irreducible polynomials with distinct roots over the rational numbers and without repeated roots. We investigate two specific cases where the quartic polynomial has the form $y^2 - x(x^2 + ax + b)$, with $a$ and $b$ being elements of the symmetric groups $S_4$ or $A_4$, and determine the possible rank increments of elliptic curves in these extensions.

A recently proposed inequality called the quantum null energy complexity (QNEC) indicates that the derivative of the logarithm of the von Neumann entropy in a specific direction is bounded by a constant, which can be used to examine the entropy changes in various quantum systems. This study investigates two distinct types of holographic models, including a holographic version of the Ising model and a specific two-dimensional topological field theory, to demonstrate how the QNEC can be utilized to determine key thermodynamic characteristics, including the adiabatic work, heat transfer, change in the internal energy, and the change in the entropy itself as well as other indicators, such as the Fisher information, within a specific time frame. Notably, we establish that the QNEC can be expressed in terms of the thermodynamic forces and the cosine of the angle between the direction of entropy change and the null energy condition direction. Moreover, we find that the quantity representing the excess over the equipartition of the entropy in relation to the temperature, known as the bound entropoy, plays a crucial role in this analysis. The QNEC is also shown to be invariant under a specific transformation known as the "surge transformation." The paper at hand is the third in a series of articles on this topic, for which we refer the reader to the original publications.

To measure the speed at which a quantum state changes, the duration it takes for two distinguishable states to become indistinguishable serves as a significant indicator.
This distinguishability time can be calculated using a variety of methods, including the worst-case scenario in which it takes the minimum time to move between two points on a sphere or, more specifically, within the parameters of a Bloch ball.
In this study, we establish a minimum time requirement to transition from an initial state to an unrecognizable state compared to a target state, defined as changing beyond a threshold of which can be detected with a certain accuracy, defined as δ.
We also examine the instances in which this time reaches its maximum possible value, achieving this record by constraining the direction in which the change occurs.
In addition, we establish that the rate at which the distance between the two states changes must be greater than a certain threshold, which can be seen as a quantum analogue of a classical principle known as the Reimann-Hartogs theorem.
Furthermore, we analyze the instances in which this rate is achieved, which includes the cases in which the state evolves in response to a variable temperature or, more specifically, a state that is non-thermally excited or, in a more general sense, any state that deviates from a state of maximum entropy.
In the process, we establish a lower bound for the rate at which the distance between the two states changes, which can be seen as a quantum analogue of a principle known

Let $X$ and $Y$ be two complex normed spaces, assuming that $X$ is continuously and densely embedded in $Y$. We establish an important inequality showing that the norm of a projector of type $\big[\cdot, C_{Y^{*}}\big]$ from $X$ to $Y$ is equivalent to a norm that takes into account the norms of functions in $X^{*}$ and the norm of the inverse of the embedding from $Y$ to $X$.

Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing and have varying levels of integration that rely on local functionality. To advance these technologies, it's essential to have a thorough understanding of defects within integrated elements. This knowledge can be gained through the analysis of defects' influence on quantum behavior using terahertz range frequencies, specifically in the realm of Josephson junctions. A study employing terahertz near-field nanoscopy and electromagnetic simulations has discovered that defects within integrated elements are often caused by frayed edges of microbridges, a previously unreported finding. Furthermore, research revealed that edge-based microbridges can be made more efficient by creating a "grain boundary" effect, which can be achieved by precisely defining the geometry of the edges, and this effect can be detected through S-parameter analysis, even at very low powers.

An atmosphere evolution model for Venus has been refined to better align with results from meteoritic and planetary differentiation models and with theoretical models of core-mantle interactions, solvation of sulfur in the core, and atmospheric chemistry. By exploring various processes including core-solid Earth interactions, atmospheric photochemistry, and the solvation of sulfur in the core, this study reveals the trajectory of Venus's atmospheric evolution over its 4.5 billion-year history. The model indicates that Venus experienced a prolonged hothouse phase during the early stages of its existence, with surface temperatures exceeding 300°C. As volcanic activity decreased, a positive feedback loop emerged in which the reduction of volcanic gas emissions led to core cooling, resulting in the increased solvation of sulfur in the core and a return to a hotter and more humid climate. This cycle repeated itself over billions of years, with the atmosphere undergoing successive cycles of runaway greenhouse effects fueled by the release of carbon and water trapped in the mantle and core. The model also accounts for the effects of impacts, core-mantle interactions, and the solvation of sulfur in the core on the atmosphere's composition and temperature, and suggests that a massive impact that occurred approximately 500 million years ago had a significant impact on the atmosphere, leading to the current observed conditions.

Point processes that take into account multiple types of events, such as natural disasters, online messages, or neuronal activity, are used extensively in various fields to analyze events of different categories. A key task with event data of this nature is to identify relevant relationships between events of the same or different types. Nonlinear Hawkes processes are widely used to model such connections, with their conditional intensities defined by past occurrences of related events. However, estimating these connections or nodes' parameters and analyzing events of the same type that have no known connection can be challenging. We developed a Bayesian method to estimate the parameters of a nonlinear Hawkes process and introduced a new diagnostic tool to investigate connections between events of the same type without prior knowledge. We applied this technique to synthetic data, showing it accurately estimated the original parameters and identified connections between events of the same type, as well as online message graphs extracted from Twitter during the 2019-2020 Greta Thunberg climate protests. We found that certain nodes with no apparent connections to others were linked to hidden events, and we were able to recover these latent components.

In intensely focused laser beams, polarization becomes significantly altered through interactions with plasmas, and can ultimately switch to a higher intensity, a phenomenon that can reach intensities comparable to those achieved by the laser itself. The intensity of a Gaussian laser beam measures as over 10 to the power of 22 watts per square meter. A new theoretical model, accounting for the effects of electron deflection due to the beating of laser light with a background magnetic field, along with rescattering of electrons with high energy levels, is presented. This model is applied to model interactions between laser beams of various intensities and interactions between laser beams and partially ionized plasmas, and is capable of explaining and predicting the phenomena of polarization alteration and amplification of laser beams. The model also provides guidance on the parameters necessary to achieve this effect in laboratory settings, including the use of a specific type of plasma, known as a two-electron gas. The model is further validated through comparison with existing experimental data and results of previous models, and is applied to model interactions between laser beams of extremely high intensities, in excess of 10 to the power of 22 watts per square meter, and interactions between laser beams and partially ionized plasmas, and is capable of predicting the phenomena of polarization alteration and amplification of laser beams in these settings. The model also provides guidance on the parameters necessary to achieve this effect in laboratory settings, including the use of a specific type of plasma, known as a two-electron

Revisiting the earlier calculation, the corrected value of the tau lepton's electric dipole moment is found to be in the range of (0.66 to 0.75) x 10^-21 cm, under the standard model with a heavy tau as a lepton. When including the effects of threshold corrections and taking into account the contributions from the heavy top and Higgs bosons, the estimated range narrows to (0.67 to 0.75) x 10^-21 cm.

A code is considered to be based on the rank metric, using a particular generating matrix, if it is possible to accurately decode it, given that the transmitted word has a Hamming distance of at least $d_h$ from the code's zero word and a rank distance of at least $d_r$ from any linear combination of the code's information words, with the condition that the information words are part of a given set of full-rank matrices. It has been proven that codes of this type, with a large enough distance of at least $d_r$, can resist errors of a certain type that occur during transmission, specifically type-$\Gamma_2$ rank metric errors, which occur when the transmitted word results from the transmitted symbol and two of the code's information words, as well as being resistant to the Bussgang criterion. In such cases, with a certain code size, it has been found that the Bussgang criterion can be met at a lower signal-to-noise ratio than with conventional codes, allowing for a gain of up to 10 dB, or even better, with the exact gain depending on the code's specific size and the type of channel it is on. It has been discovered that with codes of this type, specifically those that are Gaussian and symmetric, it is possible to determine the signal-to-noise ratio that must be met in order to maintain a certain error decoding rate, using the code's distance and error type, along with a particular measure of the

In CFT$_2$, a specific type of conformal primary field was found to be associated with a particular kind of OPE block that cannot be generated using the standard conformal bootstrap method. 
In a previous study, it was demonstrated that a particular type of spinning twist field could be incorporated into the conformal bootstrap framework by employing a complex shift in the conformal Cassimir operators' spectrum.
This resulted in the emergence of spinning twist CFT operators in an AdS$_3$ spacetime.
The twist field's spin and the cosmological constant are shown to have a linear relationship in AdS$_3$, which was not observed in higher-dimensional AdS spaces.
The relation between the spinning twist CFT operators and the Kirchhoff operator that arises in the Lorentzian OPE block is also clarified.
The incorporation of complex shifts in the AdS$_3$ context is shown to be equivalent to an alternative approach that involves employing a Lorentzian OPE block directly.
The employed method is shown to be consistent with the AdS$_3$/CFT$_2$ duality by means of an explicit calculation in a free boson compactified on a torus.
The employed method is shown to be capable of reproducing the central charge of the CFT$_2$ in an exact manner.
The employed method is also shown to be in agreement with the results obtained using the TBA method.
The employed method is shown to be associated with the Virasoro characters

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a combinatorial framework to calculate Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds using a set of rules they defined. We demonstrate that their rules can be interpreted through the lens of differential forms and de Rham cohomology, thereby providing a natural explanation for their original algorithm. We also offer an alternative derivation of their rule for calculating the Pontrjagin class of a manifold with a symmetric bilinear form, and show that every symmetric bilinear form can be represented as the sum of a positive definite form and a form with a specific characteristic matrix structure. Notably, we can calculate the Pontrjagin class of such a manifold using just the Euler class and the Todd class of a specific vector bundle.

We investigated the photometric and spectroscopic characteristics of the SN II 2020jfo using a combination of data from various sources, including the ATLAS, PASTEL, TASTE, VPHOS, VLT, and WHT instruments, and analyzed its properties in the context of relevant empirical and theoretical evidence, ultimately providing a reliable explosion energy estimate for this SN II and shedding light on its underlying physical mechanisms.

The detection of transient X-ray events in wide fields necessitates the use of large-format semikilovette (lobster-eye) optics to focus X-ray beams onto CCD chips. We propose a method for real-time signal processing that analyzes temporary variations in CCD readings along the semi-kilovette pattern. This approach allows for the rapid identification of transient events and associated coordinates. We discuss the implementation of this strategy in the context of the Wide Field Monitoring Telescope, an instrument designed for wide-field X-ray observations with a large-format CCD chip.

We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity, a concept introduced by Dafermos and Melting, which leads to multiple conservation laws and a role in understanding the stability of discontinuous solutions in a broader context.

A recent study used a deep learning model to analyze the influence of cosmic velocity dispersion on the formation of dark matter halos by "looking" at initial conditions, specifically cosmic waves, and assigning a score to the effect of velocity dispersion on halo mass. The model's predictions were compared to theoretical simulations, showing it accurately captures the relationship between velocity dispersion and halo mass, with a standard deviation of about 12%. The results also revealed that the score represents a complex, non-linear relationship that can be broken down into several simpler relationships, including a correlation between the rms of initial density fluctuations and velocity dispersion, and another between the rms of cosmic velocity field and velocity dispersion. The study demonstrated that the score can be reconstructed from these relationships, providing a non-linear, self-consistent explanation for the influence of velocity dispersion on halo mass. The analysis was initially performed using a specific simulation, but the model's findings were shown to be applicable to a broader range of simulations with different parameters, offering a general and transferable understanding of the role of velocity dispersion on halo mass.

We have revised the method for calculating the equilibrium configurations of rotating stars in general relativity, incorporating the inertia tensor into the mass-shed limit surface equation to accurately determine the angular velocity at mass shedding. We have implemented this new approach in a numerical scheme, using the Constrained HyperSurface method as a foundation. By applying the new formulation, we have calculated the mass-shed limit surface equation in the $\dot{M}$-$a_{\rm lim}$ plane for rotating neutron stars with different compositions, and our results agree with previous studies based on the Cowderoy criterion. We have also investigated the effects of various parameters on the mass-shed limit surface equation, including the density distribution, angular velocity, magnetic field, and accretion rate. Furthermore, we have compared our results with those obtained using the $\Omega_{\rm lim}$-model, and have developed an analytical fit for the mass-shed limit surface equation in the $\dot{M}$-$a_{\rm lim}$ plane, which can be used to study the evolution of rotating stars in X-ray binaries.

Documents such as invoices, medical records, and resumes contain diverse layouts and require extraction of specific information including names, quantities, and monetary amounts. Due to the time-consuming and intricate nature of these documents, manual label creation is extremely challenging, if not impossible, making automated annotation techniques crucial. We present a novel method for generating diverse label sets for complex documents by applying a combination of human intelligence tasks, Reinforcement Learning, and Generative Adversarial Networks, without the need for pre-trained models. We conduct experiments on four public datasets and the results show our approach to be highly effective in reducing annotation costs, outperforming other comparison methods by a significant margin. The annotation cost was found to be as low as $0.0005 per instance, with an accuracy of 95% on average, demonstrating the potential for substantial cost savings. The code for this project is available at the following link: https://github.com/ghrashad/Document-Extraction-Annotation.

The analysis of neutron star-black hole (NSBH) mergers with the help of gravitational waves relies heavily on the analysis of a large number of waveforms, which can be difficult to accomplish with traditional methods of model-based matching. In an attempt to overcome this challenge, the authors have developed a deep learning method that employs a convolutional neural network to identify the binary parameter of a waveform and has been tested on signals produced by the BNS and BBH mergers of the S20004729-0 sample from the third observing run of the LIGO and Virgo collaboration. The results showed that it is possible to recover the correct classification of a waveform with a high degree of confidence even when analyzing signals with a duration of 2 seconds and a signal-to-noise ratio of 8, and the developed network was found to recover the correct classification of a waveform with a high degree of confidence even when analyzing signals with a duration of 2 seconds and a signal-to-noise ratio of 8.
